Senses.Explanation: Yao and Shun, the paired sage-kings whom the Chan corpus uses as its classical measure of rule and then repeatedly puts under further questioning. In the Ancestral Guidelines Collection, Qinshan Puchu calls a ruler “a ruler like Yao and Shun,” calls the people those of Cheng and Kang, and immediately asks for the song of peace. Another recurrent line says, “The old farmer does not know the power of Yao and Shun; thump, thump, he beats the drum and sacrifices to the river god.” In the Five Lamps Complete Collection, an unnamed monk recites that inherited line and Nantang Qingyu answers, “Eyes seeing as if blind; mouth speaking as if mute.” Other texts explicitly limit the pair. Xichan Shoujing says even a ruler like Yao and Shun still has transforming activity, then contrasts this with what heaven and earth cannot contain and what Yao and Shun do not know by name. Juelang Daosheng says, “A true son of heaven does not rely on decrees from Yao and Shun,” while his lineage verse reverses the wording before a whisk opens the crown-eye. In the Touzi–Furong case, Touzi Yiqing asks whether the ruler's command relies on Yu, Tang, Yao, or Shun; as Furong Daokai prepares to answer, Touzi Yiqing strikes him with the whisk and assigns twenty blows. In the question-and-answer record of Wunian Shenyou, Wunian Shenyou answers why people today cannot accomplish what Yao and Shun did. The Zen deviation is the pair's use inside the interview: ideal rulers become lines to answer, measures explicitly exceeded, and names inside a command question enforced with the teaching-seat whisk.

Senses.Explanation: Worldly toil: literally, dust and toil, and concretely the wear, bustle, and entanglement of ordinary affairs and responsive thought. The compound occurs 1,353 times in 275 allowlisted texts. Yunmen Wenyan says worldly toil is unbroken; Zhenjing Kewen says its myriad affairs are empty; and Dahui Zonggao says there is no worldly toil to avoid. Yuanhu Miaoyong answers a complaint about the toil and commotion of the world by asking who is the worldly toil and who is the one rejecting it. Dufeng Benshan calls a quiet, easeful condition only a temporary rest from worldly toil and warns against recognizing it as final. Wuyi Yuanlai pairs dwelling in dust with leaving dust and speaks of leaving the world amid worldly toil. Yunwai Ze similarly says one may dwell in worldly toil without being invaded by it. The records therefore retain the ordinary burden while testing avoidance, temporary quiet, and non-invasion; they do not make the compound a hidden name for awakening.
Senses.Note: The frequent longer string 'worldly toil and vexation' occurs 36 times in 24 texts, but the entry preserves the headword's own concrete dust-and-labor wording. Formula searches found no stable bare self-definition; the apparent 'worldly toil is ...' strings mostly introduce a person located amid it.

Zen every mote and every land
Senses.Explanation: Across 205 occurrences in 116 allowlisted texts, Chan masters pair it with “each thing and each particular” (物物頭頭), say that every mote and land “fully displays” (全彰), and place it in public addresses as the range of an action or disclosure. One address says, “every mote and every land once manifested awe-inspiring light; each thing and each particular fully displayed the true eye” (塵塵剎剎，曾現威光。物物頭頭，全彰正眼). Another gives the compact parallel, “each thing and each particular—the whole body; every mote and every land—the great function” (物物頭頭全身，塵塵剎剎大用). The phrase is also made a test: “if you understand, every mote and every land; if you do not, a kick to the head” (若也會得，塵塵剎剎；若也不會，當頭一蹋). The corpus thus bends a cosmological distributive into recurring teaching-seat language for an all-pervading range; this entry makes no claim beyond those deployments.

Senses.Explanation: A face, statement, or position described this way rises sheer and precipitous like a wall a thousand fathoms high. The expression occurs 434 times in 113 allowlisted texts. Nanyuan Huiyong opens an address by saying that such a wall stands on the red flesh-lump. A reviewed unnamed monk repeats Nanyuan's line as a question, then overturns the Chan seat after Nanyuan confirms it. Dongshan Shouchu places sometimes mingling with mud and mixing with water beside sometimes standing sheer as a thousand-fathom wall, then says Dongshan is found in neither place. Yuanwu Keqin makes the contrast reciprocal: in the ash-covered and dirt-covered place, stand like the wall; in the wall-like place, be dirt-covered and ash-covered. Elsewhere Yuanwu joins the image to sitting cut off across the ten directions and the appearance of great function. Cuiyan Kezhen classifies three turning phrases as respectively standing like the wall, sailing a boat on dry land, and host and guest intermingling. Langya Huijue later raises Nanyuan's saying and appraises it as dangerous. Zen bends a visible cliff-like wall into a public saying and an appraisal of encounter positions; the stored contrasts remain the named speakers' contrasts rather than a universal equation.

Senses.Explanation: A wall so high and sheer that it gives no route over or through it. Chan records use that impossible-to-pass barrier as a stance, a predicate, and a place where a response is demanded. In Dahui Zonggao's section of the Complete Book of the Five Lamps, an unnamed monk asks why Dahui is always like such a wall; Dahui tells the recorded questioner to say a word at that very place. Yuanwu Keqin joins the wall to blocking off the ten directions, and elsewhere predicates the wall of every person without the slightest alteration or deficiency. The records also police the image: Yuanwu says people mistakenly identify silent blankness with the sheer wall, and Zhenjing Kewen says Dongshan is not to be found there. It therefore names an impassable encounter-setting, not mere silence and not a synonym for any named teacher.

Senses.Explanation: To degrade a free person into servitude is to impose a lower status on someone who was not bound to it; Chan speakers use the legal-social wrong as a charge of falsely diminishing what is already present. Foyan Qingyuan calls excessive explanation 'degrading the free into servitude.' Tianyin Yuanxiu puts the charge into a reply to an elder and also denies that saying everyone possesses the matter is such degradation. Feiyin Tongrong explicitly says equating a bound being with Shakyamuni is neither degrading the free nor calling the base noble, while Yunmen Wenyan makes 'do not degrade the free' a stock counter before a blow. Huayan Shengke turns the same charge against treating Shakyamuni as awake and the assembly as not. These cases bend a status offence into an interview accusation: the named master says the proposed distinction or explanation has needlessly lowered its subject.

Yuanwu places it after “a great dead man has already lost his breath” and says, “upon reaching one’s own ground, great rest and great cessation” (到本分地上大休大歇). Xueyan immediately refuses to make that field an endpoint: “if you wish to head directly for the field of great rest, great cessation, and great ease, there is a great living road ahead” (前頭大有活路在). A later master criticizes descendants who bite onto Linji’s four shouts and take that for the field of great rest and cessation, calling the identification “a sheep’s substance in a tiger’s hide” (羊質虎皮). The Chan deviation is therefore an explicitly named field of arrival that remains subject to public correction; the entry reports those predicates without defining an inner state.

SearchAliases: a person of great thorough awakening
Senses.Explanation: The phrase occurs 48 times in 30 allowlisted texts. It names an event or resulting qualification in biographies, appraisals, and questions. One record says that people of great thorough awakening have finished the matter of inquiry and afterward stayed by water and woods until pushed forward to address others (古人大徹大悟，參學事畢，且於水邊林下). A public exchange tests the qualification directly: Tianzhu says there is nobody of great thorough awakening in the hall; the record owner asks, "which one is not of great thorough awakening?" and the first counters, "which one is?" (那箇不是大徹大悟的；那箇是大徹大悟的). A Dahui record places it beside "the mind-ground opens and passes through" (大徹大悟，心地開通) and calls Zhaozhou's dog public case a key that opens that mind-ground. A later address jokes that its third phrase could make people greatly and thoroughly awaken, then refuses to utter it because nobody would remain to watch the Chan hall. These records attest the phrase as event, qualification, question, and comic hall claim; this entry adds no meaning beyond those recorded deployments.

Senses.Explanation: The phrase marks a decisive breakthrough or describes a person credited with one. Linji Yixuan is narrated as awakening greatly at Dayu's words. Emperor Zhuangzong asks why a greatly awakened person could nevertheless become deluded, and the answer denies reversal through the broken-mirror and fallen-flower images. Tang Shiji distinguishes reports of repeated great and small awakenings. Biographical passages narrate breakthroughs by Fayan Wenyi and Faxiu, while the Record of Pointing at the Moon applies the phrase to Shakyamuni's awakening under the morning star. A preface narrates Dingxu's sudden breakthrough under Dahui Zonggao's blows. Dahui also transmits the maxim that great doubt necessarily has great awakening beneath it. These uses establish magnitude and decisiveness while leaving later records free to test claims made about awakened persons.

Senses.Explanation: Chan records tell a practitioner to “die the great death” by letting prior discriminations and supports fall away, but they repeatedly complete the image with coming alive, turning around, and responding freely. In the Blue Cliff Record, Yuanwu Keqin compares the condition to a greatly dead person who comes alive: long and short, good and bad are made one, yet fitting response is not lost. His recorded sayings similarly say that prior views and explanations must be put in order like a greatly dead person who can rise alive, after which contention falls away. Zhongfeng Mingben urges a practitioner to die the great death once and suddenly bite through the tasteless saying. Guting Shanmi says true and false then pass together without obstruction. Langting Ting denies that either cleverness or dullness can accomplish it and pairs the great death with turning back alive. Hanyue Fazang requires conditioned dust to fall away before one turns, emerges, and breathes freely; Tianran Hanshi likewise says one dies greatly and returns alive before elaborate inherited arrangements look like minor affairs.

Senses.Explanation: Great function or great use. In one public interview an unnamed monk asks Changqing Da'an what it is like when great function manifests without preserving rules. Changqing answers, “if you can use it, then use it” (汝用得但用); the recorded questioner bares his shoulder and is struck. Another unnamed monk asks Shanhui separately, “what is great capacity?” and “what is great function?” and receives a blow across the back for each. The corpus coordinates “great capacity and great function” (大機大用, 325 occurrences) and “the whole capacity and great function” (全機大用, 128 occurrences). Yuanwu Keqin uses the first pairing in instruction to Deshan Jing and the second while describing meeting life with life and death with death. Guishan Lingyou supplies an explicit contrast: “you people have obtained only the great body, not great function” (汝等諸人只得大體不得大用). Yangshan Huiji identifies Baizhang Huaihai with great capacity and Huangbo Xiyun with great function. Xuansha Shibei asks Xuefeng Yicun what it is like when great function manifests, and Xuefeng rolls three balls together. These formulas, questions, bodily replies, pairings, and contrasts show a function publicly displayed and appraised in encounters; they do not establish a separate metaphysical object behind the term.

Senses.Explanation: Full capacity for action comes into view rather than remaining merely available or described. The expression occurs 447 times in 170 allowlisted texts and often continues with the statement that established rules are not retained. Dazhu Huihai directly equates the appearing of great function with the unequalled body of the teaching. A reviewed unnamed monk asks Changqing Da'an what happens when great function appears without retaining rules; Changqing answers, “If you can use it, just use it.” Fengxue Yanzhao tells the assembly that at the encounter great function must appear and that they must not constrain themselves to small details. Yunmen Wenyan states the stock line; a second reviewed unnamed monk immediately asks what the appearing of great function is, and Yunmen raises his staff and calls out that old man Shakyamuni has come. Yuanwu Keqin pairs the stock line with using a blade of grass as a sixteen-foot golden body and the golden body as a blade of grass. Dahui Zonggao reports that students of sayings apply the phrase to Guizong's killing a snake and Nanquan's killing a cat, then explicitly rejects that account. Zen makes a phrase about capacity becoming present into a public question, an assembly demand, and a case-commentary formula; the different answers and Dahui's rejection prevent any one action from becoming its hidden definition.

Senses.Explanation: Great doubt is an intensified mass of inquiry cultivated until its obstruction breaks open. The phrase occurs 196 times in 91 allowlisted texts. A direct definition says, ‘doubt has no large or small; only when the doubt is weighty is it called great doubt, and when light it is called small doubt’ (疑。情無大小，但疑之重，是謂大疑；疑之輕，是謂小疑). The same record says that when one cannot refrain from raising it, ‘therefore it is named great doubt.’ Across other texts it appears in the fixed contrast ‘great doubt, great awakening; small doubt, small awakening; no doubt, no awakening,’ in questions about ‘a person of great doubt,’ and in a biography that reports Xiuyun Wei ‘greatly doubted’ and investigated forcefully. Thus the corpus uses the phrase both as a named weight of doubt and verbally for becoming deeply doubtful; English ‘great doubt’ covers both without positing different referents.

Senses.Explanation: The great creature is the tiger. Konggu Daocheng gives the corpus's direct equation: “a long creature is a dragon; a great creature is a tiger” (長蟲是龍，大蟲是虎). Records then put that ordinary animal-name to work in public encounters and appraisals. Baizhang Huaihai asks Huangbo whether he saw the tiger; Huangbo makes a tiger sound, stops Baizhang's feigned axe blow, and slaps him. An unnamed questioner asks Tongfeng Anzhu what he would do on meeting a tiger; Tongfeng roars, the questioner acts frightened, and Tongfeng laughs. Rui'an Sengyin gives the recurrent answer “a tiger watches a water-mill” (大蟲看水磨) to a student's inference. Langting Jingting calls Deshan a drowsing tiger accustomed to biting without showing his teeth. Yushan Shangsi describes a singed-tail tiger crouching in the road and roaring. Yang Yi reports asking what happens when two tigers bite each other. Yangshan Huiji's comparison of Changsha Jingcen to a tiger supplies the latter's recorded epithet “Cen the Tiger” (岑大蟲). The Zen-specific bend is observable rather than secret: the ordinary tiger becomes an encounter role, an enacted roar, a recurrent answer, an appraisal of a named teacher, and an epithet.

Senses.Explanation: The headword (契悟) literally means "to tally and realize." In Chan transmission biographies it is an event verb marking a person's reported realization after a word, question, case, accident, or exchange. Huike is told "I have finished settling your mind for you" and then greatly realizes (光即大契悟). Daoquan hears "smoke rises beneath your feet" and realizes on the spot, after which he travels no farther (師當下契悟，更不他遊). Other records place it after hearing the cypress-tree case during an entering interview, and after a rider falls when his donkey's foot breaks through a bridge. The narrative can immediately report the person's next speech: after realizing, Huike runs to Bodhidharma and says that he has put external conditions to rest. The Chan deviation is institutional and documentary: lamp and sayings records use "to tally and realize" (契悟) to mark the realization event within a transmission biography and often preserve its trigger and aftermath. The word itself does not say that the realization "matches the identified master's mind," and this entry does not add that claim.

Senses.Explanation: Taking away the person but not the environment is one member of Linji’s Four Selections, stated as a rubric and answered through fresh images. The first member of Linji's four statements later called the Four Selections: ‘at times, take away the person but not the surroundings.’ Linji's own record gives the complete set and then records the unnamed monastic's question ‘what is taking away the person but not the surroundings?’ Linji answers, ‘the warming sun brings forth brocade spread over the ground; an infant's hanging hair is white as silk.’ The formula subsequently circulates as a verse heading and repeatable public question. Kefu's verse begins ‘its conditions themselves carry entangling error; if you try to seek the mysterious purport, deliberation instead reproaches you.’ Fengxue answers the inherited question with ‘a newly emerged red-furnace golden pellet strikes through the unnamed monastic's iron face-door,’ while another later master answers ‘the home country has a road that no one reaches.’ These answer-lines are recorded deployments of the formula.

Senses.Explanation: Taking away the environment but not the person is one member of Linji’s Four Selections, stated as a rubric and answered through fresh images. The second member of Linji's “four selections” (四料揀): literally, “take away the situation, not the person.” Here “situation” (境) is the presented surroundings or objects, while “person” (人) is the person. Linji first enumerates four possibilities in an evening instruction: sometimes take away the person but not the situation; sometimes take away the situation but not the person; sometimes take away both; sometimes take away neither. In the recorded follow-up he answers this member with, “the king's command has already gone throughout the realm; the general beyond the frontier has ended smoke and dust” (王令已行天下遍，將軍塞外絕煙塵). Later masters retain the exact category but supply different answers: “secretly transmit the emperor's edict; double the journey by a hundred stages,” “build the altar and appoint the general,” “muddy head and earthy face,” or paired states such as “silent, silent; alert, alert.” The category is therefore a reusable public-interview question within Linji's fourfold roster, not a proposition whose intent this entry resolves. Its Zen deviation lies in the bureaucratic verb “take away” becoming one axis of a named appraisal scheme for person and presented situation.

SearchAliases: drinking water knows cold and warmth
Senses.Explanation: In these records, drinking water supplies a recurrent comparison for knowledge reported by the drinker: cold and warmth are known by the person who drinks. Literally, “like a person drinking water.” In the Chan record the phrase normally continues “knowing cold and warmth oneself” . Its Zen-specific deployment is as a stock comparison for knowledge that the person concerned reports from his own encounter rather than receives as another person's verbal description. In the Huineng and Huiming encounter, Huiming responds after Huineng's question about his face before his parents were born: “like a person drinking water, knowing cold and warmth oneself” . Dahui says that at this point it is like drinking water and knowing its temperature oneself, and adds, “unless one has personally verified and personally understood, one can then see it” . The Record of the Mirror of the School frames a question with “understanding the way and clarifying the school are like a person drinking water, knowing cold and warmth oneself—how can their manner be spoken?” , and elsewhere pairs the comparison with “only verification knows; it is difficult to measure” . Poshan states the same deviation in domestic language: “only each person understands inside his own belly” , followed by the water comparison. Thus the corpus retains the ordinary act of drinking but makes the drinker's private knowledge of cold or warmth its recurring Chan predicate.

Daolin answers Bai Juyi with 'do no evils; carry out the many goods'; Qingyuan Xingsi asks an unnamed monk the price of rice in Luling; Linji Yixuan shouts at one unnamed monk and raises the whisk before striking another; Zhaozhou Congshen tells an unnamed monk to pay his respects and then cuts off the attempted continuation. When Ding Shangzuo asks, Linji leaves the Chan seat, seizes Ding, slaps him, and pushes him away. Xuedou Chongxian answers another unnamed monk with 'five-colored auspicious clouds.' The repeated formula is one public demand, while its recorded replies range across maxim, counter-question, shout, implement, image, and bodily action. The records supply no single answer shared by all these exchanges.

Senses.Explanation: The fixed public question, 'What is the patriarch's purpose in coming from the West?' In this corpus the patriarch in the formula is Bodhidharma, but the phrase functions as a repeatable question rather than as the name of one settled answer. An unnamed monk asks Jingshan Daoqin, who says the question is not properly put. Zhaozhou Congshen asks it while Linji Yixuan is washing his feet; Longya Judun asks Linji the same formula in another encounter. Jixian Wang puts it to Fahua Zhiyan. Other anonymous questioners receive sharply different replies from Baizhang Daoheng, Weifu Dajue, Fenyang Shanzhao, and Xianglin Chengyuan: the question misses, an announcement at the crossroads, a blue-silk fan's cooling breeze, or something presented face to face. Dahui Zonggao later raises the famous Zhaozhou exchange in which the answer is the cypress tree in the courtyard. These incompatible responses are part of the phrase's public-interview deployment; none is silently substituted for the English meaning of the question itself.
Senses.Note: Frozen-corpus concordance: 2,126 exact hits in 259 files and 254 independent works. The full interrogative is a lexicalized case-question linked to, but not merged with, the shorter nominal 'the patriarch's purpose in coming from the West' (祖師西來意). Response diversity is not polysemy in the question. Search aliases deliberately cover 'purpose', 'meaning', 'why', 'come west', 'coming from the West', 'Bodhidharma', and 'the patriarch'.

Senses.Explanation: This stock public-interview question asks what the Way is. Nanquan answers Zhaozhou, ‘the ordinary mind is the Way’ (平常心是道); when Zhaozhou asks whether one can head toward it, Nanquan says that intending to head toward it departs from it (擬向即乖). Other records preserve unlike answers without a single harmonizing gloss: ‘white clouds cover the green peaks; bees and butterflies love the courtyard flowers’ (白雲覆青嶂，蜂蝶戀庭華), ‘every household's gate opens onto Chang'an’ (家家門口通長安), and ‘what is sweet is licorice’ (甜底是甘草). Panshan Baoji merely rebuffs the question and sends the recorded questioner away. In a longer written questionnaire, the answer begins ‘unobstructed is the Way’ (無礙是道). Zhaozhou's record also makes the ordinary road-word audible: Zhaozhou first answers ‘the one outside the wall’ (墻外底); when the recorded questioner says he means the great Way, the answer is ‘the great road runs through Chang'an’ (大道透長安). The dictionary therefore retains the direct question and its observable public-interview role; the mutually different recorded answers are not converted into an interpretive menu.

SearchAliases: far side of Mighty Sound King
Senses.Explanation: Mighty-Sound King Buddha, a Buddha whom Zen records repeatedly invoke as an extreme before-and-after boundary. Huangbo Xiyun says he followed the Way before Mighty-Sound King; Nanquan Puyuan replies that Huangbo is still a descendant of old Master Wang, turning Nanquan's surname into the answer. Xuance says unaided self-awakening is acceptable before Mighty-Sound King but entirely the way of outsiders afterward. Xuedou Chongxian classifies unaided awakening before him as the second phrase. Tianyi Yihuai asks how many people Mighty-Sound King Buddha taught in his first assembly, then directs the audience to look at a ten-thousand-fathom peak. Dahui Zonggao critically reports people who call closed eyes news from the Buddha's far side. Hanyue Fazang describes paintings that place him before the seven buddhas as a circle preceding their differing verbal teachings, then gives a source-specific account of the name as outside form and sound and before writing. Juelang Daosheng asks whether his listeners have ever seen the power of Mighty-Sound King Buddha. The Zen figure is thus defined by these deployments: a named limit in lineage claims, interview questions, classification, painting, and criticism, not by a detached hagiography.
Senses.Note: The frozen allowlisted corpus has 545 exact hits in 189 files representing 184 works. Seven anchors from six works cover before, after, far side, second-phrase classification, first assembly, image and name commentary, and a public challenge about the Buddha's power. Before, after, and far side retain one named figure rather than producing different senses.

Senses.Explanation: “The Old Woman Burns the Hermitage” names the whole encounter among the old woman, the young woman, and the hermitage-dweller, not only its final fire. In its repeated narrative, an old woman supports a hermitage-dweller for twenty years and sends a young woman to attend him. The young woman embraces him and asks, ‘at just such a time, how is it?’ He answers, ‘a withered tree leans against a cold cliff; through the three winter months there is no warmth.’ On hearing the report, the old woman says that for twenty years she has supported only a common fellow, drives him out, and burns the hermitage. Later masters cite, verse, question, and re-appraise the case: one asks why various quarters support the recorded questioner; another proposes that the hermitage-dweller should have laughed when approached; another says that to uphold the school and establish the teaching requires such a person, speaking of the old woman. These opposed recorded appraisals belong to the case's reception; this entry does not decide between them.

Senses.Explanation: Confucius, the classical teacher whom Chan masters quote, compare with case figures, praise, and deliberately cut down. The record does not deploy him only as a foil. One transmission account quotes his “silently know it” and “one thread runs through it,” then explicitly says that these sayings accord with the subtle purport of the lineage. Another biography says the moment when Longtan met Tianhuang secretly accords with Confucius's statement “Do you think I conceal something? I conceal nothing from you,” making his sentence a comparator for a Chan encounter. Dahui places him beside the buddha and Laozi: after not doubting any of the three, one should borrow their nostrils and breathe out oneself. A later letter pairs Śākyamuni's flower-holding hand with Confucius's lute-playing hand as instances of the same human use of a hand. The same corpus also handles him sharply. One address says, “Confucius did not recognize written characters; Bodhidharma did not understand Chan,” while Juelang's verse says Confucius once displayed the first mechanism. Yongjue makes him hear a hall display and fall over laughing, and a recorded emperor-master exchange openly ranks Confucius, Mencius, and Laozi. An entire section titled Confucius's Staff says people know the lineage uses the staff but do not know that Confucius was skilled in using it; his sayings become blows that draw blood without leaving a mark, and the dead-letter Confucius is finally said to wield a living staff. The Zen deviation is this public re-siting: Confucius's sayings and gestures are compared directly with Chan encounters and buddha cases, while the figure can be affirmed, borrowed from, ranked, struck through staff language, or deflated without being protected as a remote authority.

Senses.Explanation: Brightness or clarity described as standing by itself and remaining unmistakably distinct. The term occurs 243 times in 112 allowed texts. Its common expansions make the constraint explicit: 'brightness standing alone, distinct and distinct' (孤明歷歷) occurs 42 times in 35 texts, while 'brightness standing alone and shining by itself' (孤明獨照) recurs in five texts. Linji Yixuan identifies 'the person right now before your eyes, listening ... distinct and distinct' (即今目前孤明歷歷地聽者此人). Dahui Zonggao likewise describes people sitting and standing plainly in that distinct clarity while speaker and listener meet. The records refuse to make the description a terminus: Xueyan Zuqin says that profound clarity and distinct brightness standing alone 'is not yet news of arriving home' (未是到家消息). Miaozhan Wenzhao asks, 'Whose radiance is this distinct brightness standing alone?' (歷歷孤明，是誰光彩), then warns that calling it 'true suchness and the actual limit' (真如實際) resembles cutting a sore into sound flesh. The term therefore describes a salient, self-standing clarity in these passages without naming a completed attainment or a procedure.
Senses.Note: The graph-literal translation is supported by both affirmative uses and express corrections. The records describe solitary brightness as distinct and shining alone, while also saying that it is not yet news of arriving home.

Senses.Explanation: Its central named case addresses the immortal Lü Dongbin: after he asks about hiding a world in a grain and cooking mountains and rivers in a small pot, Huanglong Huinan points and says, “this corpse-guarding ghost” (這守屍鬼). Lü invokes a drug of deathlessness; Huanglong Huinan replies, “even after eighty thousand ages, in the end you fall into empty extinction” (饒經八萬劫，終是落空亡). Other Chan records apply the same epithet to sitting inert on a cushion, a tenth-stage sage, and anyone who lives a hundred or thousand years but remains “a corpse-guarding ghost; its ghost does not disperse; a dead person” (守屍鬼魂、不散底死人). Yet Gaofeng Yuanmiao also instructs someone to guard on and on like a corpse-guarding ghost until the doubt-clump bursts with a sound. The Chan deviation is the use of this macabre epithet across case verdict, criticism, and an attested simile in instruction. The differing appraisals are preserved rather than harmonized.

Senses.Explanation: To guard a stump waiting for a rabbit is to repeat the site of a past accident as though the same result must return. Huanglong Huinan addresses the image to bewildered students; Yuanwu Keqin says later imitators wait at the stump by copying Bodhidharma's silent bow as the formula for receiving the marrow. Po'an Zuxian and Zhongfeng Mingben similarly criticize treating inherited words or postures as fixed proof. Linji Yixuan gives the phrase as his answer for a crowd pressing at the gate. In these cases the stump is a recorded precedent and the awaited rabbit is a result expected from copying it.

Senses.Explanation: Setting the mind at ease is posed as a request and answered through the famous demand to bring the mind forward, with later records retelling and testing that exchange. To set the mind at ease or to be at ease. The expression occurs 932 times in 245 allowlisted texts, and its central Chan deployment is the Bodhidharma-Huike public case. Huike says that his mind is not at peace and asks Bodhidharma to settle it; Bodhidharma tells him to bring the mind, Huike says he has searched for it and cannot find it, and Bodhidharma answers, 'I have finished setting your mind at ease.' Later records name the second patriarch's mind-settling matter, quote the closing words as an interview answer, versify searching for mind and not finding it, and openly criticize both request and response. Ordinary situational uses say that arrivals are at ease and that an unnamed attendant tells Gaofeng to rest easy while the attendant turns away a visitor. Those causative and intransitive constructions share the same mind-at-ease referent; grammar alone does not make separate senses.

Senses.Explanation: A lineage master: the designation for someone presented or judged in relation to the Chan ancestral line. The term occurs 1,445 times in 257 allowlisted texts. Daowu Wuzhen gives a direct role statement: “As for a lineage master, he takes away the poor child's pearl sewn in his clothes and examines the accomplished person's viewpoint” (夫宗師者，奪貧子之衣珠，究達人之見處). Dahui Zonggao says that a lineage master decides right and wrong and must open people's eyes rather than rely only on blind cangues and sightless blows (大凡宗師決斷是非。要得開人眼目。不可一向盲枷瞎棒). Guishan Lingyou says a lineage master must meet people with the fundamental matter. Yuanwu Keqin likewise says the lineage-master household must teach a person through, even at the cost of injuring hand and blade when the person does not understand (宗師家為人須為教徹). Yuanwu calls Zhaozhou Congshen “a great-handed lineage master” (大手宗師), saying that Zhaozhou does not discuss mystery, marvel, occasion, or object but meets people with the fundamental matter. He also calls Dongshan Shouchu, Zhimen Guangzuo, Deshan Yuanmi, and Xianglin Chengyuan “great lineage masters” (皆為大宗師). The label can be withheld or mocked: Xuedou Chongxian says of an inadequate answer, “calling oneself a lineage master like this and wanting to open the eyes of humans and gods—only in the donkey year” (如此自稱宗師，欲開人天眼目，驢年去). The noun thus works as a title and appraisal tied to public responsibilities, and as a rebuke when a claimant does not meet them.
Senses.Note: All direct-definition formulas and common modifiers were searched. The “great lineage master” form occurs 113 times in 49 texts; the lineage-master-household form occurs 87 times in 47; the lineage-master-eye form occurs 22 times in 20; and the “lineage master of a generation” form occurs nine times in eight. The role is corpus-wide and is not keyed to a single teacher.

Senses.Explanation: The lineage's house style: the recognizable way a Chan house carries and displays its inheritance. Public interviews repeatedly pair it with the song the named respondent sings and ask from whom it descends. Linji Yixuan answers by recalling his three beatings under Huangbo Xiyun; Xingyang Guijing points to Shaoshi, Shoushan Shengnian to a personal transmission there, Baizhang Zhiying to an image held in the palm, and Qingshan Hao to a charge received at Vulture Peak and enacted at Wenshui. Konggu Daocheng speaks of fanning this style until plants come alive, Juelang Dasheng asks supporters to sustain it together, and Guxue Zhe says it will greatly flourish. Chan bends ordinary school custom into an inheritance whose validity is made public in answers and conduct.
Senses.Note: Frozen-corpus concordance: 2,159 exact hits in 337 files and 331 works. One referent covers inheritance, activation, support, and flourishing; response differences are lineage claims, not separate senses.

Senses.Explanation: A paired term for stability and discernment. It occurs 962 times in 196 allowed texts. Huineng devotes a named section to it and gives the richest direct relation: 'Stability and discernment are one body, not two. Stability is the substance of discernment; discernment is the function of stability' (定慧一體，不是二。定是慧體，慧是定用). He continues, 'At the time of discernment, stability is in discernment; at the time of stability, discernment is in stability' (即慧之時定在慧，即定之時慧在定), then names this 'equal learning in stability and discernment.' He explicitly rejects making them successive: 'Do not say first stability produces discernment or first discernment produces stability as separate' (莫言先定發慧、先慧發定各別). Hongzhi pairs 'discernment able to be stable' with 'stability able to respond' (慧而能定。定而能應) and calls this 'the power of stability and discernment' (定慧力). Huangbo answers a question about their equal learning with 'throughout the twelve periods, do not rely on a single thing' (十二時中不依倚一物). A later letter supplies a corrective naming statement: 'Provisionally it is called stability and discernment; it is not an actual thing. As for this mind, it is originally self-stable and self-discerning' (方便喚作定慧，不是實法也。若論此心，本來自定自慧). Another record directly describes the graphs: inner and outer wholly clear is called stability, while responding to conditions and things with function without end is called discernment. The entry reports these corpus definitions without recasting the pair as a staged regimen.
Senses.Note: Direct definitions, substance/function equations, order contrasts, analogies, and corrective witnesses were all harvested. 'Equal stability and discernment' (定慧等) occurs 80 times in 44 texts; 'stability and discernment are one body' occurs in two independent texts; the substance/function formulas occur in four each. The pair remains one corpus-wide sense, led by Huineng's explicit rejection of separation and sequence.

Senses.Explanation: In the inherited guest-dust image, ‘guest’ and ‘dust’ name transient troubles or stain that arrive and depart rather than the host. Literally, “guest-dust”: dust characterized as a visitor rather than the host. Much of the corpus preserves it in the inherited compound “guest-dust troubles” (客塵煩惱), something said to stain, cover, or be unrecognized. Baizhang Huaihai's distinct functional classification is separated into the Baizhang-specific sense below. Elsewhere the Records say a grown child learns explanations and does not know that these are “guest-dust troubles” (不知是客塵煩惱); Dahui speaks of the “stain of guest-dust troubles since beginningless time” (無始時來客塵煩惱之染); and the Admonitions for the Monastic Gate has the compact bodily compound “body-and-mind guest-dust” (身心客塵). The Zen record therefore keeps the inherited dust imagery while Baizhang bends the compound into an explicit ruler/function classification.
Senses.Note: The corpus-wide sense remains one article because the Baizhang classification depends on the same guest-versus-ruler morphology as the broader compound. The explanation describes the recorded classification without adding an outside account of affliction or purity.

Senses.Explanation: One's own household treasure is what is already one's own, rather than something carried in through another person's gate. Zhenjing Kewen quotes the contrast 'what enters through the gate is not household treasure' and immediately asks what the treasure is; Baichi Yuanshuo says he brings it out in a public address, while Zhongfeng Mingben calls sights, sounds, and the whole field before a person one's own household treasure. Other records test it with an unpolished jade and warn that inherited words can leave a person counting somebody else's wealth. The domestic image therefore marks direct possession, not money or a concealed jewel.

Senses.Explanation: Hanshan is the pre-Zen figure whom the records pair with Shide and Fenggan. The string occurs 1,453 times in 271 allowlisted texts, but that total mixes the person with ordinary and place-name uses. As a figure, Hanshan is quoted by name: "my mind is like the autumn moon; the clear blue pool is bright and pure; no thing can be compared with it—how can I speak?" (吾心似秋月，碧潭清皎潔，無物堪比倫，教我如何說). Masters then criticize the verse: one says "Hanshan has slipped in speech" (寒山子話墮了也); another says Hanshan "labored without result" (寒山子勞而無功). In encounter lore Hanshan and Shide are visited at Guoqing monastery, imitate fighting oxen, bare their teeth, and later ask about the encounter. Elsewhere "Hanshan visits Shide" is given as the answer to a question about Vimalakirti's silence. Zen therefore deploys Hanshan as quoted poet, paired comic figure, and an answer in public interview.

Senses.Explanation: Cold ashes are ash in which the fire has gone out. Guxue Zhe quotes Zhenxie Qingliao's sick-room verse placing cold ash in a stove beside frost on a mat, while Shanquan Wei pictures hot beans bursting in cold ash. Chan addresses put that same physical image into sharply different frames. Pin Jixiang groups one thought lasting ten thousand years and cold ashes with dead wood as still, sunken dead water. The Continued Record preserves Shishuang Qingzhu's inherited list—rest, cease, let one thought last ten thousand years, go like cold ashes and dead wood—inside a sermon where Yunfeng quotes it, identifies it as an old master's view, and criticizes a one-sided reading by supplying the contrary, noisy sequence beginning "do not rest and do not cease." Chenghui Xianxu says that downward discussion would make dead wood flower and cold ashes burst into flame. Lianfeng sets yesterday's ground-covering cold ashes against today's sky-filling news of spring. The ordinary ash, the criticized stillness formula, and the rekindling or seasonal reversals are one material image under different predicates, not different lexical things.

Senses.PreferredTarget: Complete Command of the Precious Mirror
AlternateTargets: Song of the Complete Command of the Precious Mirror
Senses.Explanation: In the records this is a transmitted Caodong verse and named textual object, described as a complete command and passed from teacher to successor. In the Chan record this is not a generic state: it is the title and transmitted Caodong text associated with Dongshan Liangjie. Dongshan tells Caoshan that he personally received the Complete Command of the Precious Mirror from his former teacher Yunyan, that its matter exhausts the essential point, and that he now entrusts it to Caoshan (吾在雲巖先師處親印寶鏡三昧，事窮的要，今付于汝). A later commentary consequently calls it a book transmitted privately by Dongshan to Caoshan (寶鏡三昧一書，洞山室中密授曹山者也). The text itself opens, “This such thing was secretly entrusted by buddhas and ancestors; you have now obtained it, so guard it well” (如是之法，佛祖密付；汝今得之，宜善保護), then gives the paired images “a silver bowl filled with snow; the bright moon hiding a heron” (銀盌盛雪，明月藏鷺) and says that although their kinds are not the same, mixed together their places are known (類之弗齊，混則知處). Across later Caodong records its title is joined to the Five Ranks, upright and crooked, ruler and minister, and the paired wording “he is not me; I am precisely he” (‘he is not me; I am precisely he’). A direct question, “What is the Complete Command of the Precious Mirror?” receives, “Do not reflect idle light and shadows; return his old face” (不照閒光影，還他舊面皮). These are the transmitted title, contents, relations, and recorded answer; the corpus supplies no single prose substitution for the whole text.
Senses.Note: #0g deviation: the phrase is deployed as the proper name of a Caodong transmission text and house inheritance, not merely as the ordinary image of a valuable mirror or the standalone word for complete command. Attribution of authorship is not fully uniform: Dongshan's record says he received it from Yunyan and entrusted it to Caoshan; later records also call it Dongshan's text or report older attributions. The entry therefore reports the transmission claims without deciding authorship. Allowlisted count: 117 hits in 49 texts; the title form “Song of the Complete Command of the Precious Mirror” occurs 3 times in one text.

Senses.Explanation: “Not a thread hanging” is tested against robes and nakedness in public exchanges: the recorded exchanges ask how a robe remains, call the departing speaker back, or reject the claim as still below the steps. Literally, not one inch of thread hanging or attached : "not a thread hanging." This graph form occurs 59 times in 43 allowlisted texts; the variant with the simplified hanging graph occurs 97 times in , and the reversal "not hanging one thread" occurs 14 times in . Chan records make the clothing image into a repeatedly tested claim. When Xuanji answers Xuefeng's weaving question, "not a thread hanging," Xuefeng calls after him that the corner of his robe is dragging; Xuanji turns his head and Xuefeng strikes him, saying, "a fine 'not a thread hanging'!" . Nanquan asks the official Lu Gen what he does throughout the twelve periods; Lu replies with the phrase, and Nanquan answers, "you are still a man below the steps" . Jifei asks Fayun where the robe on his body came from if not a thread is hanging; Fayun answers by questioning whether it can be called a robe. Another exchange answers the condition "all affairs extinguished, not a thread hanging" with "you should be ashamed," then answers formal dressing and bowing with "the bare body fully exposed" . The phrase therefore bends literal nakedness and weaving into a stock Chan claim whose own records repeatedly check it against robes, dressing, and the interlocutor’s response; the corpus does not treat the words as a sufficient verdict by themselves.

Senses.Explanation: To take an existing error and proceed by means of another error. The corpus uses the phrase both in case description and as a verdict. Gunanmen's case comment says that the World-Honored One was pressed until there was no road for turning and could only follow one error with another. The phrase can also be prohibited: after declaring each of Linji's four positions wrong, Zhongfeng Mingben asks whether anyone can speak for him and warns against following error with error. In a public test, monks bow or step forward and repeatedly receive the phrase as Sanshan Denglai's verdict. Other passages interrogate it directly: one asks what the error is and answers with eating tea when tea comes and rice when rice comes; another rejects the phrase as an excuse for preserving faulty writing, comparing it to asking directions at a fork and spitting upward. A further instruction pairs the buddha's appearance with transmitting error and Bodhidharma's arrival with following error by error. These uses show mixed stances, not separate meanings: the same act can be warned against, applied to a case, or issued as a public verdict. The exact phrase occurs 407 times in 163 allowlist texts.

Senses.Explanation: A “small convocation” is a named communal address, often held in the evening or for a special occasion, whose procedure and content are less fixed than an ordinary hall address. The Baizhang rules say it has no fixed location, may use the sleeping hall or teaching hall according to attendance, is announced by a placard, omits the release-from-consultation bell, gathers the community after the evening bell, and lets the resident master mount the seat. The same rules list occasions including installation, visiting officials or donors, special requests, instruction for the dead, and seasonal observances. Records then mark small convocations for year-end, opening or closing a retreat, memorial instruction, ordination, and ordinary evening teaching. A playful interview answers “what is a small convocation?” with “eating gruel,” contrasting a great convocation with eating rice. These uses identify an event format, not a diminutive teaching.
Senses.Note: Exact frozen-corpus count: 7,411 hits in 357 files and 353 works. Eight curated witnesses from seven works meet the floor and include both procedural definition and performed events.

Senses.Explanation: Budai, literally 'the Cloth-Bag monk,' is the non-lineage figure defined in Chan records by the bag he carries and uses in public exchanges. His title occurs 200 times in 105 allowlisted texts. Asked 'what is the cloth bag?' (如何是布袋), he puts the bag down; asked 'what is the matter beneath the cloth bag?' (如何是布袋下事), he shoulders it and leaves. Asked the great meaning of the buddha-teaching, he again puts it down and stands with folded hands; asked whether there is an upward matter, he shoulders it and goes. In the street he says he is waiting for a person and rejects the claimant who says he has arrived. Records raise his verse, 'Maitreya, true Maitreya, manifests countless hundreds of millions of bodies, constantly showing himself to people, while people do not recognize him' (彌勒真彌勒，分身千百億，時時示時人，時人自不識), and publicly comment on it. The Zen Budai is thus the bag-bearing street figure whose putting down, shouldering, waiting, displaying, and Maitreya verse are repeatedly raised and judged.

Senses.Explanation: The lion appears through cubs, roars, and full-force capture in the stored Chan encounters. A lion. Senses.Explanation: Patriarch Simha is the named twenty-fourth lineage figure: records narrate his beheading and list his place between named successors. As a personal name, Siṃha denotes the Twenty-fourth Indian Patriarch, not the animal lion. The Patriarchs' Hall Collection heads his record 'The Twenty-fourth Patriarch, Venerable Siṃha,' identifies him as a man of central India, and records his entrusting the eye of the true teaching onward. A transmission roster independently places Venerable Siṃha between the Twenty-third and Twenty-fifth Patriarchs. Qianyan's record later raises the inherited case in which the king of Kashmir cuts off Venerable Siṃha's head. A person numbered in the lineage and beheaded by a king is a different referent from the lion used in lion cub and lion's roar. The Chan corpus invokes this pre-Chinese figure through his lineage place and death case; that Zen deployment defines the person sense here.

Senses.Explanation: A lion cub is a young lion. Chan records repeatedly bend this animal image into a public test-name and appraisal for a person. Mazu asks a lecturer who boasts of expounding many texts, “are you not a lion cub?”; after the lecturer declines the name, Mazu makes a hissing sound and the exchange continues. Named teachers say “a true lion cub, well able to roar” (真師子兒，善能哮吼) after a reviewed unnamed participant shouts or answers; in one lineage narrative this appraisal is followed by entering the chamber and receiving the seal. A direct question, “what is the lion cub?” receives “the tips of its hair line up the cosmos” (毛頭排宇宙). Formal verse places the cub in the lion's cave roaring until heaven and earth split, while another warning says that a true lion cub does not eat leftover soup. Later commentary can sharpen or contest an appraisal, saying that when Dongyuan opened his mouth to roar his fathers and ancestors were already lost. The Zen-specific bend is the recurrent use of the young lion as an explicit name given, refused, tested, and confirmed in encounters, often by the observable ability to roar. The entry does not infer succession whenever the words occur.

Senses.Explanation: The lion’s roar is explicitly defined against the jackal’s cry as teaching without something gained, and later records demand, test, or appraise that roar in public exchange. In the Chan record it names forceful speech or teaching and is repeatedly opposed to the cry of a jackal. One record supplies an explicit definition: ‘teaching with something gained is the jackal's cry; teaching with nothing gained is called the lion's roar’ (說法有所得，斯則野干鳴；說法無所得，是名師子吼). The phrase is not merely an appraisal applied by compilers: Baozi Guangyun tells his interlocutor to ‘try making a lion's roar,’ and monks claim it, and it becomes a public-interview challenge. Guishan says that Shishuang's speaking of Chan is ‘like a lion's roar, frightening the foxes, wolves, and jackals to death.’ In another exchange an unnamed monastic asks what happens on meeting a lion's roar; Shoushan Xingnian answers ‘let the jackal cry as it likes,’ after which the unnamed monastic shouts. Thus an animal sound is bent into a name, test, and verdict for speech in the teaching encounter; the texts themselves establish the lion/jackal contrast without requiring an imported symbolic reading.

Senses.Explanation: The “ordinary mind” is repeatedly named as the way, but the records contest what counts as ordinary rather than equating it with unexamined habit. In the Zhaozhou–Nanquan exchange, Nanquan Puyuan answers “the ordinary mind is the way” (平常心是道), then says that aiming toward it already departs from it. Mazu Daoyi gives an explicit account: ordinary mind has no contrivance, right or wrong, grasping or rejecting, annihilation or permanence, ordinary or sage (無造作，無是非，無取捨，無斷常，無凡聖); walking, standing, sitting, lying down, and responding to circumstances are all the way. Zhongfeng Mingben warns that the ordinary mind belongs neither to knowing nor to intellectual understanding and that attempts to harmonize explanatory formulas with it become measurement by discriminating consciousness. Zhenjing Kewen criticizes taking “the whole ordinary mind is the way” as a final rule merely meaning that each conventional thing is just itself. Zhuanyu Guanheng deliberately extends ordinary mind through relations between spouses, siblings, parents and children, friends, ruler and minister, and seasonal change, then says that actually pointing it out within those relations remains difficult. Yuanwu Keqin describes meeting meals and tea as they come while according with ordinary mind, explicitly adding that views of buddha and teaching do not arise. The term therefore ranges across a case answer, direct characterization, ordinary activity, social application, and warnings against turning ordinariness into a settled conceptual formula.

Senses.Explanation: In these records, Zhaozhou Congshen's courtyard-cypress answer blocks both a symbolic explanation and the claim that he merely points to an external scene. It is transmitted as his answer when asked the meaning of the ancestral teacher's coming from the west and repeatedly reopened by later teachers. Dahui Zonggao reports Wuzu Fayan raising the answer and first saying that understanding it in that way is wrong, then repeating it and saying such understanding is right. Xutang Zhiyu transmits the fuller exchange: when the monastic objects that Zhaozhou should not show an external scene, Zhaozhou says he does not show an external scene and repeats the courtyard cypress. Wansong Xingxiu preserves the further transmission problem in which Huijue denies that his former teacher Zhaozhou ever said it. Ruibai Mingxue stresses that naming the cypress does not present an external scene. Tianran Hanshi warns that descendants die in the words, Hanyue Fazang rejects the explanatory imitation that makes the cypress a display of a cosmic body, and Langting Ting rebukes an answer that merely restates “the ancestral teacher's coming from the west.”

Senses.Explanation: Guang'e is the butcher whom Zen masters turn into a case figure, an interview answer, and a disputed example. Dongshan Jue raises the story that Guang'e slaughtered a thousand sheep each day, went to the Buddha, threw down his butcher's knife, and said, 'I am numbered among the thousand buddhas'; the Buddha answered, 'so it is, so it is' (昔廣額屠兒日殺千羊，一日至佛所，颺下屠刀，云：我是千佛一數。世尊云：如是，如是). Dongshan then rejects both the view that Guang'e had formerly been a buddha who appeared provisionally as a butcher and the view that a remorseless killer simply threw down the knife and became buddha on the spot. Fahua Quanju answers a public question about his house style with 'Guang'e Candala' (廣額旃陀羅). Bao'en Faan instead exhorts his assembly to be like 'fierce butcher Guang'e,' who cast down the knife and immediately attained the fruit of an arhat (廣額兇屠，拋下操刀，便證阿羅漢果). These sources do not agree on one explanation of the act. They do agree in deploying Guang'e through the butcher, the knife, and an abrupt claim or result; the entry preserves that disagreement rather than supplying a secret meaning.

SearchAliases: the teaching establishment's gate and court
the gate and court set up for teaching
Senses.Explanation: The expression denotes the teaching establishment's gate and court in these Chan records. Its wording is the "gate and court" established for teaching or transformation. Chan records use it for the organized framework of explanations and responsive teaching, then explicitly place it below what questioners call the matter beyond or above it. the recorded questioner says, "one question and one answer still fall within the teaching establishment's gate and court" (一問一答猶落建化門庭) and asks how to raise the first principle. A sermon supplies a direct apposition: even a shout said to contain all these features "is still the teaching establishment's gate and court—responsive expedients—called a small resting place, not yet the treasure-site" (猶是建化門庭隨機方便，謂之小歇場，未至寶所). Another says that even holding the seal, raising the banner, and moving freely still falls within it and "is not yet the recorded questioner's essential road" (未為衲僧徑要一路). The Chan-specific use is evaluative and institutional: masters name their own question-and-answer and explanatory apparatus as a constructed teaching precinct, commonly in a contrast the texts themselves draw with what is "beyond or above" (向上) or the recorded questioner's essential road.

SearchAliases: Zen Zhang Three and Li Four
Senses.Explanation: Zhang Three and Li Four are the records’ stand-in pair for unspecified, readily named people rather than two biographical figures. Baofu Congzhan says that someone passing behind the buddha hall is seen to be Zhang Three or Li Four, then publicly asks why someone passing before it is not seen. Asked “what is the student’s own self?” another answers “Zhang Three and Li Four” (如何是學人自己；張三李四); asked “what is buddha?” another gives the same answer. The Ancestral Hall Collection places their names among distinctions that arise with seeing and hearing: “there are Zhang Three and Li Four, Hu comes and Han goes, the four surnames dwell mixed together” (便有張三李四，胡來漢去，四姓雜居). A later address puts them in the marketplace: “Zhang Three and Li Four sell noisy emptiness; Shide and Hanshan dispute cheap and dear” (張三李四賣囂虛，拾得寒山爭賤貴). Zen bends ordinary stand-in names into recurring answers, visible passersby, and market figures in public addresses; the entry does not decide what any single answer intends.

ClaimAnchors.AttributionNote: Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Lianyue (蓮月禪師語錄). In his own New Year hall address, Lianyue Guangsi repeats Mingjiao's line and asks the assembly why Li is drunk if Zhang drank the wine. Lianyue Guangsi is not yet in the roster; his record supplies the provisional pinyin form.

Senses.Explanation: Mr. Zhang drinks the wine while Mr. Li becomes drunk: the proverb marks a mismatch between actor and consequence. Zhang performs the act of drinking, but Mr. Li bears its effect and gets drunk. The stock line occurs 125 times in 84 allowlisted texts. Masters use that observable mismatch as an answer to otherwise different public questions: why the monastery superintendent lost his eyebrows after Danxia burned the wooden buddha, what Yunmen Wenyan means, and why there is no buddha teaching at the start of a good year. The corpus extends the joke: “Mr. Li sobers up and questions Mr. Zhang, just making Mr. Zhang lose his good temper” (李公醉醒問張公，恰使張公無好氣). In a teaching-seat enumeration it stands beside “Zhong Kui can dance the eighteen beats, the golden cock sings dawn, and the stone woman roams in spring” (鍾馗解舞十八拍，金雞唱曉，石女游春). Lianyue Guangsi turns the mismatch back into a question: “since Mr. Zhang drank the wine, why is Mr. Li drunk?” (既是張公喫酒，因甚李公卻醉). Sixin Wuxin repeats the line, asks its import, and refuses to explain it: “Let the blue sea change as it may; in the end I will not explain it to you” (任從滄海變，終不為君通). Zen bends the comic actor/effect mismatch into a reusable interview answer, verse line, teaching-seat enumeration, and new public question. The records license that structural inference but do not equate the proverb with one universal hidden answer to every case.

SearchAliases: Deshan goes down with his bowl
Senses.Explanation: The case title “Deshan Carries His Bowl” names the complete Deshan–Xuefeng–Yantou encounter, not merely the initial movement with a meal bowl. The case records Deshan going down with his bowl before bell or drum; Xuefeng asks where he is going, Deshan returns to his quarters, Xuefeng reports this to Yantou, and Yantou says Deshan has not understood the last phrase. Deshan summons Yantou, who privately states his meaning; the next day's ascent of the seat differs from usual, and Yantou says Deshan will live only three more years. The corpus turns this named encounter into a case heading, verse topic, question asked at the teaching seat, assigned object of inquiry, and point of later prose comment. Recorded replies to 'what is its meaning?' include 'no meaning' followed by 'if he wanted to go, he went; if he wanted to sit, he sat,' and, elsewhere, 'buying dear and selling cheap.'

Senses.Explanation: Wuyi Yuanlai supplies the clearest corpus definition: there are two awakenings, “interpretive awakening obtained from written words and speech” and “thorough awakening obtained by investigating on one’s own part”; he adds, “interpretive awakening is like hearing someone describe a thing; thorough awakening is like seeing the thing with one’s own eyes” (解悟者如聞人說物，徹悟者如親眼見物). Other records say not to stop if one has not thoroughly awakened, describe the World-honored One seeing the morning star and thoroughly awakening, and contrast the many who thoroughly awaken with the equally many who misunderstand. Thus the Chan record bends an ordinary intensive verb into a named contrast with “interpretive awakening” (解悟), while also using it in lineage biographies; the direct contrast, not an imported theory of enlightenment, controls the gloss.

Senses.PreferredTarget: the lineage seal transmitted and applied to mind
Senses.Explanation: A lineage seal said to be transmitted from teacher to heir and applied to mind: the records preserve stamp grammar rather than a physical object. The term occurs 1,374 times in 280 allowed texts. Chuming Baoyin says the ancestral mind-seal is neither long nor short, square nor round, inside nor outside, nor in between (祖師心印，非長非短，非方非圓，非內非外，亦非中間). Jingjie Shoumi says it has no trace or shape and remains distinct and uninterrupted through the ages (祖師心印，無痕無狀。歷劫分明，未嘗間斷). Fengxue Yanzhao compares it to the mechanism of an iron ox: 'going, it seals and holds; staying, it seals and breaks' (去即印住。住即印破). Shishuang Chuyuan says one seal imprints empty space, water, and mud (一印印空。一印印水。一印印泥). Huangbo Xiyun says Bodhidharma 'secretly transmitted the mind-seal, imprinting your original mind; mind imprints the teaching, and the teaching imprints mind' (密傳心印，印你本心。以心印法，以法印心). Sengna says the ancestral mind-seal does not consist exclusively in harsh conduct (祖師心印非專苦行), while Weishan Huaixiu says the mind-seal of buddhas and ancestors is known only through confirmation (佛祖心印，唯證乃知). These are the corpus's formal, material, and transmission predicates; they do not turn the seal into a literal implement.
Senses.Note: Required definition formulas found no single prose gloss of the bare compound, but several direct shape-negations and seal-mechanism explanations. 'Ancestral mind-seal' (祖師心印) occurs 336 times in 145 texts, while 'mind-seal of buddhas and ancestors' occurs 23 times in 17. Proper-name uses belong to the separate personal-title sense below.

Senses.Explanation: Here the graph translated as "thing" or "what is established" (法) is contextual: in the recurring pair "this thing is mind; outside mind no thing stands; this mind is the thing; outside it no mind stands" (此法即心，心外無法；此心即法，法外無心), it names what could be set up as a thing apart, not an untranslated religious loanword. Shao's frequently quoted verse places the phrase beside visible landscape: "the summit of Tongxuan is not the human world; outside mind no thing stands; blue mountains fill the eyes" (通玄峰頂，不是人間；心外無法，滿目青山). A later master quotes that verse and says it has been "broken into two pieces" (打成兩橛). Another hall address strikes the Chan seat and asks: "mind has not arisen—where could the things be established? Where did mountains, rivers, and the great earth come from?" (心既不生，法從何立？山河大地，甚處得來). The corpus therefore records the line as a maxim, a verse, a question to the assembly, and an object of later criticism; this entry does not decide the criticism.

Senses.Explanation: The place of mental activity ceasing is a formula for thought no longer having a place to proceed; the records state it, question it, and sometimes put it in a rejected explanation. The standard companion is "the road of language is cut off" (言語道斷, 171 occurrences). A transmission record explains the parallel syntax: "when principle is clear, the road of language is cut off—what words could discuss it? When the purport is met, the place of mental activity is extinguished—what contemplation could think it?" (理明則言語道斷，何言之能議；旨會則心行處滅，何觀之能思). Hongzhi asks, "just when the road of language is cut off and the place of mental activity is extinguished, what then?" (言語道斷心行處滅，又作麼生). A later address quotes "it cannot be known by wisdom or recognized by consciousness; the road of language is cut off, the place of mental activity extinguished," then answers with a deliberate counter-formulation: "it can also be known by wisdom and recognized by consciousness; the road of language is cut off, mental activity is not extinguished" (心行不滅). Zhongfeng also reports an interpreter's equation: "cut off thought, then the place of mental activity is extinguished" (絕慮則心行處滅), before contesting that line of equation in the following passage. The entry therefore records the fixed pair, explicit parallel, question, and counter-witness rather than equating the phrase with blankness.

Senses.Explanation: Records call it a “saying” (話), say that the biography says that Fazhou Daoji showed him the saying ‘who is reciting the buddha’s name?’” (示以念佛是誰話), or command a student to “investigate ‘who is reciting the buddha’s name?’” (參念佛是誰). Wuyi Yuanlai says to “raise only one phrase” (單提一句), identifies “who” (誰) as the word in question, and compares it in that passage to a hair-cutting sword and a poison-coated drum. In a recorded interview, the student states the phrase; Juelang Daosheng replies, “who is not reciting the buddha’s name?” (不念佛是誰) and raises a ceremonial scepter. Zen thus takes vocabulary associated with buddha-name recitation and makes the literal who-question a named saying, command, biographical turning point, and public exchange. The entry reports only those recorded actions.

Senses.Explanation: This deictic expression points back to a just-demonstrated action, wording, interpretation, or state: “in this way,” “like this,” or simply “so.” Huineng asks what is coming “in this way”; Shitou Xiqian blocks “this way,” “not this way,” and both together; Yuanwu Keqin warns that understanding in this way misses the matter, but elsewhere says that seeing in this way gives a share of freedom. The phrase also forms recurrent frames: “at precisely such a time” (正當恁麼時), “if so” (恁麼則), “must be this way” (直須恁麼), and Yuanwu Keqin’s self-reference to “talking this way” (恁麼說話). Foyan Qingyuan juxtaposes repeated “this way” with repeated “not this way,” while Sixin Wuxin says a great man is not made this way. Its translation therefore follows the demonstrative relation in each turn; the word does not itself name a teaching or a single approved manner.

Senses.Explanation: “If so, then” is the student’s recurrent inference formula in public exchanges, immediately tested or overturned by the recorded reply. A conversational connective: 'being so' followed by 'then,' hence 'if so, then.' It occurs 5,426 times in 317 allowlisted texts. Chan encounter records give it a conspicuous turn-taking role: a questioner repeats or draws an inference from a respondent's answer, and that respondent may confirm, reverse, test, or reject the inference. Recorded replies call the inference wild talk, reverse its premise, block it with an image, ask for the student's own part, or demand how the claimed conclusion is carried out. These outcomes are deployments of the same connective, not new senses. Its distinctive role is the recurrent public-interview hinge where a proposed understanding becomes answerable to the next line.

Senses.Explanation: A verb phrase: “awaken” plus “the Way.” Chan records use it retrospectively in biographies and cases: Lingyun awakens on seeing peach blossoms, the Buddha on seeing the morning star, and other monks after an encounter or event; verses composed afterward are called “verses on awakening to the Way.” The stock pairing “awaken to the Way on hearing a sound; clarify mind on seeing a form” is itself raised and questioned in a hall address. The records also police the designation: one text calls memorizing two convenient sayings and naming that “awakening to the Way” one of the enumerated kinds of foolish Chan. Thus the term names an attested event and biographical verdict, while the corpus also records challenges to loose claims of it.

Senses.Explanation: The compound functions as "as I knew," "sure enough," or “I knew it.” Its frequent Chan setting is the public interview, where one turn marks the recorded respondent’s prior expectation or recognition of the other. Ziman says, “as I knew, you are at a loss” (情知汝罔措), and cuts off the unnamed monk as he is about to continue. Pingtian Puan hears that a visitor has come from Huangbo and says, “as I knew, you had been to see an adept” (情知你見作家來). Jingfu’s case commentary anticipates the reader: “as I knew, you misconstrue it here” (情知你向者裏錯會). An unnamed monk also gives the compact reply “I knew it” (情知), after which Langting Ting says, “a fierce tiger does not eat meat lying down” (猛虎不食伏肉). These grammatical forms attest recognition or expectation; they do not name a separate faculty of “feeling-knowledge.”

Senses.Explanation: A formed, subjective understanding: case commentaries describe it as something generated around sayings, clung to, warned against, or broken through. In case commentary it is something readers ‘make’ from a saying (作情解), something words cause to arise (如今却因言句。轉生情解), and something commentators are repeatedly warned not to produce (切忌妄生情解). Yuanwu contrasts such explanations with seeing the old person’s intent, and writes that following another’s words generates this understanding. Other records speak of being stuck in it, forgetting it, or breaking its lair. These are the corpus’s recorded descriptions of the term.

Senses.Explanation: Cognition operating through feeling, sentiment, and recognition: affective or feeling-bound discernment. The term is repeatedly paired with estimating, reckoning, distinguishing, and interpretive understanding. Yuanwu Keqin asks whether a case can be estimated through affective cognition and calls explanations offered in public addresses affective-cognitive reckoning. Xuedou Chongxian says that recognizing the lineage at the words may still remain dim beyond its bounds. Huanglong Fazhong excludes affective-cognitive discrimination from his stated phrase. Liao'an Qingyu contrasts uncontrived writing with people glued to affective cognition and occupied with ornamental composition. Juelang Daosheng criticizes using knowledge and affective cognition to estimate public cases and encounter moves, while Tianru Weize calls what people learn and say dependence on affective cognition and interpretive understanding. The Zen bend is therefore grammatical and public: the records name the cognitive equipment by which students estimate cases and speeches, then explicitly mark that equipment as the obstruction or limit under criticism.
Senses.Note: The frozen allowlisted corpus has 537 exact hits in 152 files representing 148 works. Seven anchors across six works cover estimating, reckoning, exclusion from discrimination, being glued to it, being dim beyond it, using it on cases, and learned explanation as reliance on it. These collocations describe one kind of cognition, not different things.

Senses.Explanation: Alert or wide-awake. The headword occurs 1,323 times in 275 allowlisted texts. One major deployment is the command “stay awake” or “stay alert” (惺惺著, 142 occurrences). Ruiyan Shiyan's case has him call “Master!” to himself, answer “Yes!”, then say, “Stay awake; after this do not be fooled by anyone” (主人公……諾……惺惺著，以後莫被人瞞). The same word describes an alert person: Tianyin Yuanxiu contrasts an alert person, for whom moving, not moving, or both are acceptable, with a person who is not alert, for whom none is acceptable (惺惺底人……未惺惺底人). A second major deployment is the fixed pair “still and alert” or “alert and still” (寂寂惺惺 / 惺惺寂寂, 47 / 35 occurrences). Yongjia Xuanjue's Verse on Stopping defines alert as not producing the signs of dull abiding or blank indeterminacy (惺惺謂不生昏住無記等相), then ranks alert-and-still as right, blank-and-still as wrong, still-and-alert as right, and scattered-and-alert as wrong (惺惺寂寂是，無記寂寂非，寂寂惺惺是，亂想惺惺非). Later records also criticize these deployments. Zhanran Yuancheng reports that all quarters called Ruiyan's self-address “playing with spirit-ghosts” (諸方謂其弄精魂). Fangrong Tongxi reverses the case by saying Ruiyan's house-master called Ruiyan rather than the reverse. Haiyin Zhaoru names still-and-alert among fetters, paired with torpor and scattering (被寂寂惺惺、昏沉散亂縛). The entry therefore keeps the attested gloss “alert” while preserving both the formulas and the named criticisms.
Senses.Note: One corpus-wide sense, used of an alert condition and, by ordinary grammatical extension, of an alert person. The still-and-alert pairing is attributed to Yongjia Xuanjue's Verse on Stopping, while the Chan record also preserves criticism of Ruiyan Shiyan's command and names the pair itself as a fetter. The target remains the attested “alert” or “awake.” Compare “still” (寂寂), “master-in-charge” (主人公), and “playing with spirit-ghosts” (弄精魂).

Senses.Explanation: To answer or act aptly at the juncture presented: respond as the occasion calls. A historical notice says Linji Yixuan frequently used shouts when responding, then immediately records his warning to followers who merely copied his shouting. Caoshan Benji is described as ordinarily responding with no fixed tracks; a lineage overview describes the five houses as each having a house style and responding in exchanges. The corpus also pairs the term with events and conditions: 'the teaching is originally without speech; it responds according to the affair,' and 'meet the occasion like lightning.' Zen bends ordinary situational responsiveness into an expectation of apt public answer and action. The occasion or juncture is what is presented; the word does not automatically mean a student's graded capacity or a generalized system.

Zen responding to things, showing a form
Senses.Explanation: The phrase occurs 209 times in 105 allowlisted texts. The records repeatedly pair it with the comparison "like the moon in water" (如水中月). They also make it a public-interview question: asked "what is responding to things, showing a form?" Zhaozhou Congshen says, "bring the bed-seat over for me" (如何是應物現形；與我拈床子過來). In another exchange the monk asks which is the moon in the water comparison and the responding master raises the whisk. A later hall address says, "the body has no form; responding to things, it shows a form" (法身無象，應物現形), then raises the staff and measures the staff against the recorded heights of the World-Honored One and Maitreya. Thus the phrase is not left as an abstract proposition in the Chan corpus: masters put it into questions and answer it with the teaching-seat furniture and implements in front of the assembly.

Senses.Explanation: Answering the call records the audible response after one person summons another, preserving the call-and-response sequence of the case. To answer when called or to acknowledge an instruction. The word occurs 1,087 times in 227 allowlisted texts. Compilers repeatedly preserve the same audible action as the hinge of an encounter: Nanyang Huizhong calls his attendant three times and receives three answers; Shakyamuni calls Ananda after Ananda asks about the former buddhas' procedure; Mahakasyapa calls Ananda in the robe-transmission case; and Huangbo Xiyun names Pei Xiu by calling him, then declares the naming complete when Pei answers. In Xingsen's record an unnamed lecture master answers the call 'Lecturer,' and Xingsen immediately appraises him. Dahui Zonggao later raises an exchange in which Luoshan calls Zhaoqing and Zhaoqing answers before Luoshan replies 'a macaque enters the site of the Way' . The same response also acknowledges an instruction: Ananda answers Shakyamuni's order to enter the city with the bowl. The Zen bend is not a special second meaning but the records' placement of this ordinary answer as the next public turn and, at times, the central action of a named case.

Senses.Explanation: Releasing one’s grip over a sheer drop figures complete relinquishment at the point where ordinary supports fail. To release one's handhold over a sheer drop, where falling and loss of life are at stake. The phrase occurs 261 times in 120 allowlisted texts and becomes a named line in public interviews, sermons, verses, and death verses. Yuanwu Keqin preserves the paired saying, 'At the cliff let go; accept and undertake it yourself. Revive after extinction; no one can deceive you' (懸崖撒手，自肯承當；絕後再蘇，欺君不得). An unnamed monk asks Xingyang Xiyin for the line about releasing one's grip at the cliff, and Xingyang answers, 'The bright moon illuminates the secluded valley' (明月照幽谷); when the unnamed monastic asks next for the line about reviving after extinction, Xingyang answers, 'White clouds arise in the great void' (白雲生太虗). Yong'an Jingwu makes 'letting go from a ten-thousand-fathom cliff' his answer to an unnamed monk's question about the affair of leaving home. Another unnamed monk asks Luopu Yuan'an how to avoid losing his life after letting go there. In a letter, Yuanwu explicitly compares the cliff act with giving up one's life and with a dead person shortly reviving. The corpus therefore supplies the danger and the recurrent death-and-revival pairing; the entry does not turn that pairing into an unstated explanation.

Senses.Explanation: Records use this phrase for words or actions that stop proliferating routes of discrimination and response. The image is “cut off all streams,” and Yunmen-house discussions place it among three phrase-functions alongside covering heaven and earth and following wave after wave. Yuanwu Keqin calls it a solitary voicing of the hidden pivot that cuts off all streams without constraint or turning back. In the Blue Cliff Record he explains that an ordinary Yunmen phrase must contain three phrases: one that covers heaven and earth, one that follows the waves, and one that cuts off all streams. Ruibai Mingxue says that in a single shout the cutting-off phrase sweeps away ordinary and sage and ends conceptual interpretation. Hanyue Fazang describes unconstrained movement as lion-like and stream-cutting, while Feiyin Tongrong pairs the image with a sword across the sky and an iron pillar. Shiyu Mingfang applies it to the power of a fragrant elephant crossing beyond the mind-ocean. Tianyin Yuanxiu nevertheless says that even cutting off all streams remains outside the gate, preventing the phrase from becoming a final attainment-label.
