Senses.Explanation: To take a seat and remain sitting. Chan records use the ordinary bodily action in institutionally loaded scenes without making the bare verb itself a separate technical noun. An unnamed monk sits every day in the sutra hall instead of reading scripture. Xuanquan Yan warns clear-eyed patch-robed monks not to 'sit in the mud.' Yuantong Xiu lists three monks in snow—one sitting with his head covered, one sucking a writing brush and composing poetry, and one sitting around the brazier talking about food—and Baichi Yuan calls the first a board-carrying Chan fellow. Hansong Zhicao permits his assembly to sleep or walk and asks why they must rigidly insist on sitting. Wuzu Fayan speaks of Shuangquan sitting amid commotion, while Fachang Yiyu describes eighteen senior men sitting silently around a brazier. The word itself names the seated bodily action; place, duration, posture, institutional setting, and each named speaker's praise or criticism come from the surrounding sentence.
Senses.Note: The corpus has 322 matches in 132 files. 'Sit every day' occurs seven times in seven files; 'sit with the head covered' eighteen times in fifteen; 'sit around a brazier' thirty-five times in twenty-six; and 'sit in the mud' four times in four. The direct nominal form occurs once, in a question about one sitting on Kunlun Mountain. No other required definition formula occurs. The entry therefore uses the plain English action and preserves the corpus's explicit descriptive and critical modifiers rather than introducing a category absent from the Chinese.

Senses.Explanation: To be made into one piece is to become continuous rather than divided by time, motion and stillness, arising and perishing, or subject and object. The records apply the phrase across sustained inquiry and all twelve periods of daily activity. Zhongfeng Mingben places it after long continuity; Tianyin Yuanxiu requires it through all twelve periods of the day; Weian Deran pairs it with arising and perishing becoming one and motion and stillness not being two. Ruibai Mingxue says subject and object both disappear. A later record quotes Xiangyan Zhixian saying that it took forty years. Yuanwu Keqin uses the phrase as a name for the one-colour side, while Zhongfeng elsewhere rejects calling a consciously recognized silver mountain and iron wall by this name. The negative witness blocks the idea that one merely imagines a separate object and pounds it together.

Senses.Explanation: To hold fast is to keep something firmly in hand or under control. Chan records characteristically load the verb against ‘release or let go’ (放行): the two can name opposed exercises of authority, yet Wansong also says each can operate inside the other, so neither word fixes one outcome by itself. The compound has 773 occurrences in 203 allowlisted storage files, and the contiguous pair ‘hold fast and release’ (把定放行) occurs 15 times in 13 texts. Wansong quotes the saying, ‘when held fast, true gold loses its color; when released, rubble shines’ (把定真金失色，放行瓦礫生光), and calls this ‘having capture and release, able to kill and bring to life’ (謂之有擒有縱，能殺能活). Xuedou preserves the same opposition: ‘when released, rubble shines; when held fast, true gold loses color; the authority is in hand, killing and bringing to life accord with the occasion’ (放行則瓦礫生光，把定則真金失色，權柄在手，殺活臨時). These lines contrast true gold and rubble under holding and release; they do not by themselves define gold as enlightenment or establish one symbolism for gold elsewhere. The common objects show the physical pressure retained by the verb: ‘hold heaven and earth fast’ (把定乾坤), ‘hold the world fast’ (把定世界), ‘hold the key crossing’ (把定要津), and ‘hold the throat’ (把定咽喉). Hongzhi calls ‘holding the throat’ the work of a good hand in commenting on an exchange. In a recorded question, Jiufeng is asked ‘what is the eye that holds heaven and earth fast?’ (如何是把定乾坤眼) and answers, ‘heaven and earth are inside it’ (乾坤在裏許), then identifies that as the heaven-and-earth eye (正是乾坤眼). Wansong elsewhere says one eye ‘is also called the eye that holds heaven and earth fast, continuously leaking not the slightest thread, and is also named the diamond eye at the crown’ (一隻眼又喚作把定乾坤眼，綿綿不漏絲毫，亦名頂門具金剛眼).
Senses.Note: The corpus uses the same verb for concrete grasping, for holding a passage or throat, and in the paired critical vocabulary ‘hold fast / release’ (把定／放行); these uses retain the literal opposition and do not require separate senses. Wansong further states, ‘where the ancients held fast, they could release and advance from the top of a pole; when releasing, they could hold firm, standing like a thousand-fathom wall’ (古人把定處放得行竿頭進步，放行時把得定壁立千仞). The record thus refuses a simple equation of holding with one fixed outcome; this entry reports the wording without assigning an intent to it.

Chan records use it as a verdict of admitted company: the identified speaker says that whoever can inspect his statement may walk hand in hand south of Mount Sumeru, that one who can seize the snake safely may walk with the old monk, or that one commentator walks with Nanquan. Its companions range from buddhas and patriarchs to named masters and interlocutors who meet the stated test. Senses.Explanation: To 把斷 is to hold something fast so that passage is completely blocked. Verses make the same pressure concrete by saying the heavy crossing is barred and difficult to pass. The word names the blocking action, not a separate metaphysical gate.

AlternateTargets: a cauldron with a broken leg
Senses.Explanation: The broken-legged cauldron is the concrete object around which poor-monastery subsistence and succession are tested in the records. Literally, a cauldron (鐺) with a broken leg (折腳). In the Chan record it is not merely damaged cookware: it is the poor mountain monastery's shared cooking vessel and, in Yaoshan's exchange with Yunyan, something the elder asks the younger man to lift and carry. Later records call an inherited monastery the former teacher's broken-legged cauldron and ask the whole assembly to put a hand to raising it. Other passages place it in a grass hut or deep mountain valley, cooking plain rice for decades without concern for wealth, reputation, rulers, or nobles. Verses retain the comic poverty of the image by cooking a jeweled-necklace gruel in it. Thus the Chan deviation is institutional and domestic: a defective pot becomes the concrete roster of sustaining, inheriting, and jointly carrying a poor Chan household; the texts do not assign it a mystical substance.
Senses.Note: The corpus has 117 exact occurrences in 71 allowlisted files. The central inherited case is Yaoshan's request that Yunyan help lift and carry his broken-legged cauldron. Later records reuse the vessel for monastery succession, shared support, hermitage food, and mountain poverty. Forms include 'broken-legged cauldron' (折腳鐺), 'broken-legged cauldron-child' (折腳鐺子), and the diminutive 'broken-legged cauldron' (折腳鐺兒).

Senses.Explanation: To hug a bridge pillar while washing is to cling to the fixed support while trying to perform an action around it. Chan records preserve the fuller forms washing while embracing a bridge pillar and washing the feet while embracing a bridge pillar. They pair the image with launching a boat while holding its cable, feeling along a wall, or remaining unable to move freely; Baizhang Yu contrasts it with his own response. The record uses the bodily awkwardness as a comparison for being impeded by the very thing one holds.

Senses.Explanation: To pick out and bring forward is a public, transitive action in these records: something is selected or taken up and put where others can hear, see, inspect, or receive it. Zhenjing Kewen brings Mazu's Sun-Face Buddha and Moon-Face Buddha wording forward again for his audience (日面佛，月面佛，一一為君重拈出). Duanqiao Miaolun says he must bring out one phrase so that what heaven and humanity have not heard or seen may be heard and seen (拈出一句子，使天上人間未聞者聞、未見者見). Gaofeng Yuanmiao brings an old doubt forward again from the beginning in a letter (今日重疑，不免從頭拈出), and Lu Hang asks that the cases of the various houses not be brought forward before requesting one direct phrase (諸家因緣，不勞拈出). The same verb governs presented objects. Pufeng Haidong tells an unnamed monk who claims to have a jewel, “try bringing it out and let us see” (試拈出看). Baichi Yuan says he will take a bright pearl from inside his robe and present it before the assembly (不免乘時拈出，對眾分付). Tian'an Sheng and Yongji Rong bring out incense for public offering. These are not two different headword senses: phrases, cases, doubts, jewels, pearls, and incense are different direct objects of one selecting-and-presenting action. Chan bends that action into a standard verb for putting inherited cases and a participant's claimed answer into the public exchange, while retaining its use for objects physically displayed and offered.

Senses.Explanation: To take up an inherited case, encounter, or saying and bring it before listeners for comment. The action belongs to the public handling of the record: the material is raised, quoted, appraised, or deliberately left without further comment. Wumen Huikai's publication notice calls his book “forty-eight cases taking up and presenting the encounters of buddhas and ancestral teachers” (拈提佛祖機緣四十八則). Jingfu says lineage descendants successively raised and voiced the inherited material and took it up for comment (舉唱之、拈提之); his editorial rules classify the collected material as masters' “statements of taking up and commenting” (諸師拈提語). Yuanwu Keqin uses the verb for a person moving within and bringing forward the upward hinge (向箇裏出沒，向箇裏拈提). Dahui Zonggao puts two opposed statements together “without further taking them up for comment” (更無拈提), leaving students to distinguish them. Yulin Tongxiu says few in the communities had taken up and commented on the old woman's burning-the-hut case (者個公案叢林中少有拈提者). Dagui Huaixiu appraises Baofu Congzhan's handling as having considerable house style, then says that under questioning it again dragged through mud and carried water (保福拈提，頗有宗風，及乎問著，又却拖泥帶水). Senses.Explanation: The flower-lifting and smile scene names the paired actions attributed to the Buddha and Kashyapa; later masters quote, judge, and sometimes reject the scene’s inherited formulation. The flower-sermon scene: Shakyamuni Buddha holds up a flower before the Vulture Peak assembly, the assembly is at a loss, and Kashyapa smiles . The compact phrase joins two different actors' gestures; it does not say that one person both holds the flower and smiles. The recorded Buddha then entrusts Kashyapa with the treasury of the true teaching eye and a transmission outside teachings. Later masters challenge the scene. Yuelin Zongshan assigns thirty blows at the moment of the flower and smile. Dongshan Shouchu says people know the compact phrase but do not know the World-Honored One. Yulin Tongxiu calls it a single transmission and says it has made clear-eyed people laugh. Zhongfeng Mingben says that if the great affair were exhausted by such gestures, holding up the flower and smiling and cutting off an arm to settle the mind would be mere plays. Tianran Hanshi calls only this purport real and all other verbal teachings false, then immediately warns against making it a fixed reality. Zen defines the invoked Buddha and Kashyapa through this public scene, entrustment, and later examinations rather than through general hagiography.

Senses.Explanation: To take up incense is the ritual gesture that introduces the words or action attached to that incense in the particular ceremony. Konggu Daocheng takes up incense and names its recipient before saying it will be burned. It is therefore not defined as invariably public, dedicatory, or restricted to named teachers, and it remains distinct from subsequently burning the incense.

Senses.Explanation: To throw a brick to draw out jade is to offer something deliberately lesser in hopes of eliciting something finer. Hanxiu Ruqian and Langting Jingting retell Zhaozhou inviting questions as throwing a brick, only to draw out another clod. Shending Yikui praises an official's attempt to elicit jade but says he still missed his household treasure. Zhufeng Zhenxu applies the image to Shakyamuni eliciting Mahakasyapa, while Tianyin Yuanxiu accepts a layman's letter as a successful brick that reveals his capacity. Chan deployment therefore tests both halves of the tactic: what bait is offered and whether the response is actually jade.

Senses.Explanation: The image is movement that drags through mud and trails water with it: cumbersome passage that does not come away clean. Chan records turn that messy, encumbered scene into an appraisal of sayings, answers, explanations, and conduct, but they can also reverse it against the apparently sheer thousand-fathom wall. In an early question-and-answer record, Luohan answers a request for ‘a phrase for people’ with ‘dragging through mud and trailing water’; when asked for its import, he says ‘no small amount of disorder’ (如何是為人一句？拖泥帶水；意旨如何？郎當不少). Zhanran is asked directly, ‘what is dragging through mud and trailing water?’ and answers ‘seven hands and eight feet’ (如何是拖泥帶水？七手八脚). Yuanwu says that ‘not mind, not buddha, not a thing’ has already dragged through mud and trailed water (不是心不是佛不是物，已拖泥帶水), and in his case commentary says that speaking the word ‘buddha’ does so while speaking the word ‘Chan’ covers the face with shame (道箇佛字，拖泥帶水；道箇禪字，滿面慚惶). Lingyin Yinwen reverses the expected opposition: in the place of dragging mud and trailing water, a thousand-fathom wall stands; in the place of the thousand-fathom wall, one trails water and drags mud (拖泥帶水處千仞壁立，千仞壁立處帶水拖泥). The base order occurs 323 times in 144 allowlisted files; the reversed form occurs 192 times in 108 files.

As a figure, Shide appears with Hanshan at Guoqing monastery in the ox-fight encounter. His verse is quoted as, "not recognizing this meaning, one labors bitterly in conduct" (不識這個意，修行徒苦辛), after which Dongshan Liangjie says this wording does not save him and foregrounds Shide's dung-basket and broom. Senses.Explanation: Dahui names agitation as deliberate, successive mental activity and pairs it with dull sinking; later records repeat, criticize, or reverse that pair. Literally, tossing or shaking and raising up . Dahui directly describes the Chan usage: deliberate attention makes thought-consciousness fly about, one thought continuing another before the previous thought stops, and the teachings call this agitation. Another record contrasts heavy dull sinking, which is hard to rouse, with fierce agitation, which is hard to suppress. It is most often paired with dull sinking as the other condition found in the Chan hall. The record does not make mere absence of both a final credential: when a student says he neither falls into dull sinking nor follows agitation and asks whether this is his entry, Yunfeng Tizong Ning prescribes thirty blows. Gaofeng says dull sinking, agitation, joy, anger, grief, and pleasure are precisely true thusness, buddha-nature, wisdom, and liberation; Daodu calls the paired conditions each person's place for establishing life. The Chan bend is therefore the masters' use of a standard fault-word both as a sharply described condition and as material they refuse to set apart from the named person.

SearchAliases: receive a place in the monks' hall
Senses.Explanation: To register for residence and receive an assigned place in a monastery. The Chan Monastic Regulations gives the procedure: a new arrival waits a day or two, presents himself at the hall office with his ordination document, and requests residence. After registration he stores his luggage, hangs his bowl, and arranges his bedding in the unnamed monks' hall. The Imperially Revised Baizhang Monastic Code states the order more compactly: one seeking residence first presents himself at the guest office, then registers at the hall office, after which his assigned place is settled. When the abbot permits registration, the attendant's office notifies the hall office; tea and the bed register follow, and the newcomer enters the common quarters. Encounter narratives use the same institutional verb. Yexian Guixing tells Fushan Fayuan and Tianyi Yihuai, 'You two want to investigate Zen; go register' (你兩箇要參禪，却去掛搭). Fayun Faxiu directs that Ziqing register elsewhere until a place becomes vacant and he can enter the hall (且令別處掛搭，候此間單位空，即令入堂). These sources make the concrete Zen bend visible: registration is not generic lodging but formal admission into the monastery's offices, hall, bed register, and common quarters.
Senses.Note: The headword occurs 145 times in 38 allowlisted texts. The regulations distinguish seeking registration, the abbot permitting it, new registrants, greater and lesser registration procedures, returning to the hall, tea for new registrants, and thanks after registration. “Seek registration” occurs 8 times in 4 texts; “permit registration” occurs twice in two. The corpus therefore supplies a concrete lodging-and-admission procedure. In some biographies the completed verb simply marks that a traveler resided at the named monastery.

Senses.Explanation: Probing pole and shadow grass names diagnostic devices for testing what lies before Linji Yixuan’s words or a participant’s conduct. Linji's own record places the phrase third in his fourfold classification of a shout, after the Diamond King's jeweled sword and the crouching golden-haired lion and before a shout that does not function as a shout. Later records preserve it as a public category: unnamed monks ask Shoushan Xingnian and Feiyin Tongrong ‘what is a shout like probing pole and shadow grass?’ Recorded answers include ‘I have tested what bones you have’ (驗得你骨出) and ‘I know whether you are a dragon or a snake’ (知你是龍是蛇). Tianyin Yuanxiu calls a particular conversational move ‘also probing pole and shadow grass,’ and another record says a staff may function this way. These attested predicates place the ordinary images in encounters as a named testing gambit. The sources quoted here retain the compound and do not separately define the pole and the grass.

Senses.Explanation: To receive someone and lead them onward. In Chan records it commonly names reception of students by named teachers and the answers given when students come before them. Asked, “how do you receive and lead?” (作麼生接引), Juelang Daosheng answers, “every house has a road open to carts and horses” (家家有路通車馬). Konggu Daocheng, asked “by which gate do you receive and lead later students?” (以那一門接引後學), answers with the recorded alternatives of staff and shout, expedient and actual, opposing and following. An unnamed questioner says, “I too hope to be received and led” (某甲亦望接引), and Konggu replies, “one cannot walk by taking another by the hand; only one's own assent is intimate” (把手牽人行不得，為人自肯乃方親). Qianshan Hanke asks whether the fundamental matter can be used to receive people, then sets “if there is receiving” against “without relying on receiving” (若有接引；不假接引). Thus the corpus uses an ordinary verb of reception as a category for named teachers' dealings with arrivals, while also recording challenges to the category itself; it supplies no single fixed procedure under the word.

Senses.Explanation: To cover one's ears while stealing a bell is to hide from oneself the noise that exposes one's own act. Muzhou Daoming says a pious-sounding account resembles covering the ears while stealing a bell. Yuan'an Feng joins it to 'clutching the stolen goods and crying injustice'; Hanyue Fazang calls his interlocutor an ear-covering bell thief and then strikes him. Yuanjie Ying forbids the move, while Konggu Daocheng applies it to people who imagine they have deceived others. Chan usage preserves the self-defeating concealment: the attempted evasion itself advertises what the named critic exposes.

Senses.Explanation: To take up the lineage's matter and keep it actively before an assembly. Its recurrent objects are “this matter,” the ancestral seal, the school's essentials, the Buddha teaching, an upward move, or the authoritative command; the action is performed in addresses, case comment, and face-to-face presentation rather than describing private possession. Wuwen Can says that he came two thousand leagues to reside at a monastery solely to sustain this matter, then raises the whisk and says, “Look! Look!” Yuanwu Keqin pairs carrying the school with upholding the ancestral seal and says the ancients entered deep mountains to sustain the school's essentials. Baiyu Jingsi describes Mazu Daoyi's sickbed answer as an all-out presentation for others. Zhean Jingfan criticizes how the ancients handled the seventeen hundred cases, while Feiyin Tongrong raises his staff and presents one move face to face. Jiguang Huo contrasts upholding the authoritative command and blocking the vital crossing with following the waves and setting up guest and host. The raw concordance has 1,140 substring matches in 261 allowlisted texts, including false joins across word boundaries; the semantic conclusions use only complete compound tokens.

Senses.PreferredTarget: to bring up and call attention to
Senses.Explanation: To bring something up and call attention to it: to prompt a person or repeatedly return a saying or matter to notice and examination. In a public exchange, an unnamed monk asks Gushan Shenyan to prompt him about the lineage matter; Gushan calls him closer and says, "This is prompting you." Hongzhi Zhengjue describes both participants in an exchange as each putting out a hand and bringing up the matter. Dahui Zonggao uses the verb both critically, for going once through an old saying and calling that freedom from words, and instructively, for bringing something up from time to time and amid walking, sitting, emotion, and responsive dealings. Wumen Huikai says many pick up Zhaozhou Congshen's answer and many bring it under examination. Foyan Qingyuan recalls receiving repeated earnest prompting from his late teacher. The Zen bend is the interpersonal and case-facing use: this ordinary act of calling attention becomes something done in the interview, received by Foyan Qingyuan from his late teacher, or repeatedly directed at a recorded saying, without naming a separate regimen.
Senses.Note: The frozen allowlisted corpus has 642 exact hits in 208 files representing 206 works. Eight exact anchors across four works cover request and response as separately attributed turns, case commentary, critical report, occasional prompting, a regional appraisal, memorial thanks, and repeated occasions. Changes of actor, object, and frequency do not create different things, so the entry remains one verb sense.

Senses.Explanation: This separate corpus sense names to take up a saying or question for sustained attention, not to lift or hold up a physical object. The stored cases keep that referent explicit. To take up a saying or question and keep it actively before attention. Zhongfeng Mingben repeatedly directs an assembly to do this with verbal objects: a saying without the flavor of meaning, one's assigned saying of inquiry, and the complete question ‘The myriad things return to one; where does the one return?’ His surrounding predicates require beginning with it, not moving from it, continuing forward with it, and sustaining questioning while walking or sitting. This is not bodily lifting of an object; it is the continued taking-up of a verbal subject.

Senses.Explanation: To have one’s eyes swapped out is a repeated warning that words, texts, sounds, or another person’s formulation can replace how one sees. Literally, "swap out the eyes" . In ordinary wording this would name a bodily exchange; Chan records use it as an accusation that a saying, written formulation, sight, sound, or teacher has displaced a person's own seeing. Miaoyun’s commentary says that the unnamed questioner who asks Xuansha about his own self has his eyes swapped out by Xuansha’s reply. Shiyu says altered wording and changed characters swap out people's eyes, and elsewhere says waterbirds, groves, bells, and gongs do it. Sanyi warns against letting the writing brush exchange black beans for one's eyes , then identifies bird-script, dragon-writing, paper, ink, and written characters as fit for ordinary circulation rather than Chan discussion. A case comment even judges the words "Where is the eminent monk?" themselves to have plainly swapped out the eyes. The distinctive Chan deployment is therefore an adversarial verdict about seeing being commandeered; the texts apply it to both words and sensory displays, not to literal surgery.

Senses.Explanation: To cast aside cause and effect is a named and condemned error: treating conduct and consequence as though they can simply be denied. The Record of Gu Xue Zhe says that misconstruing the ancients’ situation-matched talk can lead people to cast aside cause and effect and invite calamity. The Record of Gu Ting places the error after laziness gives rise to wild thoughts, and the Complete Record of Juelang asks how cause and effect could be cast aside when speaking of individual and shared karma. Dahui’s formal discourse likewise warns that hearing emptiness and then denying cause and effect is an error. The two stored expression-by-negation controls define expression by negation but do not themselves contain the no-cause-and-no-effect formula; they therefore mark a comparison that must be made from exact speech frames, not a license to equate every negative formula with causal denial.

Senses.Explanation: Clapping the hands is a narrated audible gesture, often paired with laughter or used to close a comment. The gesture occurs 746 times in 231 allowlisted texts, commonly as a visible turn in a public exchange. It may stand alone (‘clapped three times’), accompany departure, a shout, or a blow, or join laughter: ‘clapped his hands and laughed loudly’ occurs 98 times in 60 texts. The record does not assign one fixed attitude to it. Yangqi Fanghui claps and laughs before saying an answer is ‘not worth half a cent’; another monk claps once after shouting; Xiyuan claps three times when asked why he bathes without an attendant. Caoshan later explicitly calls the action ‘hand-clapping’ and distinguishes Xiyuan’s use from the same physical action elsewhere. In the Shuilao case, Shuilao rises after Mazu kicks him, claps and laughs, and speaks; later records repeatedly cite that sequence. Zen bends an ordinary gesture by making it an answer, rejoinder, appraisal, or recorded public-interview move, while the surrounding words—not the gesture alone—establish whether a given occurrence is laughter, challenge, celebration, or dismissal.

Senses.Explanation: To hit the bench or platform-seat used during an address to the assembly. The strike is public teaching-hall conduct, not merely damage to furniture: it often supplies the last percussive event before leaving the seat, but it can also become a turn in an exchange. Yuanwu Keqin raises the whisk and asks whether the assembly sees, then strikes the teaching seat and asks again. Foyin Qing makes the contrast explicit by asking whether they see the raised whisk and whether they hear the struck seat. Dahui Zonggao labels the raised whisk “form” and the seat-strike “sound.” Shishuang Chuyuan strikes once with his staff, asks whether the assembly understands, and cites the line “one strike, and what was known was forgotten.” Dayu Shouzhi answers a six-rung-reviewed unnamed questioner's question about buddha by striking once and saying it has already been forgotten. Songyuan Chongyue strikes once with the whisk and asks whether his listeners feel pain or an itch. The omitted or named instrument and the various questions change the deployment, not the physical action. The phrase has 686 matches in 141 allowlisted texts.

Senses.Note: The Zen bend is the borrowed military register: the commander's capture-and-release of an enemy becomes the cited speaker's control of the encounter, held 'in me' (擒縱非他，卷舒在我). The required definition formulas produced only one grammatical headword-plus-nominalizer occurrence and no self-definition. The repeated coordinations supply the lexical structure directly: capture contrasts with release, just as gather contrasts with release and killing contrasts with bringing to life. Senses.Explanation: In ordinary usage, ‘capture and release’ is a commander’s battlefield tactic: take the opponent, then let him go at will. Chan speakers bend that command pair toward control of an encounter, repeatedly coordinating it with rolling out and folding up or killing and giving life. That command register is the word's Zen bend. Literally, 'capture and release': 'capture' (擒) paired with 'let loose or release' (縱). The compound occurs 107 times in 73 allowed texts. Its most frequent fixed relations are 'capture and release, kill and bring to life' (擒縱殺活, 19 occurrences) and 'roll out and fold up, capture and release' (卷舒擒縱, 12). Yuanwu also records the reversed framing 'release and gather, capture and release' (放收擒縱) and says, 'capture and release are not another's; rolling out and folding up are with me' (擒縱非他。卷舒在我). In an assembly address he writes that only afterward does one 'release and gather, capture and release, and obtain great freedom' (放收擒縱得大解脫). Another address says, 'within killing there is bringing to life, capturing and releasing humans and gods; within bringing to life there is killing, weighing buddhas and ancestors' (殺中有活擒縱人天。活中有殺權衡佛祖). His Essentials states: 'able to capture and release, skilled in killing and bringing to life—great teachers do not fail to use these' (能擒縱，善殺活，得大解脫，知識無不用之). Later commemorative prose similarly says 'capture and release, killing and bringing to life, are all complete' (擒縱殺活皆全). The corpus thus deploys the pair as the cited speaker's coordinated command of the encounter, commonly placed in four-part action strings.

Senses.Explanation: A comic epithet for a one-sided person: a fellow carrying a board and seeing only one side. The stock line says that Xu Six carries a board and sees only one side, while Baiyu Jingsi states directly that each party sees one side and is precisely a board-carrying fellow (各見一邊，正是擔板漢). In a case Baiyu raises, Muezhou Daozong calls to an addressee and applies the name when the man turns; Xuedou Chongxian and Huanglong Huinan then debate its application, and Baiyu judges their opposed comments one-sided. The label extends beyond that case. Dongshan Meixi Du says that learning without awakening is overbearing pride, whereas awakening without learning is a board-carrying fellow (有學無悟謂之增上慢，有悟無學謂之擔板漢). Zhe'an Jingfan applies it both to delight at a rich feast and fear in a thorn thicket, and elsewhere says that enumerating ranks, mysteries, divisions, reality, and expedients only makes such a fellow before asking how the matter can be raised whole (只成擔板漢，此事如何舉得全). Yuanwu Keqin says that a board-carrying fellow often dies in the phrase (若是擔板漢，多向句中死却). Zen bends a comic physical image into a public epithet for the person whom a record presents as fixed on one side or trapped in wording; the entry reports those attested applications without generalizing beyond them.
Senses.Note: The headword occurs 193 times in 90 allowlisted texts; the shorter form for carrying a board (擔板) occurs 589 times in 186 texts. Six exact witnesses and one family witness cover the one-side formula, Muezhou case, paired formulas, and direct teaching-seat applications. These are local applications of one epithet, not separate referents.

Senses.Explanation: To assume and bear responsibility, especially for the teaching or its succession. Yuanwu Keqin places successful shouldering beside accepting, heading toward, and carrying out; elsewhere he says only Shenguang was permitted to bear the subtle key of Shaolin. Guangzhi Quanwu calls for someone able to shoulder it with the whole body, and Xueqiao Yuanxin calls a person with strength to come forward and bear it on one shoulder. Jiufeng Daoqian explicitly defines inward accepting and shouldering as inner succession, then contrasts it with the person who has no accepting and no shouldering. These responsibility, authority, and succession frames make the omitted load institutional and figurative. They are a different referent from physically carrying cargo, even though the metaphor retains the bodily image.
Senses.Note: The headword occurs 969 times in 265 allowlisted texts. This sense is restricted to responsibility, authority, teaching, and succession frames. Attested formations include successful shouldering, whole-body shouldering, one-shoulder shouldering, accepting and shouldering, and inability to shoulder. Physical cargo is separated below because the corpus uses the word for a different thing there.

Senses.Explanation: To bear physical cargo on the shoulder. In Xisou Shaotan's verse the object is firewood and the bodily mechanics are explicit: one shoulder carries it until the carrying pole breaks. The named cargo and broken pole make this an ordinary transport action, not responsibility for teaching or succession.
Senses.Note: This different-thing split is anchored by one unequivocal full-case witness. A corpus-wide collocation search did not locate a second independent occurrence with equally explicit cargo, so this literal sense remains provisional rather than being padded with figurative one-shoulder language.

SearchAliases: carry snow to fill a well
Senses.Explanation: Carrying snow to fill a well is a recurrent comparison for ineffective effort, applied to talk, question-and-answer, sitting Chan, and other undertakings. Literally, "carry snow to fill a well" : the load melts while the well remains unfilled. Chan records use the concrete impossibility as a compact appraisal of ineffective religious display and effort. Baishan applies it separately to "pick it up and immediately use it" , to question-and-answer exchanges in an enumeration beside "talking mysteries, drawing a cake to satisfy hunger" , and to trying to pass through by silent stillness, contrasted with trying to state it in words as "proving a turtle to be a soft-shelled turtle" . Tian'an calls sitting Chan like carrying snow to fill a well and rhymingly calls composing poetry kneading snow into a ball . Yinyuan pairs the phrase with trying to fill a net by blowing and says that even ages of such actions have no place. The Zen-specific deployment is a verdict applied not to an ordinary futile chore but to recognizable Chan-scene responses—silence, words, questions and answers, sitting, gestures, and other attempted displays.

SearchAliases: frame it in mind and miss
Senses.Explanation: “Frame it in mind and already miss” is paired with stirring thought, then corrected against inert nonmovement in repeated hall statements and interviews. Literally, "frame it in mind and already be off" . Chan records make this a compact warning and an answer: Huangbo places it after saying that mind is not to be sought with mind; another record answers "What is buddha?" with "frame it in mind and already miss; use mind and already go astray" . The fixed expansion "frame it in mind and already miss; stir a thought and already go astray" is also tested rather than left as a slogan. Two Dong'an notices add that neither framing nor stirring leaves one "working for a livelihood in dead water" , while neither framing nor stirring makes one no different from wood and clay . Fayyi answers a student's quotation of the formula by asking why someone who is always framing does not miss, and then calls the student's next move "already a miss" . Thus the Chan deviation is observable in the records' refusal to let either side—deliberation or inert non-deliberation—serve as the definition.

Senses.Explanation: Gathering the mind is the proposed finite action of collecting, drawing in, or holding in the mind. Chan records both give that action concrete work and challenge whether the wording has any stable basis: the tension belongs in the definition rather than being resolved into a system. The phrase occurs 137 times in 71 allowlisted texts. Asked to ‘show the way of gathering the mind’ (示攝心之法), Chaozong Tongren answers, ‘sit still for one stick of incense’ (靜坐一爐香), but immediately calls this ‘a fine saying’ and warns that it must not be misunderstood (好箇話頭，只是不得錯會). In a separate verse requested on the term, Chaozong says, ‘the myriad things are brightly clear—what thought and what consideration? If you intend to gather the mind, there is no basis to rely on. I now write these words for you; just this is the place of gathering the mind’ (萬法朗然，何思何慮？擬欲攝心，無本可據……只此便是攝心處).
Senses.Note: In the Extended Record of Yongjue Yuanxian, Yongjue quotes "gathering the mind is called restraint" (攝心名戒), then challenges it point by point: "what thing is mind that it can be gathered? What thing is gathering that it can gather mind? Water does not wash water" (心是何物而可攝？攝又是何物而可攝心？水不洗水). Yongming Yanshou's Source-Mirror Record states that before reaching its stated gate, "saying right makes wrong; gathering the mind is still an error" (說是成非，攝心猶錯). Shiwu Qinggong's community verse retains the ordinary finite action by listing chanting and "gathering the mind to drive off sleep" (攝心除睡). Counted forms include "gathering the mind is called restraint" (攝心名戒, two occurrences in two texts), "gather the mind to drive off sleep" (攝心除睡, two in two), "the way of gathering the mind" (攝心之法, one), "place of gathering the mind" (攝心處, one), and "gather the mind and illuminate within" (攝心內照, three in three). The entry records the action and the texts' own challenges without resolving those challenges into an external system.

Senses.Explanation: An imperative: 'put it down' or 'set it down,' with the final graph marking the command. The records use it for things held in the hands and for what a questioner says cannot be brought. When an unnamed monk raises his sitting cloth and asks for an answer, the named record subject says, 'Put it down,' then says 'withdraw' when the unnamed monk starts to spread it. In the Yan Yang–Zhaozhou case, Yan Yang asks what to do when not one thing is brought; Zhaozhou says, 'Put it down.' When Yan Yang asks what there is to put down, Zhaozhou replies, 'If you cannot put it down, carry it away.' A second recorded exchange has Shakyamuni tell the Black-Clan Brahmin three times to put things down: first each flower, then, after both hands are empty, the six external objects, six internal faculties, and six intervening discriminations. Another exchange draws the text's own contrast: scattered thoughts are answered with 'put it down,' while not producing a single thought is answered with 'raise it up.' The phrase is an instruction within these specific exchanges; the entry preserves the imperative and its stated objects.
Senses.Note: The exact form has 340 matches in 126 files. The graph variant with the shorter form of the final character has nine matches in five files. The Yan Yang question 'when not one thing is brought' occurs eighty-four times in fifty-four files, and its follow-up 'since not one thing is brought' occurs fourteen times in fourteen. 'Put everything down at once' occurs five times in three files, while the direct opposite imperative 'raise it up' occurs once. None of the seven required definition formulas occurs, so the entry is built from complete exchanges, physical deployments, the text-drawn opposition, and later quotations of the case.

AlternateTargets: let pass rather than hold fast

Senses.Explanation: In a public encounter, to open the way and allow movement instead of blocking or holding fast. The recurrent contrast is with “hold fast” or “hold in place,” and the records make the difference visible through their own images. Tianzhang Yuanshan says that holding fast freezes dripping water and stops the rivers, while releasing brings warm sun, mild wind, and mountains and streams competing in beauty; he then asks which is good. Xuedou Chongxian says that under release rubble shines, while under restraint true gold loses color. Yinyuan Longqi opens a cloth bag, opens one road of release, and lets the assembly jump east and west before asking which is release and which is restraint. Tiantong Hongjue Min is asked for “a releasing saying” after the restraining side is set aside; he answers, “open in all directions.” Yuanwu Keqin asks whether releasing for people or holding them fast is good. Wumen Huikai says that holding fast and releasing each puts out one hand to raise the ancestral vehicle. Yongjue Yuanxian contrasts Boshan Wuyi, who only knew how to hold fast, with his own release on that day. The phrase has 1,169 occurrences in 247 allowlisted texts.
Senses.Note: Corpus counts: 1,169 hits in 247 texts. Attested formations include 'release, then...' (放行則), 151 hits in 80 texts; 'drawing in and releasing' (收放), 310 in 143; 'holding fast and releasing' (把定放行), 15 in 13; 'a road of release' (放行一路), 7 in 6; 'what is release...?' (如何是放行), 11 in 11; and 'not release' (不放行), 40 in 36. No exact definitional formula equivalent to 'X means release' or 'is called release' was found. The two hits for 'one who releases' are predicative uses, not definitions.

Senses.Explanation: On a battlefield, 'defeat' (敗) is a rout and 'breach' (闕) is a gap. In Chinese Chan records the compound is a recurrent verdict of failure on an exchange, statement, answer, or speaker. The allowlisted corpus has 594 hits in 193 texts. It records the constructions 'incur a failure' (納敗闕, 130 hits in 80 texts), 'a whole episode of failure' (一場敗闕, 129 hits in 85 texts), and 'the place of the failure' (敗闕處, 39 hits in 28 texts). In one direct exchange an unnamed questioner asks, 'What failure do I have?' and receives the answer 'Wrong.' Elsewhere Dahui quotes Linji calling an old man's response 'a failure today,' then answers the question 'Where is his failure?' with 'The road is far and the night is long; stop carrying a torch, everyone, and blow it out while walking in the dark.' Yuan Cheng is asked how to have no failure and replies, 'Eat three meals.' A later comment can apply the verdict to both parties while also calling both adept: 'As failures, both are failures; as adepts, both are adepts.' These records leave the verdict attached to the cited exchange rather than supplying one universal defect that the word always names.
Senses.Note: The word carries a military register: 'rout' (敗) plus 'breach' (闕) becomes a verdict that an exchange has failed, as in 'a whole episode of failure' (一場敗闕) and 'incur a failure' (納敗闕). All seven required definition formulas were searched; none produced a lexical definition. The entry therefore foregrounds the direct 'what failure?' exchange, the 'where is the failure?' retrospective, verdict uses, and the corpus's own two-party contrast. The rare 'no failure' construction (無敗闕) has one hit in one text. Exact actors are named on every retained occurrence except the source-anonymous questioning monk, whose reviewed exception record preserves all six attribution rungs.

Senses.Explanation: Chan records use this phrase as a lineage charter, a recurring interview question, and an object of explicit qualification about what “outside” and “separate” do not mean. The flower case places it beside not setting up words and entrustment to Mahakasyapa. Yuanwu repeats it in the four-part banner, while Yunmen asks why it is asserted when the canon is hardly wordless. Unnamed monastics ask Gushan and Shishuang what the transmitted matter or phrase is. Zhongfeng Mingben distinguishes speech and writing from what is separately transmitted, calls the latter Chan and another name for the one mind, and elsewhere denies that it is some additional teaching outside mind. The corpus thus supplies a transmission claim, not a warrant to erase its recorded verbal uses.

Senses.Explanation: To appraise and distinguish is to test, sort, or discriminate people, responses, or stated teaching positions. To appraise, sort out, or distinguish; noun constructions name the resulting appraisal or classificatory distinction. The term is attested 266 times in 126 allowlisted texts. Nanyue Jiqi Hongchu's unnamed questioner sets two episodes side by side and asks Nanyue to “please appraise and distinguish” them (兩段不同，試請料揀); Wuyi Yuanlai asks who can sort out a presented conjunction. The same appraisal vocabulary appears in Linji's “Four Selections” (四料揀). The Eye of Humans and Gods records Nanyuan Huiyong asking Fengxue Yanzhao, “the Four Selections—what do the selections select?” (四料揀，料揀何法), and compiler Huiyan Zhizhao begins another exposition with people of middle and lower capacity under that heading. Zhanran Yuancheng calls paired evaluative formulas “the old so-called selection sayings” (古所謂料揀語). The public act, resulting distinction, and named set remain one appraisal-and-selection family; noun and verb grammar alone do not create different lexical things.

Senses.Explanation: Cutting the cat names Nanquan’s canonical action and functions as a later benchmark for decisive conduct. This graph form occurs 278 times in 119 allowlisted texts and is the orthographic counterpart of “cut the cat” (斬猫), not a different event. In the records it abbreviates the public case in which the east and west halls fight over a cat; Nanquan holds it up and says, “If you can speak, I will not cut it,” the assembly gives no answer, and he cuts the cat in two. When Zhaozhou returns, he puts a sandal on his head and leaves; Nanquan says that had he been there, he would have saved the cat. The phrase functions as case narration and title, an object of questions, a subject for verses, and a cited precedent. One public exchange explicitly asks, “Killing living beings is a major precept; why did Nanquan cut the cat and Guizong cut the snake?”; Miyun Yuanwu tells the questioner to repent. Another sermon quotes the rule to rescue animals from killing and asks how Nanquan's cat and Guizong's snake could have been saved. These passages establish the corpus's own precept relation without stating Nanquan's intention. Asked for the case's import, Jueyin answers only, “It takes Nanquan” (須是南泉始得). Dahui reports and rejects students' labels “timely wondrous function” and “great function appears, not retaining rules.”

Senses.Explanation: Cutting off the arm is the bodily action attributed to Huike and raised repeatedly as a named ancestral case. In the Chan record it overwhelmingly names the founding episode in which Shenguang, later named Huike, stands in the snow before Bodhidharma, cuts off his left arm, and places it before him. The lamp account has Bodhidharma say, 'you have now cut off your arm before me; your seeking may be accepted,' and then rename him Huike. Later records compress the episode into paired formulas—'standing in the snow and cutting off the arm,' 'cutting off the arm and pacifying the mind,' or 'face the wall for nine years / cut off the arm and pacify the mind'—and repeatedly reopen it as a public question. Huike asks, 'what did the cutting off of the arm accomplish?' and strikes the staff before leaving the seat. Another is asked why one cuts off an arm to seek the Way if this house style is inherent in everyone; he replies, 'there are many mistaken understandings.' Still another says, 'why cut off an arm and seek elsewhere?' The Chan-specific bend is that Huike's bodily act becomes compact lineage and interview language, quoted, challenged, and criticized across later records. These later uses do not authorize this entry to declare the act a required sacrifice or explain its intention beyond what the accounts say.

Senses.Explanation: The expression denotes every day is a good day in these Chan records. Its wording is "every day is a good day." Yunmen tells the assembly, "I do not ask you about before the fifteenth day; bring me a phrase about after the fifteenth." When the assembly gives no answer, he answers for them: "every day is a good day." The corpus thereafter quotes it as Yunmen's answer, pairs it with "every year is a good year," challenges it in questions, rebukes the recorded questioner who offers it, and expands it in later teaching-seat verse. Its specifically Chan deployment is therefore as Yunmen's public answer and a line later masters openly quote, test, contradict, and comment on; the record supplies no mystical paraphrase for "good."

Senses.PreferredTarget: become clear about mind and see nature
AlternateTargets: make the mind clear and see its nature
understand mind and see nature directly
Senses.Explanation: A fixed pair naming two claimed recognitions: becoming clear about mind and seeing nature. The records use it as an answer, a road, a requested explanation, a direct question, and a target of criticism; they do not give the formula one uniform appraisal. Yongzheng Emperor's verse unpacks the pair through wordplay: “one who clarifies clarifies the mind; one who sees sees its body; seeing nature clarifies the mind-body; clarifying mind sees the nature-principle” (明者明其心，見者見其體；見性明心體，明心見性理). In a raised case, Zhaozhou Congshen answers “what is the road without error?” with “clarifying mind and seeing nature is the road without error” (明心見性是不錯底路). A six-rung-reviewed unnamed questioner asks Konggu Daocheng what clarifying mind and seeing nature is; Konggu answers, “I do not know” (如何是明心見性？不識). The phrase occurs 146 times in 84 allowlisted texts.
Senses.Note: Critical deployments are equally explicit and must remain part of the article. Yongjue Yuanxian places “clarifying mind and seeing nature” beside three other formulas and calls it “putting grit in the eye” (明心見性是眼中著屑). A six-rung-reviewed unnamed attendant asks Yongzheng Emperor for instruction; Yongzheng compares the request to lighting a lamp under water, then asks, “how can mind be clarified? How can nature be seen?” (心如何可明？性如何可見). Poshan Haiming reports someone declaring the formula correct and responds, “what shape is mind? What thing is nature?” (心是何形？性是何物). The exact question “what is clarifying mind and seeing nature?” (如何是明心見性) occurs three times in three texts; “how to clarify mind and see nature” (如何明心見性) occurs twice in two. The entry preserves affirmative and critical deployments without making any single appraisal universal.

Senses.Explanation: The records use light and dark as a coordinated pair in visual conditions, questions, verses, and instructions; their attested relations include distinction, intermingling, reciprocity, and pairing. The graphs themselves mean “light or bright” and “dark.” The record uses the pair for visual conditions and as a coordinated pair in questions, verses, and instructions. Caoshan says, "mountains, rivers, and the great earth: light and dark are each distinct" (山河大地，明暗自殊). Another verse says, "light and dark intermingle—the pivot of killing and bringing to life" (明暗相參殺活機). A transmission verse says, "light and dark do not concern one another; each divides one half" (明暗不相干，彼此分一半). Frequent coordination with "form and emptiness" (明暗色空, 237 occurrences) places both pairs among the things named in the scene.
Senses.Note: Question forms distinguish "light within dark" and "dark within light," then ask about "light and dark together" (明暗雙雙). Ruibai says, "I do not ask about light and dark together; what about the affair facing us right now?" (明暗雙雙即不問，即今覿面事如何). Elsewhere a raised staff is said to contain mountains, rivers, earth, light, dark, form, and emptiness on its tip. The corpus supplies several relations—distinct, intermingling, unconcerned, and together—without reducing them to one abstract theory.

Senses.Explanation: Dahui directly defines dull sinking by contrast: forgetting and falling into a dark cave is called dull sinking, while deliberate mental succession is called agitation. Literally, dim or dull sinking . Dahui supplies the corpus's clearest direct description: forgetting or blanking out falls into the ghost cave beneath Black Mountain, and the teachings call this dull sinking; he contrasts it with deliberate attention, whose thought-consciousness flies about and is called agitation. Other records label dull sinking “not good” beside “binding thought strays from the real” and pair it repeatedly with agitation as the two named conditions found in the Chan hall. The Chan record also bends the inherited fault-category against simple rejection: Gaofeng says the four graphs “dull sinking and agitation” are themselves buddha-nature, Daodu calls the pair one's place for establishing life, and Dahui tells Lü Juren that whether dull-sunk or agitated, it is still only Lü Juren. The deviation lies in this combination of exact diagnosis, fixed pairing, and masters' refusal to locate the named condition outside the person who reports it.

Senses.Explanation: A reduplicated description: brightly evident (昭昭) and keenly numinous or responsive (靈靈), hence "bright and numinous." It occurs 240 times in 101 allowlisted texts. Chinese Chan records frequently use the phrase while rejecting its identification with one's true self. One address asks, "if you recognize the bright and numinous as your reality, why does it no longer remain bright and numinous when you are asleep?" (汝若認昭昭靈靈是汝真實，為甚麼瞌睡時又不成昭昭靈靈). The same address gives a direct account: the bright and numinous arises because colors, sounds, scents, and other things before one are distinguished; without those things it is like "turtle fur and rabbit horns" (昭昭靈靈，祇因前塵色聲香等法而有分別；若無前塵，同於龜毛兔角). Another record states that the fault lies in taking the presently bright and numinous as correct, since it "arises dependent on encountered objects" (昭昭靈靈乃是緣境而有). These are the corpus's explicit predicates, not an entry-level theory of consciousness.
Senses.Note: The phrase also appears in first-person retrospective description. One unnamed interlocutor says he was still "hazy and indistinct, bright and numinous, and had not yet obtained stability" (恍恍惚惚、昭昭靈靈，也未得個安穩); a later account says that this bright-and-numinous condition could not be made to arise and could not be found after a subsequent event. A verse asks, "what is the bright and numinous? By the time you blink, it has already been missed" (昭昭靈靈是什麼？眨得眼來已蹉過). Productive forms include "the bright-and-numinous one" (the nominal “bright-and-numinous one” form, 14 occurrences in 12 texts) and "recognize the bright and numinous" (認昭昭靈靈, 21 in 16). Eight texts preserve the sleep challenge's wording "the bright and numinous is your reality" (昭昭靈靈是汝真實).

Senses.Explanation: “what is it?” or “what is this?” It questions an object just indicated, a person, a place, or a phrase under discussion. It questions an object just indicated, a person, a place, or a phrase under discussion. Mazu asks about the wild ducks, "what is this?" and Baizhang answers, "wild ducks" (是什麼？野鴨子). Foyan Qingyuan points to a raised whisk and asks, "what is it—can you hear?" (是什麼，還聞麼), and Yunmen repeatedly summons his attendant, receives "yes," and asks, "what is it?" (是什麼). With a following noun the same interrogative asks "what person?" (是什麼人) or "what thing?" (是什麼物). In Chan records this bare question is repeatedly attached to a visible object, a named person, or a live exchange; the entry does not replace the question with an answer the passage does not give.

Senses.Explanation: In public interviews it rejects a proposed connection between Cuifeng Chongxian's words and the matter asked about: after an unnamed monk identifies Cuifeng Chongxian with an earlier house, the answer is "what connection does that have?" (有什麼交涉). The phrase also appears in prose criticism. The Blue Cliff Record says that treating Mazu's left and right eyes as the sun-face and moon-face has "what connection?" and that such readers have missed the old matter. Elsewhere Juehua Puzhao asks, "if lips, voice, and appearances are taken as oneself, what connection does that have?" (若以唇吻聲色以為自己，有什麼交涉). In another exchange, an unnamed monk himself uses the question after the answer "the graph 'by means of'" (以字), and receives "the graph 'eight'" (八字), a spoken play on similar-sounding graph names. Zen bends an ordinary request for relevance into a compact interview verdict: the reply or explanation offered has not connected with the exchange.

Senses.Explanation: Wooden figures appear as insensible constructed bodies that walk, sing, or answer only in the records’ impossible images and contrasts. The wooden figure is an ordinarily inert human-shaped figure that Chan records repeatedly make act: it beckons, answers, speaks, dances, embroiders, and claps a board in the clouds. The recurrent bend is the impossible agent, often paired with the barren woman, rather than a separate named person. Hongzhi Zhengjue pairs the wooden figure beckoning with the barren woman nodding. Dengzhou Zhongdu states the contrast most sharply: the wooden figure always replies, while one with nature cannot speak. Cian Shoujing says that through the scorching summer retreat the wooden figure's dirty flow does not cease. Ruibai Mingxue makes the wooden figure embroider a flowered cap at midnight while the barren woman breaks a mirror at dawn. Wuyi Yuanlai says the wooden figure rising to dance is not extraordinary, and Qingshan Shoulong answers a question about an auspicious sign with the wooden figure clapping a board in the clouds. Wuyin Zijing makes a wooden figure divine an auspicious sign at the turn of the year. Tian'an Sheng separately uses 'carved wooden man' as a disparaging person-epithet; that different referent does not prove the stock figure's physical construction; the many human actions remain predicates of that figure, not additional senses.

Senses.Explanation: The wooden buddha is a materially wooden image in Danxia Tianran’s burning case and in the fixed contrast that a wooden buddha does not pass through fire. Literally a "buddha" (佛) made of "wood" (木): a "wooden buddha," attested 663 times in 181 allowlisted texts. The principal recorded case says Danxia, encountering severe cold at Huilin Temple, took a wooden buddha and burned it. When the superintendent rebuked him, Danxia stirred the ashes and said he was looking for relics. The superintendent replied, "How could a wooden buddha have relics?" Danxia said, "Since it has no relics, bring two more honored ones to burn" (木佛何有舍利，既無舍利，更請兩尊來燒). The phrase also appears in the fixed line "a wooden buddha does not pass through fire" (木佛不度火), alongside a clay buddha not passing through water and a gold buddha not passing through a furnace.
Senses.Note: Later masters repeatedly raise the Danxia case and ask why the superintendent's eyebrows fell out. Recorded answers include "a thief does not raid a poor household" (賊不打貧兒家), "one person transmits a falsehood; ten thousand transmit it as fact" (一人傳虗，萬人傳實), "Zhang drinks the wine and Li gets drunk," and "the cat knows how to climb a tree." The ten occurrences of "What is a wooden buddha?" (the question “What is a wooden Buddha?”) and these later questions retain the literal image as their headword; the texts do not replace it with an abstract category.

Senses.Explanation: The wood-rooster is an impossible verse-image whose recorded predicates make it crow at midnight, carry an egg, sweat, announce dawn, and act where no sound is heard; one comparison also says a gaunt person looked like it. The corpus gives no manufacturing predicate and does not narrate the inherited cock-training story, so the relation of the wood modifier remains unresolved rather than being asserted as construction material. In the transmitted public case, an unnamed questioner asks Fengxue Yanzhao, “The ancient tune has no tone or rhyme; how can it be harmonized?” Fengxue replies, “The wooden rooster crows at midnight; the straw dog barks at dawn” (木雞啼子夜，芻狗吠天明). Later masters repeat the line as answers to such questions as “What is the precise meaning?” and explicitly say, “where the wooden rooster crows there is no sound” (木雞啼處無聲). Other records make it announce dawn, run carrying an egg, or sweat in summer. The Chan deviation is this use of an inert crafted bird as a recurring public-interview answer and impossible-event agent, often paired with the straw dog; the entry records the uses without resolving them into a hidden teaching.

Senses.Explanation: A wooden horse is repeatedly assigned actions that an inert carved horse does not ordinarily perform. In the Complete Book of the Five Lamps, Fachang Yiyu cooks it with its hair on, Changlu Daohe sends it chasing the wind as far as India, Zaitian Yu has it neigh in spring, and Foyin Liaoyuan has it meet spring in snow. In the Continuation of the Lamp Record, Lianhuafeng Xiang answers “A sound” when asked about Yunmen's wooden horse neighing. Shiyu Mingfang brings it back neighing in wind, Ruibai Mingxue places its summer cold beside a stone ox's winter warmth, and Tianzhu Chonghui uses its neigh in a public answer about the lineage matter. The corpus often pairs it with a mud ox or stone ox, but these pairings do not turn it into a different object. Nor does the contrast license an imported explanation about no-mind: the entry records these exact predicates and settings without deciding what hidden lesson they signify. The headword occurs 801 times in 217 allowlist texts.

Senses.Explanation: Not yet; not there yet: in the Chan corpus this is especially frequent as a teaching-seat verdict on a reply, shout, verse, or claimed understanding. The exact words (未在) also retain their ordinary temporal force. Zhaozhou Congshen says, 'Not there yet; say more' (未在更道). Gufeng Xiu tells Wanshan Zhengning, 'You have got it, but you are still not there yet' (你也得，只是未在). Fushi Tongxian likewise says, 'Not there yet; say more,' while Tianyin Yuanxiu uses the phrase to reject an attempted deception. Guangxiao Huijue says, 'Even if you reached a thousand years, you still would not yet be old' (直至千歲也未在). Thus the corpus deploys one phrase both as an evaluative reply and in ordinary statements of something not yet reached or completed.
Senses.Note: The exact headword occurs 1,247 times in 255 allowlisted texts. Searches found no self-defining formula equivalent to 'the so-called not-there-yet,' 'it is called not-there-yet,' or 'what is meant by not-there-yet?' The repeated collocation 'not there yet; say more' (未在更道) occurs 72 times in 39 texts, while 'you have got it, but are still not there yet' (你也得，只是未在) displays a further recorded shape. The subject left incomplete is sometimes named, as in 'the matter beyond is not there yet' (向上事未在).

Senses.Explanation: This is the final formidable barrier or severe checkpoint in a sequence of testing, something speakers say must be reached, passed through, or personally arrived at even after an earlier understanding. ‘Final’ marks its position and (牢) marks its formidable resistance; neither word by itself supplies the whole expression. The records speak of passing through or penetrating it, and use it as a severe last check. Yuan'an, after listing a series of named cases, calls "this whole tangle" (者一落索) the final locked barrier and criticizes estimating it through cognitive calculation. Juelang says even someone who has understood "this affair" but has "not passed through the final locked barrier" (未透末後牢關) can still mistake a shadow for a head. Yulin asks, "how many people have passed the final locked barrier?" (末後牢關幾人透得). Other formulations say it is "not measurable by humans or gods" (人天莫測) and "not understood by a thousand sages" (千聖不曉).

Senses.Explanation: The “original face” is the face a person is challenged to recognize or investigate before acquired distinctions settle the answer. The records repeatedly preserve Huineng’s question to Ming: when not thinking good and not thinking evil, “what is your original face?” (不思善不思惡，正恁麼時，如何是上座本來面目). Tianyin Yuanxiu quotes that question and the instruction to turn the light back upon one’s own original face. Guanyin Congxian deliberately removes the four words “original face” from Huineng’s demand and asks whether the alteration still belongs to Huineng’s lineage. Dahui Zonggao pairs the phrase with one’s home-ground scenery and says that the original face itself has never been deluded or awakened, locating delusion and awakening in a person’s momentary thought. Yulin Tongxiu tells the emperor to investigate the phrase in activity as well as stillness. Zhuanyu Guanheng equates the six sense-fields, when recollected without discrimination, with one’s own original face. Miyun Yuanwu urges recognition of it amid ordinary bending and looking up, then answers his own renewed question with a shout and a spatial saying. Yushan Shangsi makes his staff leap into a hall, knock down the person of no rank, and smash the original face in a deliberately extravagant hall address. Across these uses the phrase is a question, an object of investigation and recognition, an explicit equation, and a target of corrective wordplay; no single verbal reply is made its universal definition.
Senses.Note: Exact frozen-corpus count: 1,493 hits in 285 files representing 281 independent works. Seven curated occurrences from seven independent works meet the depth floor. Parallel versions of Tianyin’s record and Yulin’s exchange in later anthologies were not counted as additional evidence.

Senses.Explanation: In Chan interview and instruction, the compound names the matter proper to the person rather than an item borrowed from authoritative predecessors. Zhaozhou Congshen says a lineage teacher must receive people with it, while an unnamed monk’s question about it is answered by pointing the matter back to the questioner. Baichi Yuanshuo places inquiry, eating, bodily functions, and ordinary activity within one’s own matter but still demands that it be stated directly. Danxia Dangui warns that merely speaking of it has already made it extraneous, and Xiuyelin defines it as where one’s own root-destiny comes to rest. Bai Juyi challenges a scripture-reciting monk about a cleric’s own matter. Yuanwu Keqin says that even cloudless clarity in it cannot simply be let pass. Nanquan Puyuan likewise demands it directly without pointing east or west. Across these uses, the phrase marks what cannot be outsourced or replaced by discursive display, while remaining a demand made in concrete encounters rather than an imported abstract teaching.
Senses.Note: Exact frozen-corpus count: 975 hits in 205 files and 201 independent works. Eight exact witnesses across seven independent works meet the packet floor; the work-based count prevents two volumes of one work from being treated as independent sources.

SearchAliases: the case one is working on
Senses.Explanation: The saying, question, or public case singled out as a person's main subject of inquiry. The possessives and verbal predicates in later Chinese Chan records make this local use concrete. Jiexian tells a hall leader to know each person's own word or saying under primary investigation; another passage says that not knowing it leaves the leader without a way to act. Zhanran Yuancheng tells people to place the selected saying before their eyes, Konggu Daocheng says to raise it, and Langting Jingting warns Qianyun that he has dropped one line of it behind his head. The compound can take 'public case' or 'word, saying, conversational thread' after it, and can itself be said to be broken through. Yongzheng asks, 'What is primary investigation?' and gives one particular example: if one trusts the gate of recollecting buddha, investigate who is recollecting buddha. Wuyi Yuanlai says that the Chan house relies on primary investigation and that when it breaks through it is like the moon reflected in a thousand rivers. These predicates describe the assigned subject and the act of investigating it without turning the term into a named system.
Senses.Note: The corpus has 232 matches in 100 files. The expanded phrase 'word or saying under primary investigation' has eighty-nine matches in fifty files; 'raise the primary investigation' has twenty matches in fifteen; 'public case of primary investigation' has four in four; and 'one line of primary investigation' has three in three. One text has the only direct 'what is primary investigation?' formula and its own example; two texts use 'the so-called primary investigation.' The phrase is strongly possessive: texts say 'each person's,' 'one's own,' 'the one assigned,' and 'not knowing his.' No evidence supports treating it as an untranslated foreign object or as a person-specific sense.

Senses.Explanation: A person's native ground is that person's own ground, most often deployed in the fixed phrase “native-ground scenery.” Records say to recognize one's original face and tread one's native-ground scenery, warn that wrong roads conceal each person's native-ground scenery, and ask that it be illuminated or fully seen through. A preface says the records return to the person's own native-ground scenery; teaching-seat records place it in bowing, turning, daily activity, or the lifting of a staff. The corpus treats this ground and its scenery as something belonging to each person and subject to public demand and display. It does not define it as a metaphysical substrate.

Senses.Explanation: Chan records use “original landscape” for what is disclosed as one's own, often pairing it with the original face and contrasting its presence with seeking outside, clinging to purity, or remaining blocked by distinctions. Yuanwu Keqin and Dahui Zonggao place the expression beside the original face and say it is present through ordinary modes of activity or belongs to each person. Mi'an Xianjie says it suddenly appears when inquiry reaches the end of explanations, while Tianyin Yuanxiu says paired categories such as illumination and function appear upon this landscape. Jie'an Wujin's verse says it was never sought outside and is not absent in walking, sitting, or lying down. Zhongfeng Mingben provocatively says dullness and distraction are wholly this landscape, but immediately warns that merely accepting that formulation is another error. Sanyi Mingyu likewise denies that settling into undifferentiated purity is the original landscape.

Senses.Explanation: The mind identified in a record as original or fundamental. The word occurs 748 times in 157 allowlisted texts. The Mirror Record says mind has no form, color, root, lodging, arising, extinction, or observable contemplation; if something observable can be carried out, that text assigns it to reception, conception, activity, and discrimination rather than original mind. The Platform Record pairs recognizing one’s original mind with seeing one’s original nature (若識自本心，見自本性). Other records say it is neither joined nor separate, reject the claim that it first needs stillness, and place original nature and original mind together. These are differing corpus predicates of one textual term, not a menu of interpretations.
Senses.Note: Primary corpus-wide original-mind sense. Cross-check original nature (本性), true mind, and no-mind as neighboring entries with their own predicates. No single imported metaphysical definition is imposed.

Senses.Explanation: One's nature as it is from the outset. Chan records repeatedly use 'see one's own original nature' beside 'recognize one's own original mind.' The Platform Record makes seeing it the distinction between remaining outside the gate and entering, and describes it as not arising or extinguishing. The Mirror Record says that original nature has no difference and is not obtained because of conduct. These are the texts' recorded descriptions; the English should preserve the plain noun phrase rather than substitute a later explanatory system. The omitted collocation "original nature empty" (本性空) occurs forty times in thirty texts, but it has more than one syntax. Twenty-seven occurrences in twenty-five texts belong to the fixed line, "understand body and mind, original nature empty; how would this person differ from buddha?" (了得身心本性空，斯人與佛何殊別). A later Chan address raises that line and immediately comments, "the buddha-body is neither real nor empty; buddha-as-appearance is not appearance" (佛身無實亦無虗，佛幻非幻). The Source-Mirror Record gives a separate explicit definition: "as for original-nature empty, it is the own-nature clear-and-clean mind; original nature is own nature; empty means clear and clean" (本性空者，即是自性清淨心；本性即自性；空，即清淨義).
Senses.Note: The corpus has 667 matches in 152 files. The compound occurs in direct corrections, statements linking it with original mind, and descriptions of it as without difference. Six matches in six files explicitly pair original nature and original mind. The evidence supports one corpus-wide sense. The forty "original nature empty" matches are therefore not treated as forty copies of one bare equation. The fixed body-and-mind verse, the Source-Mirror definition, and the critical construction "rely on original-nature empty" (恃本性空, two occurrences in two texts) are distinct deployments. One Source-Mirror list criticizes people who follow binding impulses while relying on original-nature empty, alongside people who cling to coverings and wrongly add removal and severing (或隨結使而恃本性空，或執纏蓋而妄加除斷). Each predicate is reported as that text's wording rather than generalized beyond its occurrence.

Senses.Explanation: “Fundamentally, not one thing” occurs as assertion, verse line, and interview question; the records place it beside what can be presented, displayed, or investigated. Literally, ‘fundamentally, not one thing.’ The exact shorter phrase occurs 34 times in 30 allowlisted texts. Yangshan's record predicates it of one's own mind-source and contrasts immediate recognition there with gradual certification through myriad deeds. Yinyuan Longqi says there is fundamentally not one thing to present. Yulin Tongxiu places three heads, six arms, a thousand hands, and a thousand eyes beside the statement that fundamentally there is not one thing, while also saying the myriad forms run crosswise. In a public exchange, Miyin is asked what the student investigates if fundamentally there is not one thing and answers, ‘take yourself out.’ Huineng's longer ‘originally, not one thing’ is a close morphological family form, preserved as family evidence rather than counted as the exact headword. The shorter phrase is thus a predicate, verse line, and publicly tested proposition, not an imported metaphysical definition.

The recorded answer is, "because not one thing can be obtained, it is called complete" (因無一物可得，所以說具足). A prose criticism asks, "complete from the start—who picks it up or puts it down?" (本自具足，阿誰拈起放下). Other records set the phrase against outside acquisition: living beings are complete from the start and "do not depend on seeking outside" (不假外求). The Zen deployment therefore joins the phrase to the nature, direct questioning, the impossibility of picking it up or putting it down, and explicit refusal of outside acquisition; this entry reports those statements without converting them into a system of cultivation.

Senses.Explanation: The compound occurs 381 times in 145 allowed texts as a verdict on a person, answer, explanation, or speech, and as a verb for making such material up. A late direct naming statement criticizes assigning difficult cases to newcomers without matching the person and the case: after comparing it to fitting a square timber into a round hole and losing people's time, Jiexian says, 'To call it fabricated—is that not fitting?' (謂之杜撰，不亦宜乎). A playful assembly exchange separates the graphs as a surname and personal name: the staff says, 'My surname is Du, given name Zhuan'; asked why it is called 'fabricated,' it answers, 'If the elder did not fabricate, how could he spend all day talking about Zhang and Li?' (長老若不杜撰，如何終日與人說張說李). Dahui uses the word self-deprecatingly when he says, 'I have not read Guo Xiang's explanation or the various commentators' explanations; I only rely on my own fabrication to explain your silence' (我也不曾看郭象解并諸家注解，只據我杜撰說破爾這默然). The stock rebuke 'fabricated elder' (杜撰長老) occurs 68 times in 40 texts, often in the fuller comparison 'fabricated elders are like hemp and millet'—that is, extremely numerous (杜撰長老如麻似粟). 'Fabricated Chan fellow' (杜撰禪和) likewise appears as a verdict on a respondent, while 'fabricated conjectural talk' (杜撰臆說) names speech. These are grammatical deployments of one shared judgment; the texts do not establish a distinct sense from the proper name Du Mo, whose 18 hits refer to a person or to being silent.
Senses.Note: No corpus witness derives the headword from the person Du Mo. Those proper-name and silence occurrences were excluded rather than used to repeat an external etymology. The alternate 'bogus' is reserved for personal epithets such as 'bogus elder' or 'bogus Chan fellow'; 'fabricated' remains the broad target for speech, explanations, and claims.

Senses.Explanation: East Mountain walks on water is Yunmen’s compact saying, repeatedly cited, questioned, and commented upon as a named case. Yunmen Wenyan's fixed answer to ‘What is the buddhas' place of emergence?’ is ‘East Mountain walks on water’ (如何是諸佛出身處。師曰。東山水上行). The phrase occurs 290 times in 131 allowlisted texts. Later masters keep this impossible-looking sentence in public circulation as a named case-saying rather than using it as an ordinary report about a mountain. Yuanwu Keqin repeats Yunmen's exchange and gives a different answer to the same question: ‘The fragrant wind comes from the south; the halls give rise to a slight coolness.’ Xiatang Huiyuan is asked directly for the saying's import and answers, ‘The thirty-first day of the first month; no need to choose a date.’ Chaozong receives the same question in a hall exchange. Juebao Qing quotes Yunmen and then makes the sentence the opening line of his own verse. Tianran Shi titles a verse with Yunmen's saying and closes it by saying that the conversational thread has been transmitted to the present. The corpus therefore establishes what the phrase is and how it is used, but supplies no stable decoding of how or why the mountain walks.

Senses.Explanation: A withered or dead tree. Chan speakers use its cold, apparently lifeless condition as a test image, then make it do what such a tree cannot: grow branches, bloom, roar like a lion, or carry hidden news of warmth. Damei Fachang describes himself as a damaged dead tree unchanged by repeated springs; the hermit in the burned-hut case says a dead tree against a cold cliff has no warmth through three winters. Yunfeng Zudeng warns that treating cold ash and dead wood as the old masters' final position falls into a one-color understanding. The phrase therefore keeps the ordinary dead tree visible while public sayings test whether stillness has been mistaken for completion.
