Senses.Explanation: The lantern is a concrete hall object that the records repeatedly make the subject of questions, answers, speech, movement, and comparison. A lantern is the visible light-holder that Chan records repeatedly turn into a public-stage object and impossible participant. The word occurs 1,681 times in 293 allowlisted texts. Dizang Guichen points to one; in another exchange an unnamed monk names the lantern as form and asks which is mind, and Longji Shaoxiu answers that the lantern is mind. Guishan Lingyou answers a question about the ancestral teacher's coming from the west by pointing to the lantern and saying, 'a very good lantern.' The same object becomes a stock participant beside the exposed pillar: Dongshan Xiaocong says it dozes while the pillar is alert; Feiyin Tongrong makes lanterns dance while pillars knit their brows; Huitang Zuxin puts the three gates atop a lantern; and Fachang Yu says the lantern exposes sealed-mouth sitters. These are attributed answers and personifications; the records continue to name the same lantern without supplying another referent.

Senses.Explanation: To burn incense and bow is a public monastic act of reverence, ordered in hall routines and conspicuous when a visitor omits it. Occurrences.AttributionNote: Zhongfeng Mingben, in (天目中峰廣錄) (Extensive Record of Zhongfeng at Tianmu), says the handle is gone while the game remains unfinished.

Occurrences.Kwic: 已有爛柯樵子本傳。前頌雪峯末後句。亦有挂樹壺公本傳
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Wansong Xingxiu, in (萬松老人評唱天童覺和尚頌古從容庵錄) (Wansong's Commentary in the Book of Serenity), identifies the original Lanke woodcutter account.

Senses.Explanation: The rotted axe handle is the records’ time-lapse allusion: a woodcutter watches an immortal chess game and returns after his handle has decayed. The Chan corpus does not usually retell that background in full; it repeatedly names its visible pieces. Fang'an Xian says that when the game ends no one knows where to go, leaving “the Lanke man” sorrowful in the empty mountain (局罷不知何處去，空山惆悵爛柯人). Yuan'an Feng repeats, “the Lanke woodcutter doubts there is a road” (爛柯樵子疑無路). Yongjue Yuanxian lists taking up “the Lanke axe” beside propping a broken-legged pot, while Zhongfeng Mingben says the axe handle has rotted and vanished but the game is not yet finished. Wansong Xingxiu explicitly says that an earlier verse already has the original account of the Lanke woodcutter (已有爛柯樵子本傳). The Zen-specific bend is this repeated use of the rotted handle, woodcutter, unfinished game, and lost road as a compact allusion in case verse and formal speech. The outside story remains an inherited historical lead except where the Chan text names these elements directly.

Senses.Note: Mount Lanke occurs as a compound place-name in several allowlisted texts. One exact place witness is sufficient to establish the distinct referent; the entry makes no claim about the mountain's outside history.

Occurrences.Kwic: 爛柯山雨似傾盆，龜嶺峯額頭汗出
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Xiatang Huiyuan, in (瞎堂慧遠禪師廣錄) (Extensive Record of Chan Master Xiatang Huiyuan), names rain on Mount Lanke.

Senses.Explanation: The same graph pair also forms the proper place-name Mount Lanke. Xiatang Huiyuan says that rain on Mount Lanke pours like a basin while Turtle Ridge's forehead sweats. This geographic referent is not the rotted axe handle or its woodcutter, even though the place-name inherits the same graphs; it therefore has its own sense.

Occurrences.Kwic: 一句父母未生前
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Juelang Daosheng, in the Complete Record of Chan Master Tianjie Juelang Daosheng (天界覺浪盛禪師全錄), presents one phrase as “before one’s parents gave birth.”

Senses.Explanation: Chan records turn the time before one’s birth into a pointed interview location from which a person’s original face, identity, or decisive word is demanded. Xueyan Zuqin asks what it ultimately is before one’s parents gave birth. An identified lay questioner surnamed Wan turns his surname into a challenge about what he was called before that time. A verse attributed to Huineng answers with ‘originally not a single thing,’ while Tianyin Yuanxiu reports the phrase as a question repeatedly assigned for investigation. Other records keep the answers concrete and discordant: an unnamed monastic asks for the original face, Yushan Shangsi pairs before-birth with a stone mortar fried in oil and after-birth with a steelyard weight dipped in snow, and Zhe’an Jingfan says that recognizing the person in a crowd also reveals this original face. These witnesses support the recurring temporal challenge without promoting any one answer into its definition.

Senses.Explanation: The clause asks about the time before one's parents were born; the six exact witnesses use it as a teaching contrast, a question, and a measure of what is already complete. Yuanwu Keqin sets 'before father and mother were born' (父母未生已前) against 'after father and mother were born' and the completed body. Gulin Qingmao says that before one's parents were born there was already a line for repaying beneficence (父母未生已前，便有報德酧恩一句). Taiyuan Fu asks Gushan where the nostrils were before one's parents were born (父母未生已前，鼻孔在什麼處). Chushi Fanqi asks how the time before one's parents were born compares with the current occasion (父母未生已前，何似這個時節). Cijue Puyin asks a respondent where he traveled before his parents were born and strikes him as he prepares to answer (父母未生已前，在甚麼處行履). Yinyuan Longqi says that, as for recommendation, it was already finished before one's parents were born (父母未生已前薦拔已竟). The corpus thus bends the temporal clause into a recurring interview boundary; these witnesses do not supply one uniform answer.

Senses.Explanation: A tight barrier or secured pass: a checkpoint represented as shut against passage and therefore as something to hold, close, break, or get through. In Luopu Yuanan's recorded formula, the last phrase first reaches this barrier, which shuts the critical crossing so that neither ordinary nor sage passes. Yuanwu Keqin repeats the same formula. The records also make the image operational: Puming holds the barrier shut through a ninety-day restriction period and then breaks it open; Baiyu Jingsi holds it with no inside or outside; Juelang Daosheng asks for the phrase that gets free of it. When an unnamed monk asks Tianyin Yuanxiu what the barrier is, Tianyin answers, "Break through it and come meet me." The Zen-loaded phrase is thus not merely a difficult obstacle: it names the deliberately secured final checkpoint that a named record speaker can hold fast and a respondent must break through.
Senses.Note: The frozen allowlisted corpus has 670 exact hits in 209 files representing 207 works. Seven anchors from seven works cover the inherited formula, a later quotation of that formula, breaking, holding, getting free, and a direct question asking what the barrier is. The compact form "final tight barrier" and action collocations were used as discovery leads, not as separate senses. The object remains one barrier across these actions; differences between holding, closing, breaking, and passing it are deployments rather than different things.

Senses.Explanation: Herding an ox is an action and image, while Oxherding sequences are named picture-or-verse sets and remain a different object. The farm action of tending or herding an ox. In Chan records this action is repeatedly deployed as a comparison. When Mazu Daoyi asks Shigong Huizang what he is doing, Shigong answers that he is herding the ox; he says that whenever it enters the grass he seizes its nose and pulls it back (一回入草去，驀鼻拽將回), and Mazu replies that he truly knows how to herd it (子真牧牛). Baizhang Huaihai compares his handling of an addressee to an oxherd who holds a staff and prevents the animal from trespassing on crops (如牧牛人執杖視之，不令犯他苗稼). Yunqi Zhuhong's preface traces the expression to the comparison of watching an ox with a staff (譬如牧牛，執杖視之，不令縱逸，犯人苗稼), while Guting Shanjian explicitly says that its illustrated use compares the ox with the wild restlessness of human nature (夫謂牧牛者，譬人性之狂掉也). Yunyan Tianyou also attacks the inherited image: after the nose-rope breaks, his verse asks what excrement or wind remains to herd (牧甚屎屁). Zen bends the ordinary action into a publicly tested comparison, while the last witness shows that masters could also overturn it.

Senses.Note: Picture-and-verse and verse-only forms are variants of the same kind of titled sequence, not separate senses.

Senses.Explanation: A child who tends cattle: a herdboy, cowherd boy, or oxherd boy. The term occurs 334 times in 139 allowlisted texts, and Chan records concentrate its distinctive use in oxherding songs, pictures, public questions, and verse. In Puming's ten oxherding verses, the boy holds the grass rope without slack and works all day; later, when there is no ox anywhere, the boy is idle, claps, sings under the moon, and still returns to “one further barrier.” Fenyang Shanzhao's Herdboy Song says that the boy does not copy texts or read a single graph, yet unfolds countless scrolls and handles question and answer. Asked “what is the herdboy's song?” Xuefeng Yicun dances and leaves the teaching hall. Jiashan Lingquan Ziying answers “who is the person within Jiashan's scene?” with “the herdboy sings in the open fields; the woodcutter laughs deep in the clouds.” Dizang Shouen, Danxia Zichun, Hongzhi Zhengjue, and Furong Daokai further place the boy in teaching-seat and portrait verse. Zen bends the ordinary cattle-tending child into a recurring actor in staged ox-and-herder sequences, direct interview answers, and teaching-seat songs; different stages of the same herdboy-and-ox deployment are not separate senses.

Senses.Explanation: The rhinoceros, chiefly as the animal demanded back from Yanguan Qian's broken rhinoceros-fan case. Yanguan calls for the fan; when his attendant says it is broken, Yanguan demands, ‘Then bring me back the rhinoceros’ (扇子既破。還我犀牛兒來). Later speakers repeatedly raise, verse, answer, and dispute this exchange. Yinyuan Longqi says that once the fan is broken, its head and horns are fully displayed (犀牛扇既破。頭角已全彰). In Shiyu Mingfang's exchange, an unnamed monk claims that Yanguan wrongly called the fan a rhinoceros; Shiyu demands what else it should be called and sets a community fine if the questioner cannot say. Asked what the rhinoceros itself is like, Feiyin Tongrong answers, ‘Its head and horns stand high’ (頭角崢嶸). Baishan Dekai's verse puts down a rabbit-horn staff and picks up the rhinoceros fan; Xuefeng Huikong says that when the fan breaks, the rhinoceros remains; and Pin Jixiang depicts the rhinoceros falling into water when Yanguan uses the fan. The animal-name is thus repeatedly pulled out of its broken fan and handled as a public case-object. The texts do not supply one symbolic meaning for the rhinoceros.

Senses.Explanation: The mysterious or profound purport: a hidden or difficult-to-reach gist that is asked about, sought, recognized, or awakened to. The records do not replace it with one stable explanatory proposition. An unnamed monk asks Guizong Zhichang what it is; after saying that no one can understand it and that directing oneself toward it departs from it, Guizong asks, "Who is seeking the mysterious purport?" Other questioners receive deliberately different replies from Zhaozhou Congshen and Zhangyi Daoqin. Jiashan Shanhui gives a reciprocal formulation in which the interlocutor's mysterious purport is Jiashan's tongue and Jiashan's is the interlocutor's tongue. A verse attributed to Sengcan warns that failing to recognize it makes quieting thoughts futile, while a lamp biography says Zhongshan Tancui greatly awakened to it. The Zen bend is the public question itself: this purport is repeatedly demanded from a named respondent, yet the recorded answers redirect the demand rather than reducing it to a portable statement.
Senses.Note: The frozen allowlisted corpus has 662 exact hits in 181 files representing 178 works. Seven exact anchors cover three public questions, Guizong Zhichang's own return question, Jiashan Shanhui's reciprocal formulation, a verse warning, and a biographical awakening. Different answers and grammatical roles remain deployments of one sought purport, not separate master-specific senses.

Senses.Explanation: A named Caodong road or course: the first graph qualifies the road as dark, hidden, or mysterious, without establishing a physically dark roadway. The allowlisted corpus records 268 occurrences across 116 texts. Dongshan Liangjie himself names it as one of his Three Roads: ‘I have three roads for receiving people: bird course, hidden road, extending the hands’ (我有三路接人，鳥道玄路展手). The compound then moves through independently attributable teaching-seat uses rather than one fixed explanation. Fenyang Shanzhao asks his assembly, ‘What is the hidden road? Is there anyone who understands? Tell Fenyang’ (作麼生是玄路／與汾陽說看). Hongzhi Zhengjue says, ‘One step secretly shifted, the hidden road turns; the whole body released, the aeon-vessel is empty’ (一步密移玄路轉，全身放下劫壺空). Xisou Shaotan puts it at the grass tips—‘penetrate the hidden road’—while Xueguan Zhiyin says a spirit horse may gallop and a numinous crane soar, ‘crossing the hidden road freely, without touching the bird course’ (玄路縱橫，不觸鳥道). Touzi Yiqing says that even after host and guest and spoken question and answer have been established, raising the hidden road from the side is still only halfway (問答言陳，仍玄路旁提為唱／猶在半途). Shanfeng Xian turns it into teaching-hall action: ‘Holding the white staff crosswise, open the hidden road’ (橫拈白棒開玄路). The longer golden-lock family is locally explicit rather than a gloss of the bare road: Caoshan Benji says ordinary feelings and holy views are ‘the golden-lock hidden road’ and must be interchanged, while Yongjue Yuanxian calls exhaustion without the ability to turn the same compound. The Chan bend is therefore the conversion of a hidden or mysterious road into a named Caodong category that can receive, turn, be penetrated, be crossed, be opened, be appraised as halfway, and enter the golden-lock compound. None of those predicates makes it a physically dark roadway or licenses replacing every occurrence with ‘the Way.’
Senses.Note: The English road/path/way/route forms are retrieval aliases for one attested road-or-course sense, not a display menu and not a global equation between every occurrence of the graph for road and the English phrase ‘the Way.’ Five earlier rows were removed because the headword occurred in an anonymous monk's question or report while the named master only answered or examined it. The retained primary rows put the headword in the named speaker's own turn. The golden-lock rows are nested lexical family evidence and do not buy primary depth.

Senses.Explanation: The hidden barrier is a gate to be opened, penetrated, or locked, and it appears in interview questions and barrier imagery across the records. The expression occurs 593 times in 212 allowlisted texts. One penetrates, passes, strikes, breaks, or kicks it down. Speakers ask about ‘the higher hidden barrier,’ call for one who has passed it, and ask publicly how it is passed. One discourse warns that ‘clinging to the hidden barrier’ loses the larger function; another says those not through it often construe Bodhidharma’s wall-gazing merely as facing a wall. Zen bends the gate into a public-interview checkpoint, but no corpus-wide sentence defines fixed content behind it.

Senses.Explanation: ‘Old Master Wang’ is Nanquan Puyuan’s recurrent self-designation and the label under which later records quote him. Literally, Wang, old master or teacher. In the Chan record this is Nanquan Puyuan's recurrent self-designation and the label later writers use when quoting or commenting on him. The compound occurs 760 times in 193 allowlisted texts. Nanquan's biography identifies him as Puyuan, a son of the Wang family of Zhengzhou, and immediately records him saying, 'Old Master Wang is selling himself; is there anyone who will buy?' Other self-references include the water-buffalo saying, 'Old Master Wang has raised a water buffalo since he was young,' asking Zhaozhou, 'Where is Old Master Wang at fault?' and saying that Old Master Wang, unlike Mazu, does not say 'mind is buddha' but 'not mind, not buddha, not a thing.' Later comments preserve the title while explicitly naming Nanquan.
Senses.Note: This is a person-title, not a generic entry for every teacher surnamed Wang. The explicit biography and repeated Nanquan section headings fix its principal referent. The full name 'Nanquan Old Master Wang' occurs 17 times in 12 texts; the selling-himself phrase occurs 41 times in 37.

Senses.PreferredTarget: already present and ready at hand
Senses.Explanation: Already present, complete, or ready at hand rather than newly produced. Named Chan speakers apply the word to each encountered matter, a public case, immediate use, scenery before the eyes, and everything disclosed in the present scene. Yuanwu Keqin pairs 'this very thing is ready' with 'this very thing is for use'; Ruibai Mingxue asks who lacks what is originally ready, while Hanxiu Xingyun pairs original completeness with everything already present. Chan bends an ordinary word for something ready-made by using it to challenge the search for a result elsewhere, yet the word itself does not tell the reader what the ready thing is in every passage.
Senses.Note: Canonical concordance: 1,895 exact hits in 315 files and 311 works. Seven distinct deployments across six works. Grammatical shifts do not create different referents.

Senses.Explanation: A public case that is already complete, present, or ready to hand. The expression is fully attested in Chinese Chan records as a case-term and an utterance. One address says, 'One who comes this way is a ready-made public case.' Another named record subject waits for the assembly to settle, says only that even a ready-made public case cannot be arranged, and steps down. A later record says that whenever an unnamed monk came, Muzhou said, 'Ready-made public case.' Teachers also ask directly what a ready-made public case is and answer with such lines as 'the eastern ravine's water flows into the western ravine; clouds rise on the southern mountain and the northern mountain.' Yuanwu says that before the ready-made public case is spoken its pattern is already manifest, and when its root is raised it leaks through layer after layer. The expression is also followed by 'there is no need to investigate' in fourteen matches across fourteen files. These Chinese uses supply both the literal compound and its deployment as an actual public-case expression.
Senses.Note: The corpus has 382 matches in 154 files. Six passages in six files ask, 'What is a ready-made public case?' One text uses 'this is called a ready-made public case,' another places it among a series of naming formulas, and the reversed order 'public case ready-made' occurs fifty-five times in forty-three files. Further fixed lines include 'ready-made public case, no need to investigate' (14/14), 'ready-made public case, already many-sided' (5/5), 'ready-made public case, without error or deception' (3/3), and 'ready-made public case, already overcomplicated' (7/7). All evidence here is from Chinese Chan sources.

Senses.Explanation: A coordinate pair naming “principle” and “affairs, events, or matters.” Chan records ask how principle and affairs are unobstructed, say that both sides have been penetrated or are fully provided, and require them to be clearly distinguished. The Mirror Record gives one explicit account of their relation: “This principle is the principle that completes affairs; this affair is the affair that displays principle.” Ying’an says, “Penetrated on the side of principle and penetrated on the side of affairs: this is called principle and affairs fused through.” Other records speak of both being complete or ask directly, “What are principle and affairs?” The expression is translated as the coordinate pair stated by the texts rather than collapsed into one abstract category.
Senses.Note: The corpus has 850 matches in 198 files. Recurrent constructions include 'principle and affairs unobstructed' (117 matches in 63 files), 'principle and affairs perfectly fused' (24 in 21), 'principle and affairs both complete' (11 in 9), and 'principle and affairs distinct and clear' (9 in 6). Forty-six occurrences in thirty files ask, 'What are principle and affairs?' or use that wording within a fuller question. These distributions support one corpus-wide sense rather than a named Chan figure-specific one.

Senses.Explanation: The formula says that birth and death is the great matter: the records make it an urgent reason to seek clarification, and several directly explain it as not knowing where birth comes from or where death goes. Dahui Zonggao calls not knowing one's coming the greatness of birth and not knowing one's destination the greatness of death, and names that condition with the formula. Tianru Weize gives the same paired explanation, while Xueyan Zuqin urges listeners to take it as a matter of unsurpassed weight and get it clear. Yuanwu Keqin describes declaring this great matter and one's own affair still unclear as the proper initial reason for approaching an established lineage instructor. Zhongfeng Mingben rebukes people who carry the words in their mouths while hunting a phrase from old paper. Dufeng Xingjian says neither saying nor knowing it is enough, and Shending Yunwai Ze says it cannot be finished through oral proof or acceptance in thought. The entry therefore records urgency, definition, and corrective use without treating repetition of the slogan as its resolution.

Senses.Explanation: One sense asks a person’s place of origin in interviews; a separate use names a condition of arising. A person's place or circumstance of origin. Dongshan asks Lingyun, 'where is your place of origin?' (闍黎生緣何處), and Lingyun answers that he is a man of Min. Dazhu is asked the same question and answers, 'the sun rises in the east; the moon sets in the west' (日出東，月落西). Huanglong Huinan bends this ordinary origin question into one of his three chamber checkpoints: 'everyone has a place of origin; where is yours?' (人人盡有生緣，上座生緣在何處). His biography says the monasteries called the set Huanglong's Three Checkpoints. Later records quote, versify, appraise, and answer the same question. One later exchange answers 'face to face, you do not recognize it' (覿面不識), then explicitly asks what happens beyond the three checkpoints. These are different answers and institutional deployments of the same origin question, not additional lexical senses.

Senses.Explanation: "different kinds." In Chan questions it can stand alone: asked "what are the other kinds?" (如何是異類), the identified master strikes a bowl and calls a servant to eat, while another answers "the foot is short, the inch is long" (尺短寸長). Its defining Zen deployment is the fixed expression "move among other kinds" (異類中行). Nanquan says people of the time must move among other kinds; challenged on "kind," he puts both hands on the ground. Another witness places the expression beside "although moving in an animal's conduct, one does not receive an animal's recompense" (雖行畜生行，不得畜生報). Cao Dong's record supplies the sharpest lexical boundary: the ancients provisionally borrowed the water buffalo as an "other kind"; it is an other kind in the matter, not an other kind in language (古人權借水牯牛為異類。秖是事上異類。非言語中異類). The entry records these answers and boundaries without deciding what spiritual condition they express.

Senses.Explanation: The phrase names movement or conduct “among different kinds,” and Chan records make it a contested classification of how a person goes rather than a zoological destination. Nanquan Puyuan says that Chan monks “must move among different kinds” (須向異類中行), answers Guizong Zhichang’s animal-conduct objection, and elsewhere classifies Daowu Yuanzhi’s withdrawal from an exchange as “moving among different kinds” (他却是異類中行). Caoshan Benji repeats Nanquan’s classification while discussing forms of speech. Langting Ting distinguishes moving among different kinds without cutting off sound and form as the “following fall” (隨墮), alongside the kind-fall and honored-fall. Xieyun Ji uses the phrase of a cat in a playful letter, while Juelang Daosheng tells Huang that earlier people required moving among different kinds and contrasts this with being soaked dead in still water. The shared wording therefore covers named conduct, classification, question-and-answer, and later explanation; the records do not reduce these deployments to a single animal act.

Senses.Explanation: To draw a snake and add feet is to spoil a sufficient figure by adding what does not belong. Langting Jingting applies the phrase to describing an incomparable mind with an added moon image. Huanglong Huinan uses it for saying more than one's share requires; Shanfeng Xian calls his own further remark an added foot; Juelang Daosheng says the ancestral style never needed such additions. Yuan'an Feng playfully reverses the result—adding feet makes a dragon—while Danxia Dangui tags an old question as the needless addition. The shared Chan test is whether extra speech clarifies the live matter or merely decorates and distorts it.

SearchAliases: a painted cake cannot satisfy hunger
Senses.Explanation: A painted cake is repeatedly named as something that cannot feed: the records apply that bodily limit to words, talk, blows, and shouts that likewise fail to satisfy hunger. Literally a cake drawn or painted rather than edible. Chan records make it a stock verdict by completing the image: “a painted cake cannot fill hunger” . In the Xiangyan case, after he cannot answer Guishan's question and searches all the writings he has read for a reply, he sighs, “a painted cake cannot fill hunger” ; the record then has him burn those writings. Dahui's verse pairs it with another ineffective likeness: “how could a shimmering mirage ever stop thirst? When could a painted cake fill hunger?” . The verdict extends beyond writings. One discourse says “discussing the obscure and speaking of the marvelous is like using a painted cake to fill hunger” ; another asks whether wielding the staff and shouting differs from filling hunger with a painted cake . A verse explicitly places it beside “speaking of food never makes one full” . Thus the object keeps its literal non-feeding property while the corpus repeatedly applies it to quoted words, explanations, stock gestures, and other substitutes that it says do not fill hunger.

Right then and there: a temporal expression marking something as occurring without an intervening interval. Shanglan Shun's verse says accumulated ignorance disappears right then; the Five Lamps narrator says Zhitian awakens on the spot when shown the blowing-a-hair case. Huangbo Xiyun uses it for the time of becoming clear without retaining a mark of clarity, while Linji Yixuan uses it for being without further business after turning the light back and recognizing no difference from the patriarchs and buddhas. Huqiu Shaolong says that if listeners trust the presented mind-settling scene, the mind is settled right then. Wuyi Yuanlai attaches the expression to one thought not arising, Miyin to the ice-like disappearance of a raised repentance case, Xuedou Chongxian to a mirror distinguishing beautiful and ugly as soon as it is set up, and the Yongzheng Emperor to a selected saying and discriminating consciousness shattering on the spot. The Zen record prizes the compressed timing, but the word itself remains a temporal modifier: it does not by itself name a teaching, a prescribed exercise, or a distinct temporal entity.
Senses.Note: Frozen-corpus concordance: 1,568 exact hits in 319 files and 315 independent works. Verbal, verse, and narrative uses all mark immediate timing. English noun phrases such as 'the present' are excluded from the preferred gloss because the curated evidence consistently modifies events or states rather than naming a distinct temporal object.

Senses.Explanation: “at / meet the trigger or occasion.” In Chan records the occasion is repeatedly public and interpersonal: one account says that in all his questions and answers he “did not yield when meeting the occasion” (問答，當機不讓); a verse pairs a clear question and a direct answer with “meeting face-to-face on the occasion” (當機覿面). The phrase can introduce a request—“with one phrase meeting the occasion, please speak the teaching” (一句當機請師說法)—or appraise an immediate response. Feiyin Tongrong strikes the staff and says, “freed through on the occasion; it is no other thing” (當機透脫，更非別物). Yuanwu's verse says that buddhas and patriarchs “value what is ready-made when meeting the occasion” (佛祖當機貴見成) and immediately calls for someone to come before the assembly and settle doubt. Thus the corpus bends a general word for apt timing toward the live occasion of encounter, question, answer, and response.

SearchAliases: to let it pass right before one's face
to miss what is directly before one
Senses.Explanation: To miss something face-to-face is to fail to recognize what is directly present; speakers apply the warning to a person, ordinary sights, a staff, and an encounter before the assembly. The phrase occurs as a verdict, a warning, and an author's acknowledgment. Meixi Du pairs two kinds of people: those who stand out shoulder it directly, while those confused about the head and recognizing a shadow miss it face-to-face (超群拔萃的，直下荷擔；迷頭認影的，當面錯過). In a letter he says that on first meeting a correspondent he did not recognize the correspondent's freedom and literary quality, “truly what is called missing it face-to-face” (誠所謂當面錯過也); this is the corpus's only formula using “what is called” for the term. Boshan Wuyi says, after asking whether anyone can assess the value of what he has presented, “one still must not miss it face-to-face” (也不可當面錯過). Elsewhere Boshan lists “rice comes from grain, soup from water, and a nun is a woman,” then says “do not miss it face-to-face” (飯是米做底、湯是水做底、師姑是女人做底，切莫當面錯過). Yunxi's record places the warning after “kites fly and fish leap; mountains stand and water flows” (鳶飛魚躍，山峙水流，切莫當面錯過). Panlong calls on his staff to bring news to the assembly, warns them not to miss it face-to-face, raises the staff, and asks whether they understand. The exact phrase occurs 134 times in 67 allowlisted files.

Senses.Explanation: A mass of doubt is something cultivated until it becomes concentrated and then breaks open or is shattered at awakening. The Chan record makes doubt materially mass-like: a discourse says that inside and outside ‘roll into one mass of doubt’ (滾作一箇疑團), and other records speak of making the whole body, sitting, walking, dressing, eating, and even the encountered world into that mass. The same physical grammar governs its end: it is ‘broken through’ (打破疑團), or remains ‘unbroken’ (疑團不破). In an autobiographical public account, repeated blows make Gaofeng Yuanmiao's mass of doubt more acute (疑團愈切). Thus the phrase is not merely ordinary uncertainty; these later Chan records deploy it as the consolidated, bodily condition named around sustained investigation and its reported breaking. The corpus does not make the mass a separate object from the doubt or state a further gloss for the breaking.

Senses.Explanation: The phrase names a sustained, felt condition of doubt used in inquiry, not a passing uncertainty about a proposition. Wuyi Yuanlai explicitly asks what this doubt is and describes it erupting, knotting at the brows, and becoming impossible to put down or drive off. Dahui Zonggao says that while it remains unbroken, life and death press in. Gaofeng Yuanmiao recounts it suddenly arising while he held the question where the one returns, leaving him unable to distinguish directions. Librarian Lai tells Xueyan Zuqin that investigating Chan requires raising it and connects small doubt with small awakening. Preface author Ding Libiao calls not knowing a parent's destination or one's own beginning and end the great doubt of life and death shared across time. Zhongfeng Mingben warns that even uninterrupted conjunction of saying and doubt can become a subtle stealing mind. The corpus thus presents a concentrated condition to be raised and broken, while also warning against treating its continuity as achievement.

Senses.Explanation: To make something clear or bring it to light. Chan biographies repeatedly say that someone brings “the great matter,” “the mind-ground,” or “the essentials of mind” to light. One record lists bringing the great matter to light alongside having one's mind-ground opened through mountains and waters and recognizing one's original face through things encountered; the text supplies these neighboring predicates without making them synonyms. A later address states its aim as having each person “directly bring to light one's own fundamental great matter” (直下發明自己本分大事), anchoring direct instruction rather than retrospective biography. Other biographies say “there will certainly be clarification” (必有發明) or that someone was “not greatly clarified” (不大發明). Those result and degree constructions name the outcome of the same bringing-to-light event, not another lexical referent.

Senses.Explanation: To swear an oath is to make an explicit pledge; the surviving witnesses record different oath contents and do not all describe a public performance. The Xuefeng Genxin row is compiler biography: it says he vowed to travel and then went to Gushan, not that he utters the headword. The common element is an explicit pledge, while publicity is not established as defining.

Senses.Explanation: Baizhang’s wild fox names the canonical causality case and the fox-body at the center of its retelling. In the received account an old man says that his answer 'does not fall under cause and effect' led to five hundred lives as a wild fox. Baizhang answers the repeated question 'is not blind to cause and effect'; the old man reports release and asks for a monastic funeral. Guishan later responds to the raised story by shaking a door panel, and two monks dispute the easy fall-and-release opposition. Later masters repeatedly reopen the named case: Daxin raises it in the chamber, Wansong heads it as the eighth case, Foyan Qingyuan is tested on it, Shita Xuanmi Li comments on it in a hall address, Hongfu Ziwen versifies it, and Yunju Shuai'an Fancong gives another verse. A fox narrative thus becomes a stable public-case label; the entry reports its documentary parts and later testing without adjudicating cause and effect.

Senses.Explanation: Chan records make the top of a hundred-foot pole the place where gaining entry is still insufficient and a further step is demanded, questioned, or refused. Changsha Jingcen’s verse says that even one who has gained entry is not yet genuine and must step forward from the pole-top, with the ten directions as the whole body. Wumen transmits Shishuang’s question asking how to advance, and Fojian Huiqin comments on the moment of advancement. An unnamed monastic puts the fixed question to Fadeng, while Yanguan Qi’an counters by asking what use advancement would have. These divergent responses preserve the pole-top as a public challenge rather than a fixed ladder stage.

Senses.Explanation: Blood under the skin is the records' bodily image for someone who registers pain and itching, unlike unresponsive earth and wood. It is consequently used by Gulin Qingmao as a qualification for people addressed in the hall: "you people must have blood under the skin" (汝諸人須是皮下有血始得), and "if he has blood under the skin, he will certainly have another livelihood" (他若皮下有血，必定別有生涯). A garden exchange also keeps the literal body image audible: seeing a cook cut melons, Yu'an Zhiji asks the head cook, "which one has blood under the skin?" (那個皮下有血). Zen bends the bodily phrase into a recurrent test for someone who registers a touch or blow, while the records themselves ground that use in pain and itching rather than an imported psychological category.

Senses.Explanation: The monastery supervisor is the administrator who records, allocates, and safeguards communal property and practical business. A dying elder orders the supervisor to record the division of robes and bowls; public records thank incoming and outgoing supervisors, and named officeholders request formal addresses or receive verses and memorial rites. Senses.Explanation: People described as unable to see, hear, and speak. In the Chan record, the full phrase becomes the stable wording of Xuansha Shibei's “three kinds of invalids” public case. Xuansha asks how one receives people who cannot see a raised mallet or whisk, hear spoken command, or answer. Yuanwu Keqin warns his audience against treating his discussion as nothing more than the disability list, then asks where the blind, deaf, and mute fellow stands; Xuedou Chongxian begins his verse with the same phrase. In a Yunmen case, Yunmen tests an unnamed monk for deafness and muteness, and Xuedou applies the full phrase to him. Yuelin Shiguan later labels and re-asks Xuansha's case. Guting Shanjian also compares people unable to resolve doubt with the blind, deaf, and mute. Zen bends a literal description into repeatable wording for a public case and an interview about receiving people when visible, audible, and spoken exchange fails; the entry does not invent a diagnosis beyond each recorded deployment.

Senses.Explanation: The records define straight mind against bends, twists, crookedness, and falseness: ‘straight mind means without bends or twists.’ Literally, a straight or straightforward mind. The term occurs 163 times in 89 allowed texts. The corpus supplies two compact definitions: 'straight mind means without bends or twists' (直心者，無委曲故), and 'straight mind is the site of the Way because it has no falseness' (直心是道場，無虛假故). The Platform Record repeats 'straight mind is the site; straight mind is the clean land' (直心是道場，straight mind is the clean land, ‘straight mind is the site; straight mind is the clean land’), then contrasts inwardly acting crookedly while verbally speaking straight with actually carrying out straight mind. Its positive clause is 'only carry out straight mind; regarding all things, have no grasping' (但行直心，於一切法上，無有執著). Another address expands the pattern into four coordinated expressions: 'straight mind is the site; straight speech is the subtle teaching; straight conduct is subtle conduct; straight verification is the subtle result' (直心是道場，直說是妙法，直行是妙行，直證是妙果). The common collocation 'straight mind and straight conduct' (直心直行) occurs 22 times in 16 texts. One record describes it by the absence of self-versus-other, right-versus-wrong, falseness, and crookedness; another uses 'straight mind, straight conduct, original color, original share' (直心直行，本色本分) to characterize a named Chan figure's meetings with people.
Senses.Note: The English follows the graph meaning 'straight' (直) and the texts' own oppositions: straight versus crooked (直／曲), genuine versus false (genuine / false), and straight conduct versus flattering crookedness (諂曲). The direct definition 'without bends or twists' occurs once, while the site-of-the-Way formula occurs across multiple independent records. No master-specific sense is warranted.

Senses.Explanation: Chan records make this action a lineage banner for Bodhidharma’s coming while also turning it into a question and a claim that teachers qualify in their own words. Dahui Zonggao twice states the Bodhidharma formula and glosses direct pointing as what every person already has. Huitang Zuxin and Yuanwu Keqin place it in lineage discourse, while Yuanwu also says the branching lineage has no destination outside it. An unnamed monastic asks Juelang Daosheng what the paired formula means. Mengan Siyue compares it to an antelope hanging by its horns, resisting a flat explanatory capture. The evidence supports the recurring banner and its public testing without treating Bodhidharma as the grammatical speaker whenever he is named.

Senses.Explanation: For two parties to deceive or lead each other astray. Frozen-corpus concordance: 207 exact hits in 111 storage files representing 109 independent works. Chan records repeatedly place this ordinary reciprocal act under negation in the assurance, ‘Only provide the assenting heart; we certainly will not deceive one another’ (但辦肯心。必不相賺), with graphic variants in the verb ‘provide’ and the adverb ‘certainly.’ Yuanwu Keqin closes an address with that formula. Dahui Zonggao uses it after answering an interlocutor's request about how to receive and keep a statement. Zhongfeng Mingben quotes the old formula and elsewhere tells a Chan student to trust his words because they will not deceive one another. Puan Yinsu repeats the assurance, but also asks whether an old worthy's saying amounts to mutual deception (古人恁麼道。莫是相賺麼). Affirmative, negative, and interrogative forms retain the same reciprocal act; the Zen-specific bend is the formula's recurring use as a public assurance tied to an assenting heart.

Senses.Explanation: The expression denotes one's eyebrows fall out in these Chan records. Its wording is the eyebrows (眉毛) fall out (墮落). Frozen-corpus concordance: 7 exact hits in 6 storage files representing 6 independent works. The wider family includes "the eyebrows fall" (眉毛落, 48 occurrences), "are the eyebrows still there?" (眉毛在麼, 79), and "the eyebrows become tangled together" (眉毛廝結, 129). Chan records use the loss of eyebrows as a stated consequence or accusation attached to handling Buddhist or Chan speech: one comment says that making a Buddhist teaching-discussion of a line "implicates Shimen, whose eyebrows fall out" (若作佛法商量，累他石門眉毛墮落); another points to "the place where Cuiyan's eyebrows fall out" while reviewing the Cuiyan exchange. A question joins the phrase to Danxia's burning of the wooden Buddha and asks why the monastery director's eyebrows fall out. The exact phrase is late and sparse, but its eyebrow-loss family is widely transmitted; the texts do not provide an anatomical explanation, and this entry adds none.

SearchAliases: look at the word or saying
Senses.Explanation: The expression denotes look at the word or saying in these Chan records. Its wording is ‘look at the talk’: look at the word, saying, question, or conversational thread singled out in a record. The compound most often occurs in ‘look at the saying's head’ (看話頭), and the local wording—not an imported technical label—determines whether English says word, saying, question, or thread. The records include the recorded questioner seeking written direction because the saying he was looking at had not opened to him. They also preserve criticism: Mingben reports people calling looking at a saying ‘doing work’ and rejects their appeal to direct transmission; Yuancheng says an old hunter neither did work nor looked at a saying before answering that there was ‘no place to set a hand,’ and contrasts this with looking left and right at one's own selected saying. Another record demands, ‘if you recognize it and can say it, come out and say it—what does the end of the talk say?’ Thus the Zen deviation is an ordinary act of looking directed at actual words in recorded exchanges and itself subjected to criticism in the record.

Senses.Explanation: The many blind people feeling an elephant each encounter a part and mistake partial contact for the whole animal. Xiangtian Jinian explicitly reads the elephant comparison as exposing the illness of clinging to one's own view. Dahui Zonggao lists it among cases that must be met personally rather than settled in speech. Xutang Zhiyu says the blind know an elephant yet do not see the whole; an unnamed questioner asks Zhaozhou what the true elephant is when each gives a different account, and Zhaozhou answers that there is no reliance—one simply does not know. The Chan bend turns the comparison into a public test of whether partial descriptions are being promoted as complete seeing.

Senses.Explanation: To deceive people is a recurring adverse judgement on words, conduct, or inherited interpretations. The phrase retains that ordinary act while Chan records put it under public pressure. Yunmen asks for a saying that does not deceive people, then supplies the substitute response, “Do not say this is the one that deceives people.” Miyun Yuanwu states that deceiving people is no good affair and that a good affair does not deceive people; Fushi Tongxian publicly raises the positive half. Shiyu Mingfang attacks people who deceive others for gain, while Wuzhun Shifan distinguishes deceiving people from deceiving oneself. In the Blue Cliff Record, Longya Judun denies that patriarchs and buddhas intend deception but says that, because people cannot pass through, they nevertheless become deceivers. The phrase therefore becomes a test of sayings, speakers, hearers, and self-deception without losing its transitive meaning or allowing the entry to infer intent where Longya denies it.

Senses.Explanation: Intellectual understanding is knowing reached through interpreting or explanation. The corpus overwhelmingly uses the term as a rebuke or warning. Its flagship form is 'a follower of the intellectual-understanding lineage' (知解宗徒, 35 occurrences), a label applied to Shenhui and Guifeng Zongmi: even Shenhui and Guifeng were rejected as followers of intellectual understanding (神會、圭峰尚斥為知解宗徒). In an origin case, a student names the matter 'Buddha-nature at the original source,' and Huineng says that even if this fellow later founds a place, he will become only a follower of intellectual understanding (此子已後設有把茅蓋頭，只成得箇知解宗徒). Another passage puts a whole list of teaching styles under the same verdict (此等見解盡屬知解宗徒). The common gate-entry warning 'harbor no intellectual understanding' (莫存知解) occurs 80 times. Mi'an Xianjie continues by comparing its non-arising to the king's sword. Other records say people are deceived by intellectual understanding and conjecture (多被知解卜度瞞過), or that the matter is not an affair on the side of intellectual understanding (不是知解邊事). The headword occurs 1,186 times in 237 allowlist texts. This entry reports the corpus's repeated pejorative deployment without turning it into a general theory of mind. Huangbo Xiyun extends the term through a food-and-digestion comparison: 'what is called intellectual understanding not digested is all poison' (所謂知解不消。皆為毒藥). Parallel witnesses preserve the same wording in two other collections.
Senses.Note: A corpus-wide pejorative. The origin rebuke and the naming of Shenhui and Zongmi as followers of intellectual understanding (知解宗徒) are raised material, while 'harbor no intellectual understanding' (莫存知解) is a stock proclamation. Compare distinguishing, deliberation, emotional consciousness, and conjecture without treating them as automatic synonyms.

Senses.Explanation: The stone woman is an impossible animated figure who bears a child, dances, sings, plays music, or acts beside a wooden man in recurrent verses and answers. The stone woman is a stock impossible mother and actor in Chan verse, answers, and formal addresses. The record repeatedly makes her bear a child, says she has no husband, or pairs her with the wooden figure while she sings, dances, nods, plays a reed organ, or calls back a dream. Pumen Xibian groups 'the stone woman bears a child' with dust rising from a well bottom, waves rising on a mountaintop, and an empty flower bearing fruit. Dongshan Liangjie pairs the wooden figure singing with the stone woman dancing. Qingshan Shoulong answers an auspicious-sign question with the wooden figure clapping a board in the clouds and the stone woman playing a reed organ beneath the water. Hongzhi Zhengjue answers a question about the person who neither comes nor goes by saying that the stone woman calls back the three-realm dream while the wooden figure cuts off the workings of the six gates. Baiyu Si compares being forced to speak with forcing the stone woman to bear a child and making a rooster lay an egg. Yandang Wenji likewise answers a lineage question with a barren woman bearing a child. Shu'an Fancong's verse says the stone woman has no husband. These reproductive and impossible-action predicates concern one stock woman; the research found no separate stone statue or named person.

Senses.Explanation: Polishing a tile to make a mirror names the task Nanyue declares impossible in his exchange with Mazu, and later records reuse it as a comparison for wasted effort. The impossible task of polishing a tile into a mirror. In the defining encounter Nanyue Huairang polishes a tile and tells Mazu Daoyi that he is making a mirror; when Mazu objects, Huairang asks how sitting Chan could then make a buddha . Later masters use the compact expression as the case-name and bend the impossible craft in several directions. Fachang Yiyu compares private explanations and forced elaboration to polishing a tile to make a mirror . Shending Yikui groups it with striking the cart or ox and calls both children's play . Tian'an Sheng includes it in a rapid list of ancestral demonstrations judged excessively solicitous . Luyan He first compares sitting Chan to making a meal from steamed sand, then says polishing a tile to make a mirror is using a straight hook to angle for a fierce dragon . Thus the records do not only label futile effort: they preserve Huairang's public correction and repeatedly reopen its impossible action in later teaching.

Senses.Explanation: The patriarch's meaning is a recurrent public-interview demand for what the ancestral transmission amounts to here. The corpus preserves incompatible object-answers, verbal answers, refusals, and later comments under the same question.

Senses.PreferredTarget: the meaning of the patriarch's coming from the West
AlternateTargets: the point of Bodhidharma's journey from the West
Senses.Explanation: The meaning or point of the patriarch's coming from the West, with the patriarch understood in these records as Bodhidharma coming to China. The words usually form a stock public question rather than a request for travel history. Named respondents answer with a cypress, washing feet, a Chan board, ripe plums, a fan, landscape lines, a refusal, or a demand that the questioner turn toward his own intent. Dahui Zonggao can also name it as a topic for which there is not yet time to speak, and Zhongfeng Mingben warns that interchangeable verbal explanations miss it. The phrase therefore names one recurring question whose Chan force lies in the publicly testable answer, not a fixed route or a single explanatory paraphrase.
Senses.Note: Frozen-corpus concordance: 2,387 exact apparatus-clean hits in 279 files and 274 independent works in the canonical f001 preflight. The bare phrase and the full question belong to one referent; response diversity does not create separate senses because every response is presented as answering or discussing the same question.

Senses.Explanation: A Chan monastery is the named residential institution in which an abbot presides and a recorded teaching career is located. Lamp colophons identify Puming and Huirì Yunwen through the Chan monasteries where they serve as abbots. Transmission rosters attach named lineage figures to Baoing Chan Monastery, while collected-record contents organize successive bodies of sayings by Ciyun, Lianfeng, and Shousheng Chan Monasteries. The Chan bend is documentary and public: the monastery is not generic scenery but the named seat that locates a lineage figure, an abbacy, a body of sayings, and the restoration or transmission of the lineage.

Senses.Explanation: The myriad things return to one: the opening clause of a stock public question (萬法歸一). It most often forms the first clause of the stock question, 'The myriad things return to one; where does the one return?' (萬法歸一；一歸何處). In Zhaozhou Congshen's case the answer is: 'When I was in Qingzhou; I made a cloth shirt, weighing seven catties' (我在青州；作一領布衫，重七斤). The corpus preserves other answers without making any of them a dictionary gloss: Wenshu Yingzhen says, 'The Yellow River has nine bends' (黃河九曲); Baizhang Mingzhao An says, 'There has not been a single person who did not ask' (未有一箇人不問); Shending Yikui answers the first clause with 'rain comes, the mountain colors darken' (雨來山色暗), then answers the second with 'clouds clear, the moon is newer' (雲淨月彌新). The phrase is therefore not merely a proposition. Zen records bend it into the opening move of a portable public-interview case whose second clause and sharply speaker-specific answers must remain attached. Juelang Daosheng answers the inherited question by challenging who taught the monk to ask it; Zhean Fan raises the Zhaozhou version and comments on its pressure. Both keep the headword as the first clause of the same public question.

Senses.Explanation: The Mirror of Qin is a named mirror repeatedly brought into Chan verse and exchange as an instrument before which a form, a speaking participant, or the person himself is exposed and distinguished. In the Recorded Sayings of Master Baiyu, Baiyu Jingsi says that before the mirror a jackal has no way to hide its original form; in the Recorded Sayings of Konggu Daocheng, Konggu Daocheng hangs the mirror at the head of a staff and says that every dust-mote land becomes responsive. In direct questioning recorded in the Recorded Sayings of Master Hansong, Hansong Zhicao answers after the absence of the mirror prompts the question how one can distinguish the matter. The compilers Jing and Yun, narrating Xuefeng Yicun's biography in the Zutang Collection, place Xuefeng face-to-face with the mirror and tell him to inspect himself. These are observable deployments of the mirror in appraisal and exposure, not a claim that every mention carries one secret fixed meaning. The headword occurs 29 times in 25 allowlist texts.

Senses.Explanation: a nest or mortar; in the Chan record, a fixed mould into which words and conduct settle. The corpus speaks of falling into another's rut (墮他窠臼, "fall into his fixed rut") as oil enters flour and cannot get out, and of both inherited gestures and current fashions as ruts: "killing buddhas and patriarchs" falls within the old people's enclosure, while wielding the staff and shout does not escape the present-day rut (殺佛殺祖，盡落古人圜繢；行棒行喝，不脫今時窠臼). One record pairs new and old while saying "jump out of the rut" (一新一舊，跳出窠臼). The decisive corpus warning is recursive: pupils may mistake the identified master's refusal to establish a rut and thereby make "no rut" into a rut (以無窠臼為窠臼, "take having no rut as a rut"). Thus the Chan deviation is not merely an ordinary habit: the term names repeatable religious speech, gestures, formats, and even anti-formulas once followers preserve them as a template.

Senses.Explanation: One instruction says that in traveling on foot and dwelling in the world one must first “establish firm footing, not be stirred by the eight winds” (立定腳跟，不被八風所鼓). A verse places it as a rock amid vast waves; a public exchange receives the direct interjection, “establish firm footing well” (立定腳跟好). The corpus also corrects a rigid use of the phrase: Zhean Jingfan says that always establishing firm footing can, upon close examination, be “a one-sided, withered understanding and a dull fellow who does not comprehend adaptation” (偏枯見解、不達權變之笨漢). Zen therefore bends bodily footing into a recurrent instruction and appraisal for remaining steady, while preserving a recorded warning that immobility itself can be faulted.

Senses.Explanation: “Where you stand is all genuine” is paired with acting as host wherever one is, then repeated as a Fayan-house characterization and as a predicate of immediate use. Literally, at the place of standing or taking one's position , all is genuine or real : "where you stand is all genuine." It occurs 35 times in 24 allowlisted texts. Linji's record supplies the governing formula twice: "act as host wherever you are; where you stand is all genuine; arriving circumstances cannot turn you around" . The second passage precedes it with "do not receive another person's delusion" and follows it by warning that a single doubtful thought gives an opening. Jingtu Huimin reverses its paired order as "where you stand is all genuine; act as host according to the place" . Zhongyan Huayan Zujue attaches it to "take it up and immediately use it" , while Zhenjing Kewen explicitly quotes Linji's wording as "bring it and immediately use it; where you stand is all genuine" . Chan bends the ordinary idea of a standing-place into a stable Linji roster phrase about taking the host position amid changing circumstances; the entry reports the formula and its transmitted predicates without adding a claim beyond those recorded predicates.

Senses.Explanation: Standing in the snow primarily recalls Huike’s vigil before Bodhidharma; a separate image compares a white heron standing in snow. Huike's vigil in the snow before Bodhidharma. Huike, still called Shenguang in the account, stands unmoving through a night of heavy snow until it rises above his knees, and Bodhidharma asks, “You have stood long in the snow; what do you seek?” (汝久立雪中，當求何事). Retrospective formulas join “standing in the snow” with “cutting off the arm” (立雪斷臂), transmission of the robe and bowl, and Huike's request for the buddhas' essential way. Later masters preserve conflicting appraisals: Shuwei Tongxuan says, “standing in snow was not yet toil; cutting off the arm was the real thing,” while Bailu Xianduan calls “the Second Patriarch standing in snow to seek mind” unworthy. It also becomes a stock public question—“what is the meaning of the Second Patriarch standing waist-deep in snow?”—to which Jiangshan Faquan answers, “a leap month comes once in three years.” The ordinary weather action has thus become the compact name of a lineage encounter and a recurring interview prompt.

Senses.Note: The heron forms (鷺鶿 and 鷺鷥) are graphic variants within one physical-action family. The direct answer and the verse comparison are different deployments of the same bird-and-snow scene, not further senses.

Senses.Explanation: To raise or hold upright the whisk, the teaching-seat implement and emblem of authority. The action occurs as an answer, demonstration, and object of public questioning rather than as a gesture with one fixed message. Nanta Guangyong answers a question about Manjusri's teacher by raising the whisk. Zhaozhou Congshen raises it when asked whether he will receive the person who sets the realm in order. Yuanwu Keqin twice raises it and says, "Just this is it." Yunmen Wenyan reopens an older exchange in which a monk asks Zifu Zhensui the import of the ancients picking up the mallet and raising the whisk. Deshan Yuanming classifies raising a finger and raising the whisk as a dead phrase. In the dominant spelling, Baiyu Jingsi raises the whisk and asks whether the assembly sees, while Yinyuan Longqi raises it as his answer to a new-command question and then tests the monk's shouts. The Zen bend is the action's institutional and interview setting: it is the presiding master's implement raised as an answer or challenge, while the corpus refuses a universal symbolic decoding. Xueyan Zuqin twice raises the whisk within hall addresses—once before calling unfreed affective dust blindness, and once before a moon verse. The surrounding sayings differ, but the referent remains the same public action with the teaching-seat implement.

Nine anchors cover direct answers, repeated demonstration, a raised old case, critical classification, and two governed dominant-spelling variants. The two spellings are readings of the same action, never separate senses.

Senses.Explanation: The step beyond the top of a hundred-foot pole, where the image leaves no footing for another step. The fixed phrase and case title are drawn from Changsha Jingcen's verse: the person sitting atop a hundred-foot pole, although having gained entry, is not yet real; the verse then requires a step forward and says that the worlds in the ten directions are the whole body (百尺竿頭坐底人，雖然得入，未為真；百尺竿頭須進步，十方世界現全身). Wumen Huikai's Case 46 titles the case Stepping Forward from the Pole-top and attributes the question “atop a hundred-foot pole, how does one step forward?” to Shishuang Qingzhu (石霜和尚云，百尺竿頭如何進步). Fojian Huiqin's later verse explicitly names Old Changsha at the time of the pole-top step (百尺竿頭進步時……老長沙). The phrase then circulates as a public question: Yexian Guixing answers “the southern continent, the northern continent” (南贍部洲，北欝單越), Linye Qi answers “then retreat” (退後即得), and Shanduo Zhenzai answers “a beheaded boatman goes down to Yangzhou” (斷頭船子下揚州). Langye Huijue places the pole-top step beside a saying with no intent in the phrase and no phrase in the intent, then asks how to breathe out. Zen bends the impossible ordinary action into a named case, a quoted verse-line, and a repeatedly answered public question; the records give different answers without changing the action denoted.

Senses.Explanation: Dafang Xinghai's mountain verse is the corpus's direct plant action: he is too indolent to gather purple fungus beside the stream (懶去溪邊採紫芝). The plant-name circulates much more widely in the compound Purple Fungus Song. Tiantong Shanxin is publicly asked what that song is and answers by clapping; Fahua Quanju answers an independent transmission of the question by saying that it is not a Wu sound but must be Han speech (不是吳音，切湏漢語). Yongjue Yuanxian asks who will join a solitary recluse in singing it (中有幽人守貞獨，誰來同唱紫芝歌), Xisou Shaotan places groups of two and three singing it on stones under pine roots (三三兩兩松根石上唱紫芝歌), and Yuanwu Keqin asks who can sing it in the season of high mountains, autumn wind, and a single goose (誰當此時節，解唱紫芝歌). Wuwen Daocan separately invokes the Four Hoaryheads of Mount Shang and their heart of withdrawal, but his verse does not contain the headword. Zen bends the plant-name into a song asked about in public interviews and sung in mountain-retreat verse. The evidence does not make the bare word itself the title of a second thing.

Senses.Explanation: To begin the monastic restriction period is to formally open a fixed seasonal interval in which the resident community follows its established schedule and limits. Recorded-sayings collections commonly use the term as an occasion heading before an address or short evening instruction. Paired references to releasing the restriction mark the opposite boundary. The stored headings therefore attest an institutional calendar action, not an utterance by the record owner whose address follows.
Senses.Note: The frozen corpus has 2,188 exact hits in 273 files representing 270 independent works. Eight anchors from eight works show winter and summer openings, hall addresses, evening instruction, an imperial opening date, and explicit pairing with release of the restriction. Table-of-contents-only hits were excluded.

Senses.Explanation: To revive after being cut off: the records use a death-and-revival image in a recurrent teaching-seat formula and in explicit criticism of that formula. Its dominant fixed formula is ‘let go at the cliff and personally assent and undertake it; revive after being cut off, and you cannot deceive anyone’ (懸崖撒手，自肯承當；絕後再甦，欺君不得). Records also place it after ‘the life-root is severed’ (命根斷), beside ‘shed skin and exchange bones’ (去皮換骨), and compare it with a cold ember flaming and a withered tree flourishing again. The identified master explicitly departs from the inherited formula: ‘the former sages all wanted to revive after being cut off; I am not like that.’ The entry reports this recurrent sequence and its criticism without deciding what state the phrase denotes.

Senses.Explanation: The term names an observable walking circuit or action, with records specifying its timing, direction, companions, and coordination with rest. Literally, to 'go along walking' or 'walk about.' The term occurs 1,022 times in 273 allowed texts and names an observable bodily action. A late biography makes the direction explicit: at night a recluse goes outside the crag to walk about, the visiting master follows, and 'each walks east and west' (隱者出巖外經行，師亦隨之，第東西各步). A Five Lamps address pairs physical condition and action: 'when well, walk about; when tired, rest' (健即經行困即歇). The same collection records Layman Feng Ji walking about the teaching hall with Foyan when a child recites a line, and records another unnamed questioner 'walking under the pines one evening' when he hears a mountain spring (一夕，松下經行，聞巖泉聲). In the collected old cases, Sudhana searches in all four directions for seven days and finds Meghashri 'walking slowly on another peak' (在別峰上徐步經行). Daily timing is also explicit: a biography says an unnamed questioner ate only after serving the assembly, while Bingseng watched him 'walk about after each meal' (每飯罷經行時). The term is frequently coordinated with sitting and lying as one of the body's recorded activities. These places, times, directions, companions, and contrasts support the plain action word.
Senses.Note: All required definition formulas were searched; no stable nominal self-definition was found. Distinct deployment shapes retained are walking east-west at night, walking when well versus resting when tired, walking with another person in a hall, walking under pines, slow walking on another peak, and walking after a meal. The entry adds no special category beyond what the people in the records physically do.

Senses.Explanation: Vimalakirti is the pre-Zen householder whom Chan masters repeatedly raise in public interviews and comments. His exact name occurs 263 times in 116 allowlisted texts. Linquan Conglun directly notes that the Sanskrit Vimalakirti means 'Stainless Renown' and is also rendered Jingming (梵語維摩詰，此云無垢稱，亦云淨名). The dominant Chan deployment is his sickroom and silence: Manjusri asks him about entry into the gate of not-two, Vimalakirti remains silent, and later masters test that silence rather than merely repeat it. Yuanwu raises the exchange as a case; Dahui cites both Vimalakirti's account of illness and his silence; Weilin Daopei invokes the empty sickroom while addressing illness. Xuedou asks what Vimalakirti said, Fenyang would give Vimalakirti and Manjusri thirty blows, and Yun'e Xi calls his closing his mouth 'eating salt to stop thirst.' The Zen Vimalakirti is therefore the seated, sick, silent figure whom masters question, rebuke, praise, and reuse—not an imported life story.

Senses.Explanation: The hall coordinator is a senior monastic officer who organizes communal procedure, announcements, seating, and voiced ceremonial cues. The Revised Baizhang Pure Rules has the hall coordinator prepare paper with the hall office before a ceremony; the Practical Pure Rules places this office among librarian, guest prefect, and attendants according to rank. Another pure-rules contents list groups it with the prior, cook, and work supervisor. In recorded events the officer strikes the announcing mallet for communal attendance, proclaims a written address before the named teaching figure mounts the seat, and is appointed alongside librarian and attendant. Liaoan Qingyu pairs the head seat’s example with the hall coordinator’s vocal leading. Qingman’s comic hall image even sends the wooden hall figure to this officer, who slaps it twice. The Chan-specific deployment is therefore public and procedural: this is the officer whose actions make the assembly’s formal encounter happen, not merely a generic administrator.

Senses.Explanation: The organizing framework by which a lineage's inherited sayings and distinctions are arranged and identified. The image joins a net's main cord (綱) to an ancestral line or school (宗). Huiyan Zhizhao's preface to the Eye of Humans and Gods (人天眼目) places 'the key outlines of the five houses' (五宗綱要) beside 'the terms of the lineage framework' (綱宗語句), including the names and decisive details that an abbot is expected to know. Named-house compounds show the same category applied to particular lineages: Lin Xuan speaks of 'the Linji lineage framework' (臨濟綱宗), while Lin Zhifan writes of 'the Caodong lineage framework' (曹洞綱宗) being restored after confusion. Zhean Jingfan quotes Yantou Quanhuo: 'Only recognize the lineage framework; originally there is no actual thing' (但識綱宗，本無實法). Juelang Daosheng raises Yantou's other formula: 'For the great governing lineage framework, first one must recognize the phrase' (大統綱宗，先須識句). The term travels with verbs such as establish, uphold, display, grasp, and restore. Zen bends the net's main cord into the named structural vocabulary by which a teaching house recognizes, transmits, and publicly tests its inherited distinctions. Tianyin Yuanxiu says one must first reach the root and then know the lineage framework; Chaozong Tongren speaks of establishing that framework while distinguishing deviant alternatives. The added uses preserve an institutional-discursive framework rather than a new object.
Senses.Note: The exact headword occurs 796 times in 213 allowlisted storage files. Standard self-definition searches did not produce a simple equation; their zero results are preserved in WORK rather than printed as unattested Chinese evidence. The strongest structural evidence is Huiyan Zhizhao's explicit pairing of five-house key outlines with lineage-framework terms, Yantou Quanhuo's two transmitted formulas, and the named-house compounds. Linji and Caodong qualification does not change the referent, so one corpus-wide sense remains warranted.

Senses.Explanation: Close-woven, tightly knit, and allowing no gap; by extension, continuously and meticulously joined. Wuyi Yuanlai gives the clearest in-record definition: the brows knit with empty space, a needle cannot enter, water cannot wet it, and no hairbreadth gap is allowed. Dahui Zonggao critically reports respondents who stick an answer directly to a student's question and call that close-woven and free of affective dust; he also reports one-sentence answers called close-woven and not running away. An unnamed monk asks Yongjue Yuanxian for the close-woven house style and receives, "The golden needle does not permit knowing." Cizhou Fangnian appraises Zhanran Yuancheng's phrases as close-woven and not falling into beginning or end. Yuanwu Keqin uses the reduplicated form for what is continuous and close when set down. Yinyuan Longqi says a single mystery has three essentials, layered and close-woven so that no wind passes. The Zen bend is the qualitative transfer from textile closeness to public speech, house style, and lineage phrases: a saying or presentation is judged by whether any seam, temporal edge, or opening remains, while Dahui's reports preserve the possibility that this label itself is being criticized.

Senses.Explanation: To climb a tree seeking fish is to pursue a goal by a route whose direction cannot reach it. Zhongfeng Mingben pairs the phrase with guarding a stump when inherited sayings are treated as certificates. Kaifu Daoning applies it to seeking the subtle point through conceptual knowledge; Yuejiang Zhengyin joins it to rigidly waiting for verification. Tianyin Yuanxiu contrasts it with the unobstructed movement of skilled encounter, and Foyan Qingyuan warns students not to wait for it. The records use the impossible search as a procedural criticism: effort continues, but the chosen means and sought result do not meet.

Senses.Explanation: An antelope hanging by its horns is a recurrent Chan image defined inside the corpus by the absence of anything a hunter can follow. One instruction says that when the antelope hangs by its horns, not only its tracks but even its scent cannot be found. The phrase is then moved into several public forms. Yunju is asked what it is like at that time and answers “six times six is thirty-six,” adding that there are no tracks. Buhui answers a question about taking the person but not the surroundings with “the antelope hangs by its horns without a trace; the mountain is naturally high and the water naturally deep.” A later instruction applies the comparison directly to a lineage teacher's speaking, saying that it has a small measure of correspondence only when it is like the horn-hanging antelope. Thus the corpus does not leave the image as animal lore: it makes the missing track and scent a question, numerical answer, position answer, verse line, and appraisal of teaching-seat speech. The exact phrase occurs 77 times in 38 allowlist texts.

Senses.Explanation: ‘Old monk’ is both an ordinary designation for an elderly monk and the conventional first-person self-reference used by named teachers such as Baizhang Huaihai, Linji Yixuan, Zhaozhou Congshen, and Yunju Daoqi. The human role remains the same across narration, address, and self-reference; those grammatical settings do not create separate senses. Its characteristic Chan deployment is humble first-person self-reference in monastic speech, conventionally translated ‘this old monk’ and grammatically serving as ‘I’ or ‘me.’ Baizhang Huaihai recalls receiving Mazu Daoyi’s shout; Linji Yixuan says he sits securely and distinguishes the visitors who come; Zhaozhou Congshen redirects a public interview by saying, ‘this old monk is hard of hearing; ask loudly’; and Yunju Daoqi addresses the assembly at his final meeting. The same noun phrase also refers in narration to an old monk: Wuzhuo meets one, a raised case begins with an old monk carried by two disciples, and a record introduces ‘an old monk named Puhui.’ Speaker self-reference, third-person reference, and definiteness are contextual readings of the same human-role noun, not different things.

Senses.Explanation: Grandmotherly concern is an elder’s solicitous willingness to explain, protect, or labour for someone even at the risk of being called overindulgent. Linji recognizes Huangbo’s repeated blows as such concern; commentators apply it to a protecting phrase or to inherited explanations, sometimes gratefully and sometimes as criticism for entering the mud. The local verdict controls the tone.

Senses.PreferredTarget: an old woman's concern is pressing
AlternateTargets: old-woman concern pressed to the utmost
pressing concern like an old woman's
Senses.Explanation: The phrase appraises urgently solicitous intervention: records sometimes praise it and sometimes compare it to poisoned honey. Literally, "an old woman's concern is pressing": old woman or granny (老婆) plus the concern being urgent or pressed hard (心切). The phrase occurs 270 times in 129 allowlisted texts. It is a predicate applied to an unnamed interlocutor's insistent words or actions toward someone else, not the name of an inner state or a sentimental ideal. In the Linji–Huangbo–Dayu case, Dayu says Huangbo's old-woman concern was so pressing that "for you he exhausted himself completely" (為汝得徹困); when Linji returns, he says it was "only because the old-woman concern was pressing" (祇為老婆心切). In another exchange, a layman calls Huitang's concern pressing and Huitang replies, "I only want you to arrive home" (秖要公到家耳). The records thus show the idiom through predicates, agents, and replies rather than through a modern emotional gloss.
Senses.Note: The phrase is neither automatically praise nor a guarantee that the action described is harmless. A commentary reports that people call Jinniu's carrying rice and dancing "pressing old-woman concern," then rejects their reading: it is "arsenic soaked in honey to entice people to put it in their mouths" (以蜜浸砒霜誘人下口). Elsewhere the location of Yaoshan's pressing concern is itself made the next interview question: "where is the place of his pressing old-woman concern?" (那裏是他老婆心切處). It can also enter verse, as in "pressing old-woman concern, laughing ha-ha, letting bystanders say long or short" (老婆心切呵呵笑，一任傍人說短長). Common frames include "only because" (the “only because” form, 24 occurrences; variant 祇為, 7) and "so very" (得恁麼老婆心切, 18). These uses support a forceful relational appraisal while preserving the possibility of criticism.

Senses.Explanation: Old-woman Chan is an appraisal label for talk or handling compared in the records with an old woman's solicitous speech. Masters apply it approvingly, critically, and ironically to sayings and encounters; it is not the name of a separate lineage. Dahui Zonggao asks whether the National Teacher's three calls may be called 'speaking old-woman Chan, dragging through mud and water' (說老婆禪，拕泥帶水, ‘speaking old-woman Chan, dragging through mud and water’), and elsewhere says that if he had initially explained everything this way, the student would later have cursed him. Huang Yuangong's letter contrasts Miyun Yuanwu's 'pungent handling' (手段辛辣) with people elsewhere who speak old-woman Chan. The label is also attached to actual old-woman encounters in the Floating Cup and Mount Wutai cases. Dahui Zonggao calls a line 'old-woman Chan in the great Tang country' (大唐國裏老婆禪), and Wansong Xingxiu asks whether someone with firm heels would consent to learn old-woman Chan. The term is therefore an attested appraisal label rather than the name of a separate lineage: records apply it approvingly, critically, and ironically to different sayings and encounters.
Senses.Note: The entry retains the literal gendered image because the corpus repeatedly connects the compound with an old woman's speech and with the broader collocation 'old-woman heart', which occurs 706 times in 214 texts; 'old-woman heart is urgent' (老婆心切) occurs 270 times in 129. The exact definition formulas yield two occurrences of 'one who speaks old-woman Chan' (說老婆禪者) and two of 'call it old-woman Chan' (喚作老婆禪), but no stable equation that narrows the label beyond the recorded comparisons and deployments.

Senses.Explanation: Laozi is the pre-Chan Chinese figure whom Chan records quote and place beside Confucius, Zhuangzi, and Gautama. Yongming Yanshou assigns Laozi to the ‘empty mystery’ in a threefold comparison; Fushi Tongxian and Guxue Zhe juxtapose his ‘holding to the one’ with sayings of Confucius and Gautama. Yanxi Guangwen turns the story that Laozi transformed the foreigners into buddhas into a public question: why did he not transform them into Daoists? The Chan bend is not a new biography of Laozi but his deployment as a named voice and case figure within comparative instruction and teaching-seat questioning.

Senses.Explanation: As a productive noun or epithet, old fellow means an ‘old fellow’ and lets Chan speakers refer to teachers and case figures with striking familiarity. Nanyue Jiqi calls Xuefeng ‘this old fellow’ after raising his words; Dahui uses the same form for the named teaching figure in a self-narrated confrontation. Yinyuan asks who will vindicate ‘this old fellow,’ meaning Shakyamuni, while Zhean groups Dongshan, Shishuang, and Ming’an as ‘three old fellows.’ The Chan bend lies in this flexible familiarity: revered lineage and pre-lineage figures can be praised, tested, blamed, or handled as participants in a present public exchange rather than kept at ceremonial distance.
