SearchAliases: a rat entering an ox horn
the rat driven into the ox horn
Zen a rat entering an ox horn
Senses.Explanation: A rat entering an ox horn is a narrowing image whose endpoints are stated differently in different passages. Dahui says to press inquiry until there is no further place to investigate, “like a rat entering an ox horn,” when the stealing mind suddenly ends. In a winter-solstice exchange, an unnamed monk asks how a patch-robed monk turns around when the yin forces are exhausted and one yang returns; Xutang Zhiyu answers with the phrase. Another instruction says to press forward day after day and month after month like the rat in the horn, and explicitly says that then a living road appears. The image can also be used as criticism: one record says that a declining lineage becomes narrower and narrower like the rat in the horn, while Ciming scolds an answer consisting of the phrase. These attested contrasts prevent the dictionary from turning the image into a fixed declaration of either hopeless dead end or guaranteed success. Chan makes the narrowing horn a public answer, an instruction, a rebuked reply, and an appraisal of a lineage's contraction. The exact phrase occurs 30 times in 24 allowlist texts.

Senses.Explanation: The sacred monk is the enshrined monastic guardian figure seated in the communal hall or represented at the monastery. Monastic rules assign the figure a seat and greetings; Fayin Shanning and Foyan Qingyuan send their assemblies back to it, while Yunju Yineng asks an unnamed monastic questioner what it said. Senses.Explanation: To continue the lineage lamps is to carry Chan succession from predecessor to successor and from generation to generation. Yongjue Yuanxian defines the governing lamp image in the Extensive Record of Chan Master Yongjue Yuanxian: successive transmission is compared to a lamp because it breaks darkness and reveals things, and because its illumination can continue without end. His histories then call more than seventy generations an unbroken chain of linked lamps and describe them as linking the lamps while continuing the flame. Hanxiu Ruqian uses the phrase in memorial verses for succession after receiving his predecessor's blows and for two named lineage holders carrying the line in different regions. Zefeng Yue applies it to an ancestral portrait during a teaching-seat address. These uses concern public lineage continuity, not ordinary lamps physically fastened together.
Senses.Note: The exact headword has 104 occurrences in 28 allowed texts. Most belong to the book title treated in the second sense; the free phrase recurs with being unbroken, continuing the flame, succession, generations, ancestral portraits, and separate teaching regions. A complete concordance review found no independently attested hardware sense. A festival line about lamps and the moon reverses the graph order and therefore does not establish one.

Senses.Explanation: The book Linked-Lamp Essentials is a specific Chan compilation, not the act of continuing a lineage. In his self-preface, Huiweng Wuming says that he selected material from more than six hundred teachers, arranged encounters, questions and answers, comments on old and recent cases, and essential statements under each person's chapter, divided the work into thirty fascicles, and gave it this title. Li Yong's preface says the title was placed on the work and the blocks were carved for circulation. Yongjue Yuanxian later places Wuming's compilation among the five lamp records. A lineage biography records Wuming as its compiler, while Sichong's republication preface calls it the Linked-Lamp Record and recounts its printing history.
Senses.Note: This is a different thing from lineage succession: it is a named thirty-fascicle text with a compiler, contents, prefaces, printing blocks, circulation history, and an abbreviated record title. The full title occurs 77 times in 13 allowed texts; the shorter title occurs once. The explicit referent label in the preferred target keeps the distinction visible without relying on capitalization alone.

Senses.Explanation: Asked “what is the phrase before sound?” Xuanquan Yan answers with the vocalization “un” (吽), and Heyushan Guanghui says, “it is just like not saying” (恰似不道). Huanglian directly answers, “before sound there is no phrase; after the sound, bring your question” (聲前無句，聲後問將來). Later addresses make contrary predicates within the same public record: one says “everyone originally has” the phrase, while the Blue Cliff Record says “the thousand sages do not transmit” it. These are attested answers and claims, not grounds for choosing an ineffable reading. Zen bends the temporal phrase into a recurrent interview prompt whose answers may themselves be spoken sounds; this entry preserves that observable deployment and the corpus’s own disagreement.

Senses.Explanation: The paired sensory objects of ear and eye: sound (聲) and visible form or color (色). Chan records do more than repeat the pair abstractly. Yongjia's exchange explicitly assigns them to the faculties — 'when eyes and ears meet sound and form' (眼耳緣聲色時) — and asks what is the substance of sound and form. Dahui makes the pair demonstrable during a public address: he raises the whisk and says, 'this is form,' strikes the Chan seat and says, 'this is sound' (這箇是色／這箇是聲). Another record gives ordinary audible examples: wind in pine trees, frogs, and crows are all sound, while saying that what one discriminates is sound and form. The corpus also predicates 'pass through all sound and form without obstruction' (透一切聲色，無有滯礙) and draws its own distinction between function 'together with sound and form' and 'the affairs of sound and form' (用同聲色而不是聲色之事). The Zen deviation is this repeated use as a named field of public testing and concrete demonstration; the graphs still denote what is heard and seen.

Senses.Explanation: “Right under your heels” locates what is immediately beneath one’s stance and recurs in demands to inspect, cut off, or pass what lies there. Chan interviews repeatedly turn this ordinary location back upon the person questioned. A reply can be appraised with 'right under your heels, thirty blows would be fitting'; Poshan Haiming can ask 'how deep is the water under your heels?', direct a questioner to 'recognize it right under your heels,' or answer a request for direct pointing with 'look clearly right under your heels.' The phrase also marks relative position in a public comparison: if the unnamed monastic can distinguish the kinds of leakage, Dongshan is under his heels; if not, he is under Dongshan's heels. A stock question asks about 'the matter under your heels' and receives 'putting a head atop your head.' The Chan-specific bend is consistent and observable: the spatial phrase becomes the immediate locus of an interviewer's demand, appraisal, or reversal, often contrasted with what the questioner seeks elsewhere or above. The texts do not supply a further object hidden beneath the feet, and neither does this entry.

Senses.Explanation: Linji’s shout is a named Chan device, repeatedly paired or contrasted with Deshan’s staff and tested in later encounters. The named shout associated by the Chan record with Linji Yixuan. Device lists pair 'Linji's shout' with 'Deshan's staff,' and later sermons compare the shout to rushing thunder. The phrase is not merely a historical label: masters publicly ask what its purport is, demand that an unnamed monastic produce it, or declare that they have no use for it today. The corpus also polices the inherited emblem. In a later Fushi exchange, the presiding teacher strikes after being asked what indication lies beyond Deshan's staff and Linji's shout, then says that calling it 'staff-and-shout' sends one to hell like an arrow. Thus Zen bends an ordinary shout into a named lineage implement and object of later interview, imitation, comparison, and criticism; the entry reports only those recorded deployments.

Senses.Explanation: Able to act, come and go, or respond without constraint: free and at ease, at liberty, or freely. The word is attested 4,537 times in 388 allowlisted texts. Foyan Qingyuan closes an address by telling everyone to drink tea in the hall, free and at ease (堂中喫茶，自由自在). Yunmen Wenyan says that only upon arriving here can one roll up and extend freely, with response and function unimpaired (卷舒自在，應用無虧). The Yongzheng Emperor uses the result phrase “obtain great freedom” (獲大自在), while Zhean Jingfan says “unconstrained and unbound in every place; without fault at every time” (一切處自在無繫，一切時無所過患). Dahui Zonggao says that one then enters birth and death and obtains great freedom (出生入死得大自在). Other records pair freedom in birth and death with freedom in coming and going, and explicitly test whether freedom at death matches ordinary freedom amid encountered objects. Zen bends an everyday freedom word into public tests about response, movement, birth, and death, while Baizhang Huaihai warns against casually declaring a buddha free or not free. Adjective, adverb, result noun, and the repeated form “free and at ease” remain grammatical deployments of the same condition.

Occurrences.Kwic: 從本已來。性自滿足。處染不垢。修治不淨。故云自性清淨。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source text Record of the Source-Mirror (宗鏡錄): Yongming Yanshou is the exact author, explaining “one’s own nature is pure” by saying it is complete from the beginning, unstained amid defilement, and not purified by cultivation.

Senses.Explanation: One’s own nature is the nature attributed to the person or mind itself. The records place it in public questions, explanations of what it contains, compound names such as ‘the naturally true buddha of one’s own nature,’ and claims about what does or does not depart from it. The expression occurs 2,091 times in 260 allowlisted texts. The Platform Record says that one's own nature is originally clean, contains the ten thousand things, and is not apart from them; another recension lists it as originally clean, not arising or perishing, complete in itself, unmoving, and able to produce the ten thousand things. These are the record's predicates, not an imported definition. Other Chan records use the term in questions about seeing, clarifying, or being unaware of one's own nature. One discourse says that what is reluctantly named the naturally true buddha of one's own nature is also called the cited speaker of one's own house. Direct answers do not settle into a single formula: asked 'What is one's own nature?' the cited speaker says, 'I will not say'; asked about the naturally true buddha of one's own nature while tending a fire, another tells the cited participant to bring a bundle of firewood.

Senses.Explanation: As a figure for speech, the tongue is said to lack bones, be cut off, or be restrained from moving in public exchange. A person's capacity to speak is what Chan verdicts test, trust, disable, or demand under the image of the tongue. Yungai Jipeng and Chengtian Weijian each answer a public question by saying that the tongue has no bone. Guanghui Yuanlian says that he no longer doubts the tongues of old masters, and Shoushan Xingnian immediately asks him to state his understanding. Huangbo Xiyun predicts that Linji Yixuan will cut off the tongues of everyone under heaven. Longyuan Fa says that a demon king has cut off the Buddha's tongue and offers to redress the wrong. Huiyun Benchong Sheng orders a respondent to produce a statement without moving the tongue, then says the respondent's shout still involves lips and mouth. These are speech acts and verdicts, not reports of bodily injury, so they establish a Zen-loaded referent separate from the organ that can be bitten.

Senses.Note: Two independent bodily witnesses establish the ordinary anatomical referent. No special Zen deviation is asserted for it.

Senses.Explanation: The tiny mustard seed is the records’ scale-comparison object, repeatedly paired with reversals in which Mount Sumeru is contained within it. The graphs name a mustard seed. The allowlisted corpus has 442 hits in 146 texts. Its small size supplies the comparison ‘mustard-seed-sized’ (芥子許, 67 hits in 50 texts), as when a named record subject speaks of a doubt as small as a mustard seed. The corpus also repeatedly pairs the seed with Mount Sumeru in both directions: ‘Sumeru contains a mustard seed’ (須彌納芥子, 46 hits in 30 texts) and ‘a mustard seed contains Sumeru’ (芥子納須彌, 59 hits in 44 texts). In the Guizong encounter, Li Bo accepts the first statement but asks whether the second is false; Guizong asks where Li Bo’s ten thousand books are held in a body the size of a coconut. In another exchange, the two directions receive the one-word answers ‘easy’ and ‘difficult.’ A later address records mountains, earth, trees, monastics, laypeople, sages, and ordinary people placed inside a mustard seed without the seed becoming narrow. These are the corpus’s recorded scale constructions; the entry does not turn them into a symbolic meaning for the seed.
Senses.Note: All required definition formulas were searched. One ‘What is the mustard seed?’ question is included because its answer, ‘It blocks your eye,’ is an attested direct response, not adopted here as a universal lexical equation. Deployment inventory includes the small-measure construction, both Sumeru constructions, question-and-answer use, and a later expanded list of what is placed inside the seed.

Senses.Explanation: To be blankly at a loss. In Chan encounter narratives it is an observable failure to answer or proceed: after being asked "who observes, and what is quiet?" the recorded questioner is at a loss; after being seized and ordered "speak! speak!" the recorded questioner is at a loss and is pushed away. The record makes the absence of an answer explicit in "the identified master was at a loss and did not know how to reply" (師茫然不知對). It also applies collectively: after the answer "clear conversation face to face—if not buddha, then who?" the assembly is all at a loss (眾皆茫然). A training biography records a student being required to give one fitting word and withdrawing at a loss (師茫然退). The Zen deviation lies in this recurring public-interview function: the adjective marks the recorded point where a participant or assembly has no response, not a mystical state and not an explanation of why the exchange defeated them.

Senses.Explanation: Straw sandals remain literal footwear while serving as the ordinary equipment and expense of traveling on foot through the Chan record. Footwear woven from grass or straw. In Chan records the sandals belong especially to going on foot between teachers: “to wear out straw sandals” and “buy more straw sandals and travel on foot for thirty years” make the ordinary shoe part of the institutional life of itinerant inquiry. The object also enters named encounters: Deshan turns his back on the hall, puts on his sandals, and leaves; Zhaozhou puts a sandal on his head after Nanquan recounts cutting the cat. Huangbo calls “the patriarchs' dark purport” “worn-out straw sandals” and says bare feet would be better. The corpus records these concrete actions and comparisons without supplying a symbolic gloss for the sandals.

Senses.Explanation: Zhuang Zhou is the pre-Chan figure whom the corpus invokes through a small roster of named stories and stock lines, rather than through a general biography. The name occurs 168 times in 93 allowlisted texts. Chan records cite “Zhuang Zhou dreamed of the butterfly; he is not me; the butterfly dreamed of Zhuang Zhou; I am not him” (莊周夢蝶，渠不是我；蝶夢莊周，我不是渠), recount that when his wife died he drummed on a basin and sang, and list learning connected with Confucius, Laozi, Zhuang Zhou, and the Hundred Schools. The corpus also deploys his name in the recurring sword line “Zhuang Zhou’s sword killed three thousand guests; from then on the road to Peach Spring did not go through” (莊周劍殺三千客，從此桃源路不通). A separate teaching-seat formula asks, “where are the three thousand swordsmen now?” and answers, “Zhuang Zhou alone is permitted to bring great peace” (三千劒客今何在？獨許莊周致太平). Another verse directly addresses him: “a message to Zhuang Zhou: stop deliberating” (寄語莊周休擬議). Thus the Zen Zhuang Zhou is the named dreamer, basin-drummer, learned figure, sword-line figure, and addressee that masters quote and redeploy. This entry does not supplement those deployments with an outside life story.

SearchAliases: Zen do not get it wrong
Senses.Explanation: An imperative: do not (莫) understand or take it (會) wrongly (錯). Its distinct Chan deployment is as warnings that named speakers attach directly to a saying or answer in public discourse. Asked the intention of the coming from the West, Anguo Hongtao answers 'it is so, but do not get it wrong.' An extended address says not to infer 'not round and not sudden' from the preceding words and not to present borrowed, similar, or calculated phrases as one's own understanding, repeating 'do not get it wrong.' Elsewhere Bao’en Huiming warns an assembly not to say that speech, silence, movement, and stillness are all buddha-affairs. The formula can also follow an unexplained seasonal statement — 'yesterday snow, today it melts' — leaving the warning itself as the only explicit appraisal. These contexts establish the public-interview function without supplying an interpretation of what the preceding words secretly mean.

Senses.Explanation: In case collections and recorded sayings, an interjected comment (著語) is compact wording inserted against a cited exchange, often immediately after one of its lines and introduced by “appends a comment and says” (著語云). The Blue Cliff Record preserves Xuedou Chongxian's repeated comments such as “seen through,” and Yuanwu Keqin's recorded sayings insert “wrong” after successive turns of an older case. Wansong Xingxiu explicitly quotes comments by Yuanwu and then answers them from his own position. Tianyin Yuanxiu and Hongzhi Zhengjue likewise interrupt cited exchanges with short verdicts. A reviewed unnamed monastic questioner asks Langting Ting for a comment on a named case, while Xiangtian Jinian says he will place a comment against each line. The form can therefore name either the inserted wording or the act of adding it; it does not denote ordinary authorship where the verb authored merely precedes the noun recorded sayings.

Senses.Explanation: The records warn against collapsing into blank nothing, then answer that blankness itself is absent or is not blank. Literally, 'fall into emptiness,' but in these records the observable warning is against falling into a blank nothing. The term occurs 325 times in 128 allowed texts; the expanded form 'fall into blank annihilation' (落空亡) occurs 63 times in 37 texts. Dahui reports people who hear 'a teaching in which nothing is obtained' (無所得法) and become afraid that they will fall into blankness; he answers by asking whether the very one who fears falling into blankness is empty. A lamp dialogue answers the charge that Chan teachers mostly fall into blankness by saying that letters and other things arise from wisdom and that, when 'great function appears before one' (大用現前), there can be no falling into blankness. Another exchange dismantles the spatial wording itself: asked whether 'originally there is nothing' falls into blankness, the reply asks, 'Since blankness is absent, from where could falling be established?' (空既是無，墮從何立). The same collection says that people fear forgetting mind because they fear falling into blankness with nowhere to get hold, then says 'blankness itself is originally not blank' (空本無空). There are 37 occurrences of 'not fall into blankness' (不落空) and 21 of the warning 'do not fall into blankness' (莫落空).
Senses.Note: The translation 'blankness' follows the records' direct corrections: 'Since blankness is absent, from where could falling be established?' (空既是無，墮從何立), and 'blankness itself is originally not blank' (空本無空). The entry records the corpus's accusations, warnings, and replies.

Senses.Explanation: The phrase asks or states the place where something comes down, settles, or finds its point of application. Chan exchanges use that ordinary landing-place relation to press where a saying, action, or person’s understanding actually comes to rest. Chan records apply it to words, answers, cases, actions, people, and one's life: 'know where it lands' (知落處) occurs 770 times in 205 texts, while 'not know where it lands' (不知落處) occurs 172 times in 89 texts. Yuanwu says that as soon as Danxia raised it, he knew where it landed (才方舉起便知落處), and his Blue Cliff prose twice contrasts knowing and not knowing where Mazu's public case lands. Dahui asks whether the assembly knows where his teacher's words land and says that knowing it identifies the top graduate (還知師翁落處麼。若知落處便識得狀元). Changqing asks the cited participant, 'Do you understand where it lands?' (還委落處麼). A lamp record joins origin and destination: 'if you know where it arises, then you know where life lands' (若知起處。便知身命落處). Xiuyelin gives the richest explicit relation found: 'the fundamental matter is precisely where the person's own life-source lands' (本分事者，即當人本命元辰之落處也). The article therefore keeps the verbal image and reports what the texts assign a landing point; it does not replace that image with an imported abstraction.

Senses.Explanation: In Chan records, the image of intertwining vines denotes language that proliferates, entangles, or demands cutting through. Yuanwu Keqin directly joins the tangle to the need to cut off words, calls old cases vine-tangle cases, and elsewhere praises action that cuts the tangle straight off. Zhongfeng Mingben lists vine-Chan among defective labels and describes later students caught where vines spread everywhere. Qingshan Puning self-deprecatingly calls his unavoidable address tangling with the assembly. Dahui Zonggao says Wushang had already entered mud and water for the assembly and produced no little tangle. Lingyao Liang offers a vine-entangled proclamation for the community to disentangle together. The metaphor can criticize interpretive or case language, describe a named speaker's own speech, or name material deliberately presented for disentangling; it is not a flat synonym for every use of words. A literal-plant control searched plant predicates and collocations such as sprouting, spreading, branching, rooting, binding, covering the ground, and filling the ground. In the retained Chan uses these extend the same speech-and-case tangle—lineage talk sprouts, sayings branch, cases cover the ground, or words bind a participant—rather than describing cultivated or botanical vines. The selected evidence therefore supports one loaded tangle referent, not a hidden second plant article.
Senses.Note: Literal vegetation/concrete-entanglement controls were run across all 2,876 exact hits. Apparent plant grammar repeatedly governs discourse, sayings, cases, or lineage proliferation; no independently active botanical referent survived for this entry. Eight witnesses from five distinct works remain sufficient for the loaded sense.

Senses.Explanation: A round sitting mat is the portable mat on which a person sits in the hall or quarters. Chan records place bodies on the mat, speak of wearing one through long use, carry it, break it, or cite it in encounters. These are uses of monastery furniture; the mat remains concrete rather than becoming the name of a procedure.

Senses.Explanation: Empty space is the open expanse in which things can be located or compared. The term is attested 5,943 times in 279 allowlisted texts. Chan records also make that ordinary expanse measurable, containable, breakable, and fillable. Productive forms include "in empty space" (虛空中, 90 occurrences), "inside empty space" (虛空裏, 136), and "like empty space" (如虛空, 364). They also record impossible or emphatic actions: "empty space shattered" (虛空粉碎, 167), "break empty space" (打破虛空, 85), and "empty space burst apart" (虛空迸裂). Zhongfeng says of an incense offering, "empty space cannot contain it; the great earth cannot support it" (虛空包不住，大地載不起). Zhe'an Fan says that if one understands at a stated point, "empty space can be measured" (虛空可量). A memorial narrative describes one who raised his head and suddenly forgot confusion and awakening, "lucid like empty space, impossible to approach or lodge in" (如虛空玲瓏不可湊泊). The corpus also says "empty space has no inside or outside" (虛空無內外, 9), while a formal address says that the Chan lineage's defining feature "fills empty space, with nowhere to evade it" (充塞虛空，無處回避). These are literal comparisons and recorded predicates; no single further sense is imposed on all 5,943 occurrences.

Senses.Explanation: “Empty space shatters” is an impossible breakage used to describe a decisive collapse of the field that had seemed to contain everything. Accounts of Gaofeng's awakening pair it with the great earth sinking and self and objects being forgotten; public addresses then reuse the phrase as a challenge—before a saying space is packed full, after it space is shattered, so where is it between? The records present a reported event and interview formula, not physical cosmology.

Senses.Note: The corpus has 578 hits in 188 allowlisted texts; Toad Chan (蝦蟆禪) occurs 11 times in 10 texts. Five exact headword witnesses and one marked graphic-variant witness cover definition, answer, verse-like pairing, public exchange, appraisal, and ordinary animal enumeration. These deployments still denote the animal or its image; direct human epithets are separated below.

Senses.Explanation: The animal appears both in ordinary lists and in striking Chan sayings. Baima Ai answers a question about the pure teaching-body with a toad at the bottom of a well swallowing the moon (井底蝦蟆吞却月). Sanyi Mingyu pairs a monkey accustomed to climbing a tree with a toad jumping into a well (猢猻慣上樹，蝦蟆跳入井). In an exchange with Xinghua Cuyuan, Yang Yi says that a three-legged toad jumps into the sky (三脚蝦蟆跳上天), and Xinghua lets it jump as it pleases. Dongshan Xiaocong lists the variant-written toad with earthworms as creatures having holes. The animal also enters the named appraisal Toad Chan. Tian'an Sheng explicitly asks what Toad Chan is and describes a toad croaking like a drum in the rain and crying, “what suffering?” (蝦蟆遇天雨，叫喚聲如鼓……何苦？何苦？). Juelang Dasheng applies the same label in a public exchange. Zen bends the ordinary animal-name into answers, impossible animal actions, and a named Chan appraisal, while the records continue to use it for the creature itself.

Senses.Note: Three exact witnesses from three independent records establish direct naming and comparison of human respondents. The local rebukes differ, but each headword refers to the person rather than supplying a different reading of the animal scene.

Senses.Explanation: The same animal-name can denote a human target directly called or compared to a toad. When an interlocutor cannot supply another question, Yunmen Wenyan calls him “this dead toad” (這死蝦蟆). Chaozong Tongren says that he cast a hook for a giant fish but caught a toad (拋鉤釣鯤鯨，釣得箇蝦蟆); the addressee protests against being pressed from free status into servitude. Yinyuan Longqi calls another respondent a forehead-marked toad (點額蝦蟆) and then says he is drowned in dead water. The human target is a different thing from a toad in a well or rain, so these direct epithets remain a separate corpus-wide sense; the entry does not project the appraisal onto every animal occurrence.

Senses.Explanation: A snail's horn supplies the minute ground for two recurrent corpus families. In prose and verse, people contend for “the minuteness of a snail's horn,” and profit and fame on a fly's head and snail's horn become an empty battle. A discussion explicitly recalls the Zhuangzi story of Chu and Man fighting over territory and leaving corpses for ten thousand miles, then places even the yielding of Yao and Shun and the conquests of Tang and Wu in “the waste of the snail's horn.” Chan verses also reverse the scale: one puts the universe on the tip of a snail's horn, while a hall address opposes the passing traveler's labor over fly-head and snail-horn matters to a great treasure hidden in the body. The minute object, its contest language, and the vast things placed on it are one image under different predicates. The Chan deviation lies in bringing the horn into hall speech and scale-reversal verse, not in assigning it a hidden meaning. The exact phrase occurs 36 times in 26 allowlist texts.

Senses.Explanation: The minute jiaoming insect is an extremely small creature. In the Collected Guidelines of the Lineage Masters, Yuejiang Yin makes the scale explicit by saying that it builds its nest on a mosquito's eyelash, hence the descriptive alternate “mosquito-eyelash insect.” Chan verses and addresses repeatedly reverse that scale: Dahui Zonggao puts a giant turtle inside its eye; Mengshan Yi has it drain the ocean; Lia'an Qingyu is asked about its swallowing a tiger; Yinshan Can puts a night market in its eye; and Zhongfang Tianlun says it swallows five Mount Sumerus. In the Surviving Draft of the Continued Lamp, Gaofeng Yuanmiao says that such an insect has blundered into his sky-spanning net; the line occurs inside Duanya Liaoyi's biography because Gaofeng is speaking about Duanya. These are distinct large-in-small actions and comparisons involving the same tiny creature, not evidence that the headword itself means the cosmos or carries one fixed interpretation. The headword occurs 394 times in 166 allowlist texts.

Senses.Explanation: A transmission line is the continuity that Chan records locate through cases, question-and-answer, sentences, and succession. Caoshan Benji answers the withered-tree dragon-hum question by saying that the line is unbroken. Yuanwu Keqin says that the ancients' line is unbroken because the question is in the answer and the answer in the question; elsewhere he says that differing speakers do not lose it sentence by sentence. Yunxi Langting Ting directly names precise question-and-answer as the line unbroken. Xueguan Zhiyin passes what he received onward as the continuation of Shouchang's line and the extension of Boshan's house style. Zen thus bends hereditary and bodily continuity into a documented connective line through public speech and teacher-successor transmission.
Senses.Note: Five curated anchors across independent works support this continuity sense, including teacher-successor transmission; hereditary bloodline and bodily circulation remain separate referents in the following senses.

Senses.Explanation: To travel on foot is to leave one community and visit teachers or monasteries as an itinerant monastic. Cases ask where the traveller is going, how many sandals the journey has cost, and what the business of travelling is; the movement is institutional and interview-facing, not tourism.

Entries.CreatedBy: Codex fresh-build lane C

Senses.Explanation: Travel on foot means to journey from place to place on one's own feet. Chan records use the expression for departing an instructor or monastery, crossing the various regions, and seeking other teachers. Dongshan Liangjie asks permission to travel and is directed toward Nanquan; Yaoshan Weiyan asks whether a visitor has travelled through the regions seeking what is hard to obtain. Later records speak of travelling a thousand miles to seek a lineage teacher and of a 'person travelling on foot' (行腳人) or 'patch-robed monk travelling on foot' (衲僧行腳). The walking journey is literal; whom the traveller visits and what is asked belong to each encounter.
Senses.Note: The corpus also turns the activity into a test. Asked "What is the affair of traveling on foot?" (如何是行腳事), Poshan answers, "face to face, looking at one another, the mouth is like wood" (面面相看口如木). Another instruction calls someone who has passed through a cited exchange a "true person traveling on foot" (真行腳人). No formula in the corpus makes the term a separate prescribed system.

Senses.PreferredTarget: monastic robe, bowl, and personal effects
Senses.Explanation: The material monastic robe, alms bowl, and, by extension, personal effects kept with them. The allowlisted corpus has 513 hits in 115 texts, including records in which the objects are thrown onto a rock, lifted, carried, guarded, inventoried, or burned with a person's other implements. Monastic regulations also name a ‘robe-and-bowl attendant’ (衣鉢侍者, 9 hits in 3 texts), who receives the seal in one installation procedure. In the Caoqi record, this attendant raises the robe associated with the object that could not be lifted at Dayu Ridge. These passages keep the material objects and their custodial office visible even where the same pair also marks succession.
Senses.Note: This first sense covers the material pair and its administrative extension to personal effects and the attendant responsible for them. It is separated from the succession-token sense because regulations can order the objects burned or placed in custody without describing succession.

Senses.PreferredTarget: the robe and bowl as evidence of lineage succession
Senses.Explanation: The same physical robe and bowl treated as passed evidence of lineage succession. The corpus records ‘transmit the robe and bowl’ (傳衣鉢, 31 hits in 26 texts), ‘entrust the robe and bowl’ (付衣鉢, 10 hits in 8 texts), and one exact occurrence of ‘robe and bowl transmitted in succession’ (衣鉢相傳). The Dayu Ridge account explicitly calls the robe ‘a token of trust.’ Yuansou Xingduan says that Huangmei's robe and bowl were entrusted to Lu, while Qining Wenyi asks which robe and bowl Lu actually transmitted. The question is recorded as a question rather than resolved here into an object different from the material robe and bowl.
Senses.Note: Historical succession does not make this sense specific to a named individual. The selected passages show the physical token, later transmission language, and a later challenge about what was transmitted. The seven required definition formulas were searched; no additional lexical self-definition was found.

Senses.Explanation: A patch-robed monk is the Chan participant marked by the patched robe and repeatedly addressed, questioned, and appraised in public encounters. The robe-word becomes a public standard in compounds asking after the patch-robed monk's eye, conduct, own affair, house, and manner. Asked “what is a patch-robed monk?” (如何是衲僧), one reviewed exchange answers, “investigating, seeking, and visiting the Way” (參尋訪道). Another exchange asks for “the patch-robed monk's own affair” (衲僧分上事) and answers, “when you want to walk, walk; when you want to sit, sit” (要行即行，要坐即坐). The corpus also asks directly about “the patch-robed monk's eye” (衲僧眼) and “the patch-robed monk's place of conduct” (衲僧行履處). It speaks institutionally of what can be used “under the patch-robed monk's gate” (衲僧門下), and appraises an assembly as lacking anyone with “the air of a patch-robed monk” (衲僧氣息). The Chan deviation lies in this public standard: the robe-word names the person expected to answer within the encounter record, while the compounds test that person's eye, conduct, handle, own affair, and house. These are attested compound deployments, not claims about an inner state.

Senses.Explanation: The wearer of patched monastic robes: a patch-robed monk or monk in patched robes. The term occurs 2,174 times in 317 allowed texts and names monks whom Chan teachers address, question, appraise, and describe through their clothing, livelihood, daily activity, and house style. Pin Jixiang gives a direct naming formula: 'Each wears a hat and waist-pack and is named a patch-robed monk; name and reality should match' (箇箇都是頂笠腰包，名為衲子，要當名實相稱). Nanquan Puyuan says, 'Dragons and snakes are easy to distinguish; patch-robed monks are hard to fool' (龍蛇易辨衲子難謾). Yushan Shangsi calls an astute patch-robed monk difficult to find (伶俐衲子難得), while Jingqing Daofu twice praises Fengxue Yanzhao as 'a fine patch-robed monk' (衲子俊哉). Zhufeng Zhenxu says, 'The patch-robed monk's eyebrows leap' (衲子眉毛𨁝跳), in an end-of-retreat hall verse. Minshu names a snow hat and cloud gourd as 'the patch-robed monk's livelihood' (雪笠雲瓢，為衲子之活計). Haizhuang Azi Jinwu says that the patch-robed monk's daily activity already has a great treasury of light and requires being such a person. Hansong Zhicao contrasts 'keeping to poverty and quiet, the patch-robed monk's house style' with 'pursuing warmth and bustle, the ordinary person's livelihood' (固窮守寂，衲子家風；附熱趨喧，常人活計). Asked directly, 'What is a patch-robed monk?' (如何是衲子), Shanhui answers, 'Bare-bodied atop Mount Sumeru; do not go toward the northern continent' (赤身須彌頂，莫向越單行). Zen bends a clothing label into an institutional and interpersonal name for the monks addressed and tested in the teaching community; it does not make praise, clothing, or house style into separate person-senses.

Senses.Explanation: The “meaning from the West” is the shortened public-interview form of the question about the patriarch’s coming from the West; the records answer it with fresh words and actions rather than one explanatory definition. Direct abbreviated questions ask simply “what is the meaning from the West?” Tianzhu Chonghui answers with a white ape carrying its young and butterflies holding flowers; Helin Xuansu answers that understanding is not understanding and doubt is not doubt. Yunfeng Zudeng answers with striking the forehead and nose, Mazu Daoyi asks what meaning is present now, Sanfeng Hanyue Fazang says “three years carrying one boat,” Linji asks Longya for the Chan board, Zhaozhou descends from the seat, and Shitou sends the questioner to ask the exposed pillar. The Chan bend is the abbreviation’s life as a public test whose many incompatible replies are preserved rather than harmonized into a hidden proposition.

Senses.Explanation: To see one's own nature. Chan records place this claim in transmission formulas, instructions, questions, and explicit challenges. Hongren links it with directly becoming a buddha; a text attributed to Bodhidharma says that seeking a buddha requires it. Huangbo Xiyun answers a direct question by refusing to make nature a second object seen by a separate seeing subject. Dahui Zonggao repeats that it is required for an unerring road and immediately asks which mind recognizes and which nature is seen. Zhongfeng Mingben says direct pointing is no longer direct once it enters speech or contrivance, while Yongming Yanshou says that once nature is seen, mind and the teaching remedies both cease. The phrase names a claimed recognition, but the records repeatedly test what the grammar of a seer looking at a separate nature would wrongly add.

Senses.Explanation: The faculty or nature of seeing, a noun phrase rather than the action of seeing one's own nature. Hanyue Fazang and Bore Gulin each quote an outside claimant who treats this seeing faculty as an unchanging witness that survives the destruction of a visible tile or stove; both speakers identify that claim as an error. Huanyou Zhengchuan groups the phrase with the nature of hearing and the nature of awareness, then says seeing and nature are not two separately visible things. This distinct segmentation matters because translating these passages as an achievement of seeing one's nature would reverse their grammar and hide the criticism.

Yaoshan Weiyan reports hearing it as the southern direct-pointing claim. Tianqi Benrui insists that the nature seen and Buddha become are not another person’s. Yuanan Feng contrasts it with accumulating deportment and marks, while an unnamed questioner asks Juelang Daosheng what the paired slogan means. The records thus retain both its compact banner form and explicit internal explanations.

AlternateTargets: what one sees, hears, senses, and knows
Senses.Explanation: The four ordinary functions of seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, named together as a fixed sequence. Chan texts warn against constructing an additional understanding from them or treating some separate entity as standing behind them. The same functions can be described as the cause of birth and death and, without changing the wording, as the root of release. Other passages say that they neither obstruct complete command nor bind a person in themselves. Translate the four actions directly; do not replace them with an imported technical noun such as 'awareness.'
Senses.Note: The corpus has 787 matches in 162 files. Sixty-six matches in forty-six files occur in constructions about leaving or being apart from seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing. Five passages in five files use the explicit nominal form 'as for seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing,' and three in three use 'the so-called seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing.' The corrective passages show that the compound names the four functions themselves, not a separate faculty.

Senses.Explanation: Huike's fixed reply in the mind-settling case: ‘having sought the mind, I could not find it. Huike says his mind is not at ease; Bodhidharma tells him to bring the mind so it can be set at ease; Huike answers with this phrase; Bodhidharma replies that the mind has now been set at ease. Subsequent records repeatedly examine the quoted sentence. Yuanwu asks why Huike answered only this. Juelang distinguishes Huike's utterance from later students repeating the same words. Zhuanyu Heng explicitly judges Huike's reply as falling into conceptual understanding when comparing it with the flower sermon, while Wanfeng asks how the sentence should be understood and comments on it in another register. Daxiu Zhu redeploys the wording in a first-person public question and is immediately asked where he is now. Huigong Xiong presses the abbreviated grammar: if it is altogether unobtainable, what remains to regulate? These disagreements and questions concern the force of one fixed quoted reply; they do not create a second referent.

Senses.Explanation: The records use this transitive appraisal for seeing through a saying, case, person, condition, or position before or after it is presented. Literally, 'look through' or 'look and break through.' The compound occurs 509 times in 154 allowed texts. It is used transitively of a saying, case, person, condition, or distinction; in passive clauses someone or something is 'seen through.' Hongzhi asks, 'What is the eye with which you can see through it?'. Comments on earlier cases say that someone saw through Lingyun and Mahakasyapa, that Tianning saw through Dahui, or that an interlocutor should see through an action before it occurs. The passive form appears in a warning about being seen through by someone at a later time (他時異日被人覷破). The fuller form 'be able to see through' occurs 40 times in 25 texts, while the emphatic 'with one look, see through' (一覷覷破) occurs 19 times in 17. The texts do not supply a separate technical definition beyond these observable objects, contrasts, questions, and active/passive constructions.
Senses.Note: The two hits for 'one who sees through this' use the final graph as the pronoun 'this,' not as a definition formula. They were therefore not treated as self-definitions. The corpus range is grammatical rather than polysemous: the same verb occurs with people, words, cases, and named distinctions as its object.

Senses.Explanation: Inspect mind or look at mind. The compound occurs 474 times in 84 allowed texts, but 257 hits are concentrated in the Record of the Source-Mirror, and the corpus does not give the action one uniform set of predicates. In the Daoxin–Niutou Farong encounter, Farong answers ‘inspecting mind’ when asked what he is doing; Daoxin asks, ‘Who is doing the inspecting, and what thing is mind?’ (觀是何人，心是何物), and Farong gives no answer. The Treatise on Breaking Appearances says, ‘Only inspecting mind, this one thing, gathers all things’ (唯觀心一法，總攝諸法), then asks, ‘How does inspecting mind count as understanding?’ (云何觀心稱之為了). Its reply distinguishes a clean mind and a soiled mind and later says, ‘Inspecting mind in this way may be called understanding’ (如是觀心可名為了). The Record of the Source-Mirror quotes a different direct formula: ‘Inspect mind as no mind; things do not dwell on things; my mind is itself empty; fault and fortune have no owner—this is called correct inspection’ (觀心無心，法不住法，我心自空，罪福無主，即是無心無數，名為正觀). Other Chan witnesses criticize particular deployments. The Yongzheng Emperor says that making silence final and ‘then devoting oneself to quietly inspecting mind’ is ‘escaping a pit and falling into a ditch’ (便務靜觀心，又所謂逃坑落塹), while Xuri Jushi’s verses say, ‘closing the eyes, vainly seek seeing; inspecting mind, mistakenly seek penetration’ (閉目妄求見，觀心誤覓通), ‘holding mind and inspecting mind divide guest and host’ (持心觀心紛主客), and ‘if inspecting mind here is clear, the undivided single flavor is itself alert’ (於此觀心若了了，混然一味自惺惺). These are text-drawn assertions and criticisms of named actions; they do not supply a single imported category for the headword.

AlternateTargets: bring an inner restriction to an end
Senses.Explanation: To release an inward restriction is a deliberate reuse of the institutional term for a different event in the person. These passages explicitly say that the restriction is formed and released in one’s own mind, or define release as an obstructing thing, net, or accumulated impediment breaking apart. A negative witness rejects merely imitative gestures as deserving this name. Because the passages change the referent from a calendar institution to a personal constraint, this is a separate sense.
Senses.Note: Four independent works explicitly define or police this personal referent. The sense is multi-source and is not inferred from the ordinary ceremony alone.

Senses.Explanation: To form an intellectual understanding is regularly rejected as construing or calculating from words rather than meeting the cited exchange. In Chan records the word commonly names understanding made from discriminations, words, or received knowledge rather than a neutral success at understanding. Yuanwu reports that many people make an emotionally conditioned construction of a public case and then explain Huichao's answer as simply meaning that Huichao himself is buddha. A record warns that seeking words and pursuing phrases in order to find such understanding produces proliferating differences and verbal facility. Huangbo's record says that construing the way as seeing, hearing, awareness, and knowing leaves one far from it. The observable Chan bend is therefore critical: the ordinary verb 'understand' repeatedly labels the very explanatory grasp that masters reject. The term can still occur neutrally in a question such as 'how should this be understood'; this is the same act under different appraisal, not a different referent or word class.

Senses.Explanation: to touch or meet the eye; in context, whatever meets the eye. It forms public questions—'what is the affair that meets the eye?' and 'what is awakening that meets the eye?'—to which Xuefeng answers with a question, 'what is it?', with 'heavens!', by lifting the whisk, or by pointing out a bare pillar. Yunmen's statement 'even if whatever meets the eye is unobstructed' becomes a repeatedly quoted and tested formula. One later master raises a whisk and says that calling it a whisk leaves obstruction in what meets the eye, while not calling it a whisk does too. Linji's record says 'whatever meets the eye is it,' and immediately supplies its own stated obstruction: feelings arise, knowledge separates, and thought changes the object. The ordinary visual phrase is thus heavily loaded as interview and teaching-seat vocabulary.

AlternateTargets: what meets the eye is awakening
Senses.Explanation: Masters raise ‘awakening wherever the eye lands’ as a public question, then enact or redirect the answer through an immediately visible object or action without making one response universal. The graphs say “meet or strike the eye” and “awakening”: “awakening wherever the eye meets.” The exact question “What is awakening wherever the eye meets?” accounts for 69 of the headword’s 127 occurrences. The answers and follow-up actions vary. When Shishuang Qingzhu asks Daowu, Daowu calls a novice, tells him to add water to the clean-water jar, later asks Shishuang what he had just asked, and leaves as Shishuang begins to repeat it; the narrative then says Shishuang woke up. Another exchange answers, “All things constantly abide”; when asked what that means, the named record subject answers with the headword again. Elsewhere the answer is “the buddha hall before you,” a named record subject kicks a dog so that it runs off making a sound, or Xuansha says, “Before a dead monk is precisely awakening wherever the eye meets.” Linquan’s later comment on the Daowu case says that it has “no empty gap.” The records preserve these named exchanges and different predicates; this entry gives no single explanation in place of their different answers.
Senses.Note: The headword occurs 127 times in 58 allowlisted texts. The direct question occurs 69 times in 31 texts, while Xuansha’s line about the dead monk occurs 8 times in 8. The related saying “what meets the eye is the Way” occurs 7 times in 7 texts. The case witnesses must not be collapsed: Daowu’s novice-and-water-jar exchange, the reciprocal “all things constantly abide” answer, the buddha-hall answer, the kicked-dog action, and Xuansha’s dead-monk statement are distinct recorded deployments.

Senses.PreferredTarget: to be greatly awakened at those words
AlternateTargets: to be greatly awakened upon hearing the words
at the words, to awaken greatly
Senses.Explanation: A narrative formula reporting that someone was greatly awakened immediately at or under spoken words. It marks the event's position in an exchange; it does not itself state what was understood. The recorded words differ in every case. Daoxin is reported awakened after Sengcan asks who binds him and why he seeks release. Damei Fachang follows Mazu Daoyi's answer "mind itself is buddha." Wuxie Lingmo follows Shitou Xiqian's challenge about turning his head away from "only this." Yanyang follows Zhaozhou Congshen's answer to carry away what he cannot put down. Fenyang Shanzhao follows Shoushan Xingnian's two answers concerning Baizhang's rolled mat, and Huanglong Huinan follows Ciming Chuyuan's question whether he takes the rebuke as scolding. Huiming is reported awakened after Huineng asks for his original face at the moment of thinking neither good nor evil. The Zen bend lies in the strict attribution chain: a named speaker's precise turn precedes a named person's reported awakening, while the narrative formula belongs to the compiler and never turns the awakening into a free-floating event without a case.
Senses.Note: The frozen allowlisted corpus has 676 exact hits in 186 files representing 181 works. Seven anchors across five works preserve seven distinct speaker-recipient pairs and a range of following actions. Related formulas such as awakening, penetration, or having an insight at the words are neighboring constructions, not alternate spellings or extra senses.

Senses.Explanation: before words or ahead of speech. Its most visible Chan deployment is the paired formula 'discern before the words' and 'accord after the phrase.' Multiple records immediately refuse both positions: discerning before the words fails one's whole life, while according after the phrase departs from the body of the Way; Yuanwu similarly quotes discernment before words as still confined by a shell. The corpus also uses the phrase nominally for 'the matter before the words' and in a preface says the mind seal may be discerned before words. These are grammatical forms of the same temporal-relational phrase. They show a stock Chan axis for examining an answer's relation to spoken words, not a named realm or separate object.

SearchAliases: the path of words is cut off
Senses.Explanation: Language's road being cut off is a formula for a point the records say cannot be reached by wording; several speakers immediately question, reverse, or delimit that formula. The phrase occurs 171 times in 71 allowlisted texts and is repeatedly paired with ‘the place of mental activity is extinguished.’ Sengcan's verse says, ‘Trust in mind is not two; not two is trust in mind; the road of language is cut off; it is not past, future, or present’ (信心不二。不二信心。言語道斷。非去來今). Hongzhi Zhengjue turns the paired formula into a public question: ‘Just when the road of language is cut off and the place of mental activity is extinguished, what then?’ (祇如言語道斷心行處滅。又作麼生). An unattributed transmitted formula says that it cannot be known by wisdom or recognized by consciousness and pairs the headword with mental activity extinguished; after the explicit marker ‘Baoning says,’ Baoning Renyong reverses the predicates, saying it can be known and recognized while the road of language remains cut off and mental activity is not extinguished. Tiantai Deshao also explicitly rejects closed eyes and seeing nothing in darkness as what the phrase is called. The corpus therefore records the fixed wording, the common pair, a counter-formulation, a direct question, and a stated exclusion without making closed eyes or mere silence its lexical definition. Baiyu Si calls the described limit “language’s road cut off and mental activity ceased,” then immediately asks about impossible animated images. The follow-up tests rather than silently absolutizes the same formula.

Senses.Explanation: Xu You, the recluse whom the Chan corpus identifies through Yao's offer of the realm, retirement at Mount Ji, washing his ears, and discarding his gourd. Wansong's commentary supplies the story in brief: Xu You lived hidden at Mount Ji, Yao yielded the imperial position to him, and Xu You washed his ears at the river after hearing it. Juelang Daosheng adds that Xu You feared being burdened by possession of the realm and would rather die than accept it. The records then put those acts into public exchanges. Jingqing answers a request for direction to what is finest before sound with “Xu You did not wash his ears,” and says washing would still leave his feet tied. Another fourfold host-and-guest exchange answers “What is the host within the guest?” with “Xu You washes his ears.” Baoning Renyong directly appraises the inherited image: Xu You's ear-washing merely displays lofty purity, while Chaofu's watering of the ox merely flaunts spirit. Hongzhi's portrait verse retains another part of the family, “Xu You discarded the gourd.” The Zen deviation is therefore observable rather than honorific: a classical refusal figure is made an answer, assigned a place in host-and-guest grammar, negated, and openly criticized from the teaching seat.

Senses.Explanation: Appraisal-commentary is the public written handling of old cases or verses, and the same word labels the resulting commentarial work or collection. Chan books make it a named layer of case literature: the named commentator addresses earlier verses, and the resulting appraisal-commentary can become a titled collection. Title constructions name Yuanwu Keqin appraising Xuedou Chongxian's verses, Wansong Xingxiu appraising Hongzhi Zhengjue's verses, and Linquan Conglun appraising verses associated with Touzi Yiqing and Danxia Zichun. Daguan Zhenke's signed preface to the Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Wushan Jingduan gives the documentary sequence: 'from recorded encounters, verses on old cases were made; from verses on old cases, appraisal-commentary collections were made' (由機緣而頌古作，由頌古而評唱集). A poem heading by Guxue Zhenzhe speaks of 'burning Wansong's appraisal-commentary on public cases' (焚萬松評唱公案). Its verbal, nominal, and title constructions are grammatical deployments of the same activity and product, not separate dictionary senses. An appended dialogue asks why widespread raising and appraisal-commentary, used to examine old material, is called mastery of the lineage. This hostile question is a stance toward the same public commentarial work, not a second referent.

Senses.Explanation: In Chan dialogue, this verdict marks a participant as caught or defeated by the words just used, and it can be turned back on either side. Muzhou and Yunmen issue the verdict to interlocutors; Luohan Guichen does likewise. Baozi Xiaowu immediately applies it both to the monastic and to his own speech, showing that the label is not reserved for one side. Dahui applies it retrospectively to Bodhidharma, an unnamed monastic turns it against Baojue Zuxin, and Sanyi Mingyu applies it to himself while inviting discernment. The records repeatedly ask where the fall lies but answer through further encounter rather than a stable prose definition.

Senses.Explanation: To construe the words is repeatedly rejected when a hearer turns an answer, gesture, or ordinary statement into a fixed verbal interpretation. In Chan records it repeatedly names an auditor's reduction of a reply or case to an explanatory category. Yuanwu reports that people construe Dongshan's 'three pounds of hemp' as an answer based on his work weighing hemp; Dahui says blind fellows construe Zhaozhou's instruction as merely 'wash the bowl'; and Fayan says that for twenty years he construed Jiashan's line only as talk about scenery. The records also expose competing constructions: a collection says people construed Vimalakirti's response as silence, a pause, remaining seated, or not answering, but none reached it. Guyin Yuncong can therefore warn, after answering 'what is buddha?', 'do not construe it as answer-buddha talk.' Elsewhere the word is itself put under interview pressure: 'without relying on the three-inch tongue, try to construe it.' The Chan-specific bend is observable and critical: construing the words (話會) is not neutral comprehension but the named act of fitting a live saying into talk about a subject. The entry does not decide what an unexplained saying ultimately means.

AlternateTargets: a word or question repeatedly brought up
Senses.Explanation: A selected word, question, or saying brought up for repeated examination. Dahui Zonggao tells listeners to look at one while moving or still; Zhongfeng Mingben says to raise one that offers no ready meaning. Hanyue Fazang and Ruibai Mingxue each give explicit but different descriptions of what counts as one. Weilin Daopei places the expression in a historical account of Song-period instruction, while Jiexian attacks lifelessly guarding one without doubt. Chan bends the ordinary sense of a spoken phrase by making it something deliberately selected, raised, watched, and disputed in named instruction.
Senses.Note: Frozen-corpus concordance: 2,779 exact hits in 325 files and 320 independent works in the canonical f001 preflight. This sense is distinct from an already-spoken conversational turn: its referent has been selected for continuing examination, not merely recalled from the preceding exchange.

Senses.Explanation: Master Zhigong is the pre-Zen figure whom Chan records quote, identify with a direct answer, and place in exchanges at Emperor Wu's court. His name occurs 494 times in 133 allowlisted texts. Asked "what is buddha?" Wanan Daoyan answers, "Master Zhigong" (誌公和尚); when challenged, he says, "Zhigong is not an idle monk" (誌公不是閑和尚). In the Fu Dashi case, Fu mounts the seat, strikes the desk once, and descends; Zhigong asks Emperor Wu whether he understands, then says, "the great man has finished lecturing the scripture" (大士講經竟). Later masters repeatedly quote and criticize that verdict. His sayings are also treated as named textual material: the Twelve-Hour Song, Fourteen Sections, and Great-Vehicle Praises. Zen therefore deploys Zhigong as a named answer to "what is buddha?," court interlocutor and adjudicator of Fu Dashi's action, and quoted author.

Senses.Explanation: Masters use the household reversal as an adverse appraisal in public exchanges and comments. It is repeatedly coupled with “point to a deer as a horse” (指鹿為馬). One address applies both verdicts even to the old advice “seek only from yourself, do not look elsewhere” (但向己求，莫從他覓); another identifies “taking the one capable of seeing and hearing as real” (認著一箇能見能聞……執以為真) as precisely mistaking servant for master. Elsewhere Xiangyan Yiduan permits bowing but warns, “you must not mistake the servant for the household head” (不得認奴作郎), while later case commentary applies the same verdict to Deshan. The ordinary status reversal becomes a portable Chan verdict on a proposed identification; which identification receives it is supplied by each passage.

Senses.Explanation: To take a shadow as the thing and lose track of one's head is to follow an image while overlooking what casts it. Juelang Daosheng says a verse has again taken the shadow and lost the head; Miyun Yuanwu applies the phrase to someone who treats worldly busyness as an external obstacle and thereby abandons himself. Shending Yunwai Ze uses it for a learned man unable to answer about his own household, and Yulin Tongxiu places it among being dazzled by sensory distinctions. Muyun Tongmen contrasts it with carrying inquiry through. The Chan bend is a diagnosis of misplaced reference: attention fixes on derivative appearances while the immediate source goes unrecognized.

Senses.Explanation: The records preserve the quoted formulation 'if what can infer is your mind, then you mistake the thief for your son,' and immediately state that 'in the patch-robed monk's gate this is called mistaking the servant for the household head' (衲僧門下謂之認奴作郎). Chan records then use the kinship error in admonition and public interview: pursuing external objects as mind is named with the phrase; an unnamed questioner asks how to judge, in darkness, mistaking thief for son and son for thief and receives 'thirty blows each'; and Huizhou Hao raises his staff and says that calling it the household head is mistaking thief for son, while denying it is fleeing the father and seeking outside. The Zen deviation is this recurrent use as a public diagnostic accusation, linked by the texts themselves to servant/master and host language. The entry reports those applications without deciding what should count as the 'true son.'

Senses.Explanation: The corpus uses ‘talking about food’ as a verdict for speech that cannot satisfy hunger: verbal display lacks the thing it names. Literally, talking (說) about food (食). Across Chan records it is a stock bodily comparison: talking about food does not fill a person, relieve hunger, or cure hunger, just as talking about drink does not cure thirst and talking about clothing does not stop cold. Masters attach the comparison to verbal fluency, borrowed understanding, and merely speaking of realization; several passages explicitly set it beside eating and drinking for oneself. One verse couples it with a painted cake: talking food never fills, and a painted cake is no remedy. A later snow-day exchange playfully reverses the inherited ranking and calls the unnamed monk talking food by the stove the most intimate of three monks, citing 'one filling forgets a hundred hungers'; this is an attested comic reversal, not the dominant sense. The Zen deviation is the term's stable use as the record's hunger test for words: the comparison remains physiological and the texts themselves state the failure.
Senses.Note: The corpus has 108 exact occurrences in 73 allowlisted files. Variants include 'talking food never fills' (說食終不飽), 'talking food cannot fill people' (說食豈能飽人), 'talking food does not cure hunger' (說食不療飢), and the paired 'talking drink and talking food' (說飲說食). The snow-day three-monks exchange is retained as a documented reversal rather than used to erase the dominant corpus comparison.

Senses.Explanation: To request instruction is to approach an instructor for an answer, clarification, or further examination. The Blue Cliff Record uses the term as a named question-type and distinguishes a long-standing student's request after seeing but not penetrating or penetrating but not clarifying. Other records use it for a first announced request, an attendant's follow-up after an exchange, and biographical visits to an instructor. These are deployments of the same act of asking to receive further explanation; noun and verb grammar do not make separate senses.
Senses.Note: The frozen corpus has 1,949 exact hits in 314 files representing 310 works. Eight anchors cover direct requests, narrated teacher-student visits, follow-up questioning, and explicit classification of the request-for-instruction question across independent works.

Senses.Explanation: 諸佛出身處 is “the place from which the buddhas emerge,” a stock question in recorded encounters. The question is normally spoken by an unnamed monk, while different masters answer locally: “East Mountain walks on the water,” “a donkey womb and horse belly,” “you asked very fittingly,” and other incompatible replies. The corpus therefore fixes the interrogative formula but supplies no single shared place-name as its answer. Later raisers explicitly quote Yunmen’s question-and-answer as an inherited case.

Senses.Explanation: Fenggan is the Tiantai eccentric whom Chan records place with Hanshan and Shide. His dossier shows him answering Hanshan's question about an unpolished mirror, travelling toward Wutai, riding a tiger, and identifying Hanshan and Shide when Lüqiu Yin asks for instruction. Later masters invoke the trio in public addresses, questions, and portrait verses—sometimes treating Fenggan's additional words as needless speech. This is Fenggan as a repeatedly deployed Chan figure, not a general saint's biography or a lineage-master claim.

Senses.Explanation: The elephant king appears through elephant-like gait, return, and royal-animal comparisons, distinct from the lion language paired with it. Chan records repeatedly take the elephant king's bearing, stride, and backward look as publicly recognizable forms of Changlu Timing's conduct. Changlu Timing looks right and says, 'the bearing of the elephant king—how could it forget the backward look?' Another stock pairing says, 'in the lion's den there is no other beast; where the elephant king walks, fox tracks cease.' The backward look itself enters encounter history: when Changlu Timing mounts the seat and says 'the lion frowns; the elephant king looks back,' an unnamed monastic awakens, enters the room, and presents his understanding. Later verse calls the lion's vigorous motion world-shaking and the elephant king's backward look effortless. The line can also be tested rather than merely praised: when an unnamed monastic quotes 'where the elephant king walks, fox tracks cease,' Changlu Timing drives him out with blows. The Chan-specific bend is this deployment of a royal animal's gait and backward glance as teaching-seat bearing and encounter language. The records assign no further gloss to the image, and neither does this entry.

Senses.Explanation: A poor child remembering old debts is someone with little present capital still occupied by liabilities carried from before. Dabo Qian makes the phrase a direct answer about the meaning of the western arrival. Chijue Daochong comments with it when an attendant cannot return the rhinoceros fan; Wufeng Ruxue uses it in answer to why Shakyamuni appeared. Tianyin Yuanxiu and Poshan Haiming apply it critically to belated review of old errors or reverence for earlier masters. The Zen bend makes remembered debt a figure for being pulled back into inherited accounts precisely when a present response is required.

Senses.Explanation: To buy a hat by measuring the head is to choose the hat by first taking the wearer’s measure. Tiantong Jue pairs the phrase with deciding whether someone is son or thief and removing bones before eating fish. Xutang says simply, “here I buy a hat by measuring the head,” while the Collected Essentials calls an exact fit difficult. These clauses establish measured fitting and discriminating selection; they do not by themselves define it as conceptual calculation.

Senses.Explanation: To draw the bow after the thief has passed is to act only after the decisive moment has already gone. Xuedou Chongxian applies the line after Zhaozhou's exchange with Huangbo and laughs at the belated move. Yuanwu Keqin gives it as an answer to a follow-up that arrives after the point; Ying'an Tanhua, Yuejiang Zhengyin, Liao'an Qingyu, and Tianyin Yuanxiu likewise use it to mark commentary or rescue that comes too late. The Chan bend is temporal and procedural: a response may be sharp in itself yet miss because the live encounter has already passed.

Senses.Explanation: The host within the guest names a guest–host position whose interpretation is explicitly system-dependent in later Chan analysis. In the later systematic account of Linji's four guest-host configurations, this is the configuration named when ‘the student has a nose-hole’ (學人有鼻孔). Records then raise the label as a public question and preserve different answers, including 'facing him, there is no companion.' This is one member of the fourfold set alongside host-within-host, guest-within-host, and guest-within-guest. The texts explicitly say that Linji's guest-host system differs from Caodong's, so the shared graphs must not blur the two school-specific things.

Senses.Explanation: This separate sense denotes Caodong host-within-guest position, not Linji host-within-guest configuration. In Caodong guest-host discourse the same words name a position paired with host-within-guest's converse and with the bent-and-upright vocabulary. The Eye of Humans and Gods explicitly glosses Caodong's host-within-guest as 'function within essence' (用中體) and says this fourfold guest-host system is not the same as Linji's. In the Dongshan encounter, Dongshan asks 'what is host within guest?' and receives 'white clouds cover the green mountain'; another transmitted version assigns 'long years not leaving the house.' Later verse can say 'host within guest is precisely guest within host' and tell the hearer not to recognize a fixed pattern in reversal and accord. These are recorded formulas and answers, not an invitation to supply an interpretation beyond them.

Senses.Explanation: Guest and host are the paired roles through which an encounter's initiative and response are described. Records ask whether the roles are distinguished, show one role questioning the other, and speak of their positions turning or being exchanged. Interchange does not name a second thing: it is an action performed with the same guest-host pair. The phrase can refer to literal social positions, but in encounter analysis it marks who sets and who receives the situation.
Senses.Note: The frozen corpus has 2,692 exact hits in 355 files representing 351 works. Ten standalone anchors span role distinction, questioning, reversal, exchange, criticism, and later commentary across independent works. A legacy witness lacking the exact headword was rejected.

Senses.Explanation: A repeated descriptive expression for being bare, exposed, and without covering. The term occurs 368 times in 143 allowed texts. Its recurring parallel is 'cleanly naked' (淨裸裸); records expand it with 'without covering' (無蓋覆), 'nothing that can be grasped' (沒可把), and 'fully exposed' (全露). These textual predicates establish what the expression describes without turning it into a condition to seek. The records also qualify it. Yuanwu says that being cleanly naked, cut off from thought, bare, and with nothing to grasp has 'still not left this-side affairs' (猶未離這邊事在). Later collections likewise say that even when one is cleanly naked, bare, and has nothing to grasp, 'there is still something fine remaining' (尚有廉纖), and contrast the relative ease of being bare with the difficulty of being distinctly evident (明歷歷). The corpus has five occurrences of the adverbial extension 'in a bare and uncovered manner'.
Senses.Note: The English follows the term's directly attached predicates. It does not treat the phrase as a named experience, attainment, or procedure. Graph-level 'red' is not forced into the translation because the corpus repeatedly explains the compound through bareness, exposure, lack of covering, and lack of anything to grasp.

Senses.Explanation: The phrase marks a bodily surface or site—the top of the red flesh-lump—where Linji places the true person of no rank and Nanyuan Huiyong places a thousand-fathom wall. Its most frequent named deployment quotes Linji: "on the lump of red flesh there is a true person of no rank, constantly going in and out through the face-gate of each of you; those who have not verified this, look, look" (赤肉團上有一無位真人，常在汝諸人面門出入，未證據者看看). The phrase also heads Nanyuan Huiyong's recorded saying, "on the lump of red flesh, a wall stands a thousand fathoms" (赤肉團上，壁立千仞), followed by the cited participant repeating the sentence and overturning the Chan seat. Later records quote both formulations, combine the phrase with the "true person of no rank" (無位真人), and use it as the location of other stated predicates. The broader form "lump of red flesh" (赤肉團) occurs 441 times, while "beside the lump of red flesh" (赤肉團邊) occurs 36 times. No exact occurrence using "inside" in place of "on" was found. The entry preserves the literal bodily wording and the two principal recorded sayings without replacing them with an imported abstraction.

Senses.Explanation: The expression denotes Linji's crouching lion in these Chan records. Its wording is ‘a lion crouching on the ground.’ In Linji Yixuan's fourfold account of a shout, a shout may be like the precious sword of the Diamond King, like a crouching lion, like a probing pole and shadow-grass, or may not function as a shout; Linji then shouts when the recorded questioner hesitates. Later records preserve the four as an identification test, asking which of three successive shouts is the sword, the crouching lion, or the probing pole. They also transfer the same roster to another teaching-seat implement: a raised staff may act as the sword, crouching lion, probing pole, or not as a staff. Public questions ask ‘what is a shout like a crouching lion?’ and receive recorded replies including ‘it frightens the wild foxes to death’; another later master answers all four questions simply with a shout. The Zen bend is therefore not an ordinary zoological lion but Linji's named comparison within the four deployments of a shout, later reused to classify shouts and staffs in teaching-seat encounters. The record supplies varied replies but no separate definition of a hidden quality.

To miss it: to let what is immediately at issue pass by without meeting it. Sanjiao Zongyin says that even asking what 'this matter' is has already missed it, and answers Magu's reformulated question with the same verdict. Yuanwu Keqin says the miss occurs in the time of raising an eyebrow; Puzhao Xiaoqin says taking up what is right before one can itself become the miss. Dahui Zonggao tells a questioner that he has missed it without knowing and elsewhere says that opening the eyes misses it and closing them misses it too. Zhenjing Kewen says that merely forming an intention while he comes forward has already missed it. Nanfeng Yunbian answers a question about a matter beyond the standard fourfold alternatives with 'you miss it face to face.' Baima Guixi gives a paired limit: hurry and one misses it, go slowly and one cannot catch up. Baichi Xingyuan contrasts counting that remains plainly exact with casually saying 'I understand,' which misses it. The ordinary verb becomes a recurrent public verdict on timing, attention, and response; no single posture, speed, or verbal formula guarantees against it.
Senses.Note: Frozen-corpus concordance: 1,555 exact hits in 237 files and 232 independent works. One act covers missing, overlooking, and letting the occasion pass. Different triggers—asking, intending, opening or closing the eyes, hurrying, slowing, or claiming understanding—are attested circumstances of the same miss, not separate senses.

Senses.Explanation: “Somewhat closer” is a comparative verdict: one response is judged nearer than another without being declared complete. Somewhat closer or a little better by comparison. The phrase occurs 854 times in 224 allowlisted texts and repeatedly serves as a qualified public appraisal. Huangbo Xiyun says that among Mazu Daoyi’s eighty-four teachers only Guizong Zhichang is somewhat closer. Xitang Zhizang summons the assembly and says that the record's unnamed participant who tries to help is somewhat closer. After an interlocutor whom the record does not name says he does not understand, Guanghui Qingshun replies that this is a little closer. Baiyan Fu says that Fu Dashi, Baozhi, and Emperor Wu still do not compare quite as well with Yan's action. Yuanwu Keqin says that being entirely unlike a list of proposed identifications is only then somewhat closer, and immediately asks why. Changqing Huileng applies the phrase after a long silence. The comparison can therefore qualify speech, silence, action, withdrawal, or the condition before a question while still withholding full approval.

Senses.Explanation: A turning word is a response demanded or supplied to pivot a case or stuck encounter. In the wild-fox case the old man asks Baizhang Huaihai to provide one in his place, and Baizhang's answer releases him. Wumen Huikai challenges readers to lay one down at the decisive point of a case. Yunmen Wenyan prizes Baling's three turning words as sufficient repayment of his teaching debt. Xuedou Chongxian asks each Chan guest to supply one to the broken-fan challenge. Baiyan Mingzhe asks an interlocutor for a different turning word that would accord with him. Tianyi Yihuai asks the community to provide one on Shakyamuni's behalf against the demon king. In a reported exchange Shun Bujue criticizes Sheng for winning a monastery with only one turning word while still not having dreamed of the teaching. The term therefore names a consequential pivoting response, not any clever sentence.
Senses.Note: Exact frozen-corpus count: 1,769 hits in 294 files and 289 works. Seven witnesses across five independent works meet the packet floor and cover substitution, challenge, three-word set, case response, alternate response, representative defense, and critical use.

Senses.Explanation: To turn oneself around is the bodily action of turning the body or self. It is attested 2,135 times in 327 allowlisted texts. The action can be direct narration: Magu Baoche turns intending to sit and is struck, while Sanfeng Hanyue Fazang turns and immediately walks away. Chan records also build a productive family from the same turning action. Yuanwu Keqin defines a “place to turn oneself” by “speak at the place without words; go at the place where going cannot be done” (無言處言得，行不得處行得，謂之轉身處). Hongzhi Zhengjue says one must know a road to turn; Yinyuan Longqi directly asks what that road is and answers, “you travel in the wild grass; I again enter the deep village” (汝行荒草裏，我又入深村). An unnamed questioner asks Poshan Haiming “what is a turning phrase?” (如何是轉身句) and receives a recorded answer. Feiyin Tongrong says that bright-eyed patch-robed monks have “no road to turn” (轉身無路), and elsewhere pairs turning with shifting step. Literal motion and the road, place, and phrase compounds preserve one turning action; the former targets were paraphrases, not different referents.
