Senses.Explanation: The imperative reverses illumination from outward pursuit toward shining back. Stored cases command return, looking beneath one’s own feet, or attach a complement such as “illuminating past and present.” This written form occurs 50 times in 35 allowed texts; the common variant 'turn the light around and shine back' (回光返照) occurs 168 times in 88 texts, and the reversed order 'shine back and turn the light' (返照回光) occurs 16 times. The Record of the Transmission of the Lamp gives the literal instruction, 'turn the light around and shine back; look: what are body and mind?' (迴光返照看身心是何物). Shitou's Grass Hut Song says, 'turn the light around and shine back, then return' (迴光返照便歸來). Linji tells his listeners that at the words they should 'themselves turn the light around and shine back, seeking nothing else' (便自迴光返照，更不別求). Chengtian Cique says, 'only turn the light around and shine back; carefully search beneath your own heels and look what it is' (但自迴光返照，向自己脚根下子細推尋，看是箇什麼). Gongchen Jueke closes an address with 'each of you, please turn the light around and shine back; do not hesitate further' (各請迴光返照，休更踟躕). Fenyang's verse supplies a result-clause: 'turn the light around and shine back, illuminating present and past' (迴光返照明今古). The corpus thus records an imperative verb phrase, a poetic return, a prohibition on seeking elsewhere, and direct objects or complements such as body and mind, beneath one's heels, and present and past. Zhongfeng Mingben explicitly singles out “the four characters (回光返照),” then says merely sitting quietly with closed eyes is not what he names. This is his attested description and falsification, not a universal prescription. Miyun’s reversed (返照回光) remains a related phrase only.

Senses.Explanation: The records coordinate confusion and awakening as a tested pair, repeatedly setting it beside ordinary and holy, motion and stillness, and true and false. Literally the graphs say "be lost or confused" (迷) and "awaken or understand" (悟): "confusion and awakening," attested 1,115 times in 231 allowlisted texts. The pair is repeatedly coordinated with ordinary and holy, motion and stillness, and true and false. One verse says, "the nature of confusion and awakening is empty; that empty nature has neither end nor beginning" (迷悟性皆空，性空無終始). Zhongxuan asks, "ordinary and holy are originally not two; how could confusion and awakening have different roads?" (凡聖本來不二，迷悟豈有殊途). Zhe'an says, "confusion and awakening are not different; motion and stillness have one source" (迷悟不異，動靜一源).
Senses.Note: The records also correct bare negation of the pair. A quoted line says, "originally there is no person of confusion or awakening; only understand today" (本無迷悟人，祇要今日了); the named record subject immediately asks, "if there is no confusion or awakening, what do you understand?" (既無迷悟，了箇甚麼). Zhe'an likewise says that claiming confusion and awakening no longer exist is still halfway, then asks for confusion not to obstruct awakening and awakening not to obstruct confusion. These are explicit textual relations, not separate senses.

AlternateTargets: searching for a head that was never lost

SearchAliases: carry the head and seek it
Senses.Explanation: The error of treating a shadow as the head that casts it while searching for a head that was never lost. An unnamed monk and Tongan Pi make this physically impossible mistake a public question and response; Yulin Tongxiu appraises it, Luohan Shenming Che names a person-type with it, Qingzhou Puzhao Yibian uses it in a chamber test, and Linquan Conglun and Jifei Ruyi use it in admonition and direct naming. Xiangshan Chengzhao explains the reversed wording through Yajnadatta: while confused, his head has not been lost, and when he awakens it is not newly gained. Yuanming Jushi supplies the image's physical constraint: shadows arise beside sunlight, moonlight, or lamplight, and a head and its shadow occur together. An unnamed monk asks Tongan how the error is stopped; Tongan says that seeking from another only goes farther away and finally asks where the head is. Yulin pairs the phrase with “abandon the root and pursue the tips” (棄本逐末). Luohan answers “What is guest within guest?” with “a person who mistakes the shadow for the head” (迷頭認影人). Qingzhou uses it in a chamber question contrasting recognition before a sound with taking on after a phrase. Linquan places both word orders side by side in one warning, while Jifei calls losing the body's whereabouts after assigning away its constituent parts “mistaking a shadow for the head.” These named deployments retain one head-and-shadow error, not different things.
Senses.Note: The exact headword occurs 136 times in 76 allowlisted texts. The reversed form occurs 64 times in 40 texts and is supporting family evidence, not an exact-headword witness. Appraisal, person-type, question, and syntactic reversal are readings or deployments of the same image; the item-8 test finds no second referent.

Senses.Explanation: To roam at ease is to go or stay freely, without being tied or obstructed by what one meets. The Chan record uses it favorably but also polices the phrase against counterfeit freedom. Yongjue Yuanxian directly defines ‘what is called roaming at ease and ranging freely’ as remaining aloof and unattached amid every false scene, like a bird flying through the sky without the slightest tether and a dragon leaving the sea without the slightest obstruction (所謂逍遙放曠者，乃是於一切妄境，超然不著，如鳥飛空，而毫無所牽繫，如龍出海，而毫無所障礙). In the same address he denies that being tied by sounds, sights, wealth, or power can be called ranging freely and roaming at ease (豈曰放曠逍遙哉). Tianhuang Daowu tells Longtan Chongxin to roam at ease according to his nature, range freely following conditions, exhaust the ordinary mind, and retain no separate superior understanding (任性逍遙，隨緣放曠，但盡凡心，無別勝解). The Patriarchs' Hall Collection describes Danxia Tianran as delighting in clouds and waters and roaming at ease whether going or staying (樂乎雲水，去住逍遙). Tianyin Yuanxiu raises his staff and asks whether it is not roaming at ease and unbound; Shiyu Mingfang's community rule rejects taking crazed delusion as roaming at ease (將狂妄作逍遙者). An unnamed monk asks Lumen Fadeng about a person roaming at ease outside things, and Fadeng answers, ‘red and festering all over, unable to be supported’ (如何是逍遙物外底人；遍身紅爛，不可扶持). Yongjia Xuanjue's letter uses the ordinary motion frame ‘roam through mountains and valleys’ (逍遙山谷), which is not the place name Mount Xiaoyao. Juelang Daosheng also uses the word inside the longer title ‘Remarks on Free and Easy Wandering’; that family compound is not a fourth sense of the bare headword.
Senses.Note: Allowlisted concordance: 974 hits in 245 texts. Definition formulas yield three hits for ‘roaming-at-ease one(s)’, one direct ‘what is called roaming at ease’ formula, no exact hits for the other standard naming formulas, and seven ‘what is roaming at ease’ questions. Family counts include 53 hits for ‘roaming at ease and unbound’ (逍遙自在), 66 for ‘roam at ease according to one's nature’ (任性逍遙), nine for ‘range freely and roam at ease’ (放曠逍遙), 24 for ‘roaming at ease outside things’ (逍遙物外), and two for ‘roam through mountains and valleys’ (逍遙山谷). The 974-hit pool also contains the distinct personal title Master Xiaoyao, the place name Mount Xiaoyao, longer book-title language, and ordinary syntax; these were separated before the lexical depth count. Seven independent lexical witnesses remain after the longer-title family row is excluded. Favorable, critical, literal-motion, staff, instruction, narrative, and public-interview deployments all concern the same free-roaming action or state rather than different lexical things.

Senses.Explanation: Master Xiaoyao is the title by which the records preserve an otherwise unnamed successor of Jiashan Shanhui at Gao'an. This is a person, not the action of roaming at ease and not Huaizhong of Mount Xiaoyao. The Jingde Record places Xiaoyao Heshang on the Chan seat: Luxi states that thought after thought climbs after conditions while mind after mind is forever still; Xiaoyao says someone said that the previous evening, answers ‘I don't know,’ strikes Luxi across the mouth with the fly-whisk, and then addresses the assembly. The Patriarchs' Hall Collection independently says that Xiaoyao succeeded Jiashan and was at Gao'an, while acknowledging that it had not seen his conduct record and could not determine his beginning or end.

SearchAliases: a golden-scaled fish through the net
Senses.Explanation: A golden-scaled fish that has passed through the net figures an exceptional adept no longer caught by ordinary devices. The phrase is anchored in Sansheng’s public question to Xuefeng: “What does the golden-scaled fish through the net feed on?” (透網金鱗未審以何為食); Xuefeng replies that he will tell him after he comes out of the net. Yuanwu’s prose supplies the corpus’s direct definition: “only with an eye at the crown is one called a golden-scaled fish through the net” (頂門有眼方謂之透網金鱗). The image then becomes an appraisal of monks: Baowen Hongyin hails a patch-robed monastic as “excellent—a patch-robed monk, a golden-scaled fish through the net” (俊哉衲子，透網金鱗), while later interviews ask why such a fish is still held up by water.

Senses.Explanation: To pass the barrier is to get through a tested obstruction: the records contrast those already through with those still stopped, and extend the phrase to a barrier-passing eye and phrase. Huanglong Huinan distinguishes the two conditions: 'one already past the barrier swings his arms and goes straight on' (已過關者掉臂徑去), whereas 'this is one who has not passed the barrier' (此未透關者也). Zhongfeng Mingben records a corrective contrast: people thread all old and new public cases onto one string and call it 'passing the barrier' (謂之透關), while 'the tight barrier of life and death beneath their heels has not actually been passed' (脚跟下一座生死牢關，政好不曾透得). The phrase also builds 'an eye that passes the barrier' (透關眼). Yuanwu Keqin asks whether anyone present has such an eye. Chijue Daochong says, 'Passing the barrier requires a barrier-passing eye; obtaining treasure requires one who can distinguish treasure' (透關須具透關眼，得寶須還別寶人). Poshan Haiming answers the question 'What is a phrase that passes the barrier?' (如何是透關句), and Dabian Xianquan contrasts 'one already through the barrier' (已透關者) with 'one not through the barrier' (未透關者). These are recorded descriptions, corrections, and compounds; this entry adds no unrecorded destination beyond the barrier.

Senses.Explanation: A proximal demonstrative, literally 'this one,' whose referent is supplied by the immediate words, gesture, or situation. Chan records repeatedly make that ordinary dependency visible in public encounters. Guanghui Yuanlian raises a fist and asks whether the place a visitor came from has 'this'; another raises a whisk and says 'this is form,' then strikes the Chan seat and says 'this is sound.' In the Buddha-and-pig exchange, Buddha points linguistically to a pig being carried past and asks, 'what is this?' (這箇是甚麼); when challenged that an all-knowing buddha should recognize it, he answers, 'it still had to be asked' (也須問過). The phrase also points to an unspoken residue in the repeated exchange 'there is still this' / 'what is this?' (猶有這箇在／這箇是甚麼), and to a charge being handed on when a departing master raises his staff and asks, 'to whom is this entrusted?' (這箇分付阿誰). Prose and address uses show the same grammar: a record says 'set this aside' before its next case, Yuanwu asks whether there is still 'this news,' and a rebuke says the buddha teaching is not 'this reasoning.' The Zen bend is therefore not a special hidden object called 'this': the demonstrative remains grammatically open while gestures, objects, questions, discourse, and succession scenes publicly furnish its referent.

Senses.Explanation: The expression denotes the whole body is eyes in these Chan records. Its wording is 'the whole body is eyes. Chan records make the whole body an organ of seeing, commonly beside whole-body hearing, speaking, or acting. Yuanwu says, 'the whole body is eyes, yet seeing does not reach it,' and extends the same construction to ears, mouth, and mind. Another discourse pairs 'the whole body is a mouth' with 'the whole body is eyes,' then assigns the former speech and the latter use. In public questioning, 'the Great Compassionate One does not extend a hand; the whole body is eyes' answers the class 'meaning and phrase both arrive.' Later case comments use the phrase as an appraisal of Yuanwu Keqin and as wording that itself still requires investigation.

Senses.Explanation: An imperative made from “quickly” and “say.” In Chan public interviews it presses the person addressed to produce an answer at once. The formula is often doubled—“Speak, quickly! Speak, quickly!”—and appears after a question, after alternatives have been barred, or with “bring forth” to demand the reply. The records place bodily consequences directly around it: the identified master holds a fork at the recorded questioner's neck, the recorded questioner pulls the identified master from the seat, or a staff beating follows. Other occurrences put it in the recorded questioner's request, “please, Master, answer quickly.” Its distinctive Chan use is timed pressure for an answer in a public interview; the phrase denotes the demand itself.

Senses.Explanation: To put on the play when the occasion appears is to have the props ready and perform responsively when a situation calls for it. Shiyu Mingfang applies the phrase to carrying a fly-whisk into public performance and criticizes the muddy spectacle it produced. Yuan'an Feng, Buhui, Baiyu Si, and Feiyin Tongrong instead use it for responsive teaching action: a no-stringed lute, a no-hole flute, a whisk raised at the right point, or free movement amid the ten directions. The phrase therefore keeps its theatrical scene while Chan records test whether the performance is timely and capable or merely showmanship.

Senses.Explanation: “Meet a patriarch, kill the patriarch” belongs to Linji’s enumerated formula of killing whatever is encountered, and later masters quote that wording as a sharp inherited command. Literally, "meet a patriarch, kill the patriarch" . Linji's surviving record places it inside a five-member roster: "meet buddha, kill buddha; meet a patriarch, kill the patriarch; meet an arhat, kill the arhat; meet parents, kill parents; meet kin, kill kin" . This is the Chan bend: the honored religious and familial titles become the grammatical objects of the same repeated verb, and later masters preserve, question, and redeploy that severe roster. A successor record explicitly asks why a good teacher would want to kill people after quoting the three religious members, without supplying a prose gloss. Later uses attach the phrase to a sharp sword, place it opposite "carry the infant and encourage the child" in a contrast about grandmotherly kindness, or quote it in a New Year's address before comments on lineage descent. The records use killing language literally in the formula but do not record bodily killings in these deployments; this entry adds no symbolic object behind the named roster.

Senses.Explanation: “do you yet understand?” In Chan records it is a recurring public-interview question after the identified master has spoken, displayed an object, stood up, or made another gesture. The addressee may answer “I do not understand”; the identified master may then speak again, request an object, or close the address. In hall discourse it also turns from an exposition to the assembly: “Do you get it? If not yet…” A long pause, a verse, a staff gesture, or the closing “take care” is frequently recorded after the question. The distinctive Chan deployment is therefore not a private report of comprehension but an observable demand made to an emperor, official, monk, or whole assembly in a recorded encounter.

Senses.Explanation: That side, the other side, or beyond: a relational expression built from 'that bank or side' (那畔). The allowlisted record has 866 occurrences in 233 storage files. The deictic contrast is explicit. Faxi Yin asks about 'the matter on that side' (那畔事) and then 'the matter on this side' (者邊事). In another public exchange, an unnamed monk says that as soon as words are involved one falls on 'this side' (遮畔), then asks Shending Yunwai Ze for news from 'that side' (那畔底消息). The word builds noun phrases for a matter, person, saying, road, or news located there. Its most frequent fixed expansion is 'beyond Awesome Sound' (威音那畔), a locative formula used in addresses and verses. Yuanjie Ying speaks of 'one saying from beyond Awesome Sound' (威音那畔一句); Cishou Huaishen asks 'what is the road on that side?' (如何是那畔路). Zen thus bends an ordinary demonstrative into a productive way of marking what a teaching-seat question places beyond the present side, while the exact referent remains deliberately supplied by each surrounding exchange. Yinyuan Longqi places the direct-teaching gateway on the far side of Awesome Sound; Yuanwu Keqin asks who can distinguish its clue. These extend the same relational ‘far side’ into lineage address without making it a second place.
Senses.Note: Corpus counts: 866 hits in 233 storage files. The Awesome-Sound expansion has 470 hits in 173 files; 'the matter on that side,' 41/29; 'a person on that side,' 10/7; 'a saying on that side,' 4/3; and direct 'what is that side?' constructions, 5/5. Standard self-definition searches returned no Chinese Chan equation. Their zero results and excluded non-Chinese evidence are preserved in WORK rather than printed as unattested quotations.

Senses.Explanation: A pronoun rendered 'which one?' in questions and 'that one' when used distally. It drives public interviews by demanding selection or identification: which Mañjuśrī Kāśyapa intended to expel, which eye is the true eye, which is stillness and which illumination, and which is Senior Ming's original face. The same pronoun can contrast with 'this one,' as in Yaoshan's bathing-the-Buddha exchange: 'you can bathe this one; can you also bathe that one?' Another exchange contrasts 'this is the Tathāgata's nirvana' with 'that one is the lecturer's nirvana?' These interrogative and distal constructions are different contextual readings of one deictic pronoun, not different things.

Senses.Explanation: A walking-imitation allusion used as a verdict on derivative conduct: someone copies another gait and may lose the step previously his own. The records preserve two grammatical directions rather than one person called a 'Handan gait-imitator.' In the shorter 'learn the Handan gait' (邯鄲學步), attested eight times in seven allowlisted texts, Handan supplies the gait being copied. In the more frequent Chan formula 'Handan learns the Tang gait' (邯鄲學唐步), attested 48 times in 35 texts, a Handan person instead copies a Tang gait. Jingqing Daofu applies the latter verdict when an unnamed monk walks away after being asked how he understands Zhaozhou Congshen's 'drink tea'; Xuedou Chongxian then asks why someone who is not a Handan man learns the Tang gait. Xichan Wenlian attaches the formula to uneven footing, while Yulin Tongxiu warns that following the verbal thread of public cases becomes 'learning the Handan gait' and invites informed ridicule. Sanyi Mingyu speaks of forgetting Handan's former gait. Chan deployment therefore keeps the walking, imitation, and loss-of-one's-own-step scene visible while reversing who copies whom; those grammatical roles do not create separate lexical things.

Senses.Explanation: A vinegar gnat is a minute creature repeatedly placed inside a vinegar jar. Baiyan Jingfu calls a group's perspective that of “a gnat inside a jar” and asks how it could know the sky and sun; another fire instruction says to smash the sky inside the vinegar gnat's jar. A portrait verse lets such gnats and mosquitoes pass winter and summer in the vinegar jar's grassy nest. The creature also enters Chan's scale reversals: a hall address has a vinegar gnat swallow a yellow-furred otter. Elsewhere Linji's words are said to pass beyond what a well frog or vinegar gnat can peer at. The jar, restricted sky, minute creature, and impossible swallowing remain one animal referent; the corpus turns it into appraisal, fire-instruction verse, portrait language, and teaching-seat scale reversal. The exact term occurs 41 times in 29 allowlist texts.

Senses.Explanation: A further barrier names an additional gate beyond an earlier passage, commonly in lines about penetrating or emerging through layered barriers. The expression occurs 739 times in 227 allowlisted texts. Counts range from one to ten thousand barriers; one passes, breaks, opens, guards, or remains separated by them. The recurring warning says, ‘do not say no-mind is the Way; no-mind still leaves one further barrier.’ Speakers also ask who has passed it, request presentation of ‘the final barrier,’ and direct a questioner to ‘ask the gatekeeper.’ A late discourse gives its own named description of ‘passing through the further barrier’; this is preserved as that text’s account, not made universal. Zen bends the checkpoint image into a public measure, but the corpus names no fixed numbered stage shared by every use.

Senses.Explanation: Speakers use ‘wild-fox Chan’ as an adverse label for Chan they present as counterfeit, distorted, or merely clever. The phrase can allude to the Baizhang fox case, but its attested use also ranges beyond that case as a charge against other people’s teaching or performance. It is an adverse label within the Chinese Chan record, applied to claims, verbal display, or conduct that Lia’an Qingyu, Ruibai Mingxue, Fangrong Tongxi, or another named speaker rejects as counterfeit or distorted Chan. Liao'an praises lines whose every sound "tears apart wild-fox Chan" (聲聲裂破野狐禪) and elsewhere says to "painstakingly sweep away wild-fox Chan" (痛掃野狐禪). Senses.Explanation: The Diamond King’s jeweled sword figures an uncompromising cutting device in Linji-style teaching and later commentary. Linji's own record places it first in a fourfold classification: at times one shout is like this sword, at times like a crouching golden-haired lion, at times like a probing pole and shadow grass, and at times it does not function as a shout. Linji Yixuan transmits the fourfold classification; later, an unnamed monk asks about the sword-shout, Dagui Zhe extends the classification to a staff, and Yuanwu Keqin applies its cutting action in commentary. Recorded answers describe the sword-shout with such phrases as ‘body divided in two’ (分身兩段) and ‘buddhas and demons slain together’ (魔佛同誅). The image also moves beyond the shout: one record says a raised staff can function as the Diamond King's jeweled sword, alongside the other Linji classifications. In these records the weapon-name is a classified deployment of a shout and, by later extension, another teaching-seat implement. The cited answers supply the cutting language; the sources quoted here give no separate prose definition of the sword-name.

Senses.Explanation: The vajra eye is an eye speakers say people possess, test with a direct question, weigh, call blind, or equate with the worlds in all directions. The corpus says people 'possess vajra eyes' (具金剛眼睛, 58 occurrences), asks 'what are vajra eyes?' (如何是金剛眼睛, seven), and repeats the measured line 'vajra eyes weigh twelve ounces; in a patch-robed monk's hand the balance-head hangs low' (金剛眼睛十二兩。衲僧手裏秤頭低, 12). One recorded assembly says that the five thousand teaching texts and the myriad labors are 'still not vajra eyes,' then asks what vajra eyes are and, after a pause, answers 'blind' (瞎). Langye tells the assembly, 'each of you possesses vajra eyes' (各具金剛眼睛). A four-part enumeration lists 'the ancestors' handle,' 'possessing vajra eyes,' 'having a lion's claws and teeth,' and 'obtaining a patch-robed monk's killing and bringing to life.' Tiantai Deshao says, 'the worlds in all ten directions are vajra eyes' (十方世界是金剛眼睛). The records therefore use the ocular image in possession statements, a definition-question, a numbered list, a measured verse-line, and a world-wide predication. Shishuang Chuyuan requires the vajra eye for distinguishing deceptive appearances during ordinary conduct. Dahui instead jokes that the cited participant traded away Zhaozhou’s pair of vajra eyes for two mud pellets and asks what Zhaozhou will use afterward. Discrimination and something transferable or lost are distinct predicates of the same named eye-image, not evidence for a material eye or a second referent.

Senses.Explanation: The golden-haired lion appears both as Mañjuśrī’s mount and as an independently deployed animal in answers, appraisals, contrasts, and verse. Senses.Explanation: The golden-winged bird is the record's great dragon-taking bird: its characteristic scene is entering or splitting the sea and seizing or swallowing a dragon. Chan masters place that recognizable scene in public questions, appraisals, teaching-seat comparisons, and reversals. Caoshan Guanghui says that Xuefeng Yicun's way of dealing with people is like the golden-winged bird entering the sea to take a dragon. Gushan Zhiyue asks what happens if the bird appears; Huanglong answers that the dragon's life will be hard to preserve, accepts that it will be swallowed, and thanks him for the offering. Yuanwu Keqin pairs the bird splitting the sea and swallowing a dragon with a lion cub leaving its cave. Hulong Taichu Qiyuan reverses the stock scene by asking why the bird-king that splits the sea and swallows a dragon is itself swallowed by a loach. When Huangbo Rong asks for the bird's straight dragon-taking, Baichi Yuan advances, makes as if to overturn the Chan seat, and leaves; Huangbo Rong recognizes him. Huangbo Yiwei An says his staff is at times the bird-king taking a dragon straightaway. Baiyun Shouduan and Ciyun Langting Jingting give two further reversals: a minute jiaoming insect swallows the bird, while the great-roc golden-winged bird's dragon-taking is called hungry indiscrimination. These are predicates, comparisons, and tests involving one creature, not different referents or an abstract quality.

Senses.Explanation: A gold-lock barrier is a controlled calque for an obstructing lock or fastening whose first modifier remains unresolved; the witnesses establish neither solid-gold hardware, ornament, nor an awakening code. The underlying scene is a gold-lock or fastening at palace halls and layered gates, not solid-gold hardware. Dadian Baotong says palace halls will not be closed with such locks when he returns to his mountain because white clouds will seal them by themselves. Zhuanyu Heng places the expression in a palace sequence of jade steps, blue-green locked gates, layered gates, a precious glazed hall, and a jewel curtain. A parallel verse by Zhe'an Jingfan pairs jade palace gates with gold doors and ninefold gates. These controls establish palace diction; they do not establish solid gold, gilding, gold color, an imperial code, or enlightenment symbolism. The records carry the same obstructing lock scene into the dominant Chan deployment at a pass or dark road. Yongjue Yuanxian calls an approving mind ‘the gold-lock dark road’ (只此肯心，便是金鎖玄路) and likewise says that ordinary feelings and holy views are that road (凡情聖見，是金鎖玄路). Baichi Yuan says even ‘the person with nothing going on’ remains a difficult lock (無為無事人，猶是金鎖難). Other records open or smash the lock-barrier, or call both hidden barrier and this lock expedient means that need opening. The Zen bend places approving mind, ordinary and holy views, and a seemingly unoccupied person behind the gold-lock barrier without turning the modifier into a material claim.

Senses.Note: The split follows incompatible governing verbs and scenes, not two readings of one occurrence: a barrier-lock is opened, closed, pierced, or smashed at a pass; a chain or fetter entangles a flying bird and is escaped or pulled apart by a lion or elephant. Longer bone and relic compounds remain separate lexical objects. The adjective is classified as unresolved within this headword, while the complete animal-chain image is directly attested as figurative binding.

Senses.Explanation: This separate sense denotes a binding chain, not the gold-lock barrier. A second corpus-wide image is a binding chain or animal fetter rather than a lock at a barrier. Its verbs require something that binds an animal and can be broken, pulled apart, or escaped. Baiyu Si pictures a soaring phoenix entangled in it (翀霄鸞鳳縈金鎖). Wuming Huijing speaks of a lion cub bursting it after an awakening exchange, but immediately says that both the exchange and this appraisal still incur fault. Baichi Yuan compares direct acceptance to an elephant-king pulling it apart and not turning back when called. Shiyu Mingfang’s inscription likewise places breaking it beside the movements of a fragrant elephant. These animal-and-binding frames establish a chain or fetter as a different object from the openable or smashable barrier-lock. The source still modifies the restraint with gold, but the corpus does not establish material composition or explain the modifier in these verses, so the displayed target names only the attested binding object.

Senses.Explanation: The gold-lock compound names an obstruction on the dark or hidden road and is repeatedly tied to ordinary feelings and holy views. Caoshan Benji equates those feelings and views with the complete gold-lock/dark-road compound and calls for reciprocal interpenetration; Yongjue Yuanxian repeats the equation and says earlier sages winnowed it. A Dongshan-linked verse places it beside intertwined light and dark, difficulty after merit is complete, and exhausted advance and retreat. An unnamed monk asks for it and Langting Ting answers ‘this side, that side.’ Gold modifies the lock-name here; none of the four passages presents precious-metal hardware.
Senses.Note: Modifier-control audit on the frozen fresh corpus: the exact two-graph gold-lock compound has 386 hits in 160 files and 158 works, while its expanded ‘yellow-gold lock’ form has 46 hits in 39 files and 38 works. Controls include barrier, gate, opening, smashing, and restraint frames, not manufacture, weight, possession, or precious-metal hardware. The entry therefore keeps gold as a lexical modifier but avoids the materially misleading English ‘golden lock.’ Four headword witnesses from four distinct works support the compound.

Senses.Explanation: The expression pictures a mountain-and-wall barrier with no route through: speakers collide with it, are stopped by it, pass through it, or report it collapsing. Foyan asks, 'What is the silver-mountain, iron-wall barrier?' (如何是銀山鐵壁) and answers, 'originally it is an affair inside one's own house' (元來是自家屋裏事); the same passage says that before he understood, it was like this barrier and after understanding, 'originally I am the iron wall' (元來我是鐵壁). Xueyan records cases 'without a route of meaning, like the silver-mountain, iron-wall barrier' (無義路如銀山鐵壁者), and separately quotes Baiyun Duan: an inherited word or half-phrase not yet passed through is like it, while after passage oneself is it. Zhongfeng applies the comparison when the words 'life and death' stop someone and says that 'impermanence of life and death, silver mountain and iron wall' are all present in Zhaozhou's question. A verse records it collapsing under one press (一拶銀山鐵壁摧). The source wording modifies mountain with 'silver' and wall with 'iron,' but the compound's 339 occurrences supply no direct predicate that the mountain is made of silver or the wall made of iron. Corpus controls show that silver and iron can mark actual material elsewhere, appearance elsewhere, and conventional or figurative compounds elsewhere; those separate uses do not decide these modifiers, so the displayed target names only the attested barrier image and does not assign symbolism.

a silver bowl filled with snow
Senses.Explanation: The expression denotes snow heaped in a silver bowl in these Chan records. Its wording is "snow heaped in a silver bowl." In the founding public exchange, the recorded questioner asks Baling, "What is the school of Kanadeva?" and Baling answers with this phrase (如何是提婆宗？銀碗裏盛雪). The record preserves it as one of Baling's three turning phrases, alongside answers about the sharpest sword and the eye of the true teaching; Yunmen says that raising those three phrases is enough to repay Baling. Later masters continue to quote, question, and redeploy the exact wording. Tianyin quotes the answer while addressing his assembly, while Dayu sets "mountains are mountains, waters are waters—a silver bowl filled with snow" against "mountains are not mountains, waters are not waters—washing charcoal in ink" (山是山、水是水，銀碗裏盛雪；山不是山、水不是水，墨汁裏洗炭). The distinctive Chan deployment is the phrase's life as Baling's answer and a quotable turning phrase in later public teaching. The texts leave the concrete phrase without a further explicit gloss, and so does this entry.

Senses.Explanation: 鋒鋩 is the cutting edge or point by which a blade shows its capacity to wound. Chan records make exposure itself the test: monks ask how to win without displaying the edge, masters warn against touching or avoiding it, and death verses say that not even a drop of it should be conceded. The word therefore joins sharp effectiveness to whether that effectiveness leaves a visible trace; it is not merely a decorative sword part.

Senses.Explanation: To understand an action, answer, silence, or saying in a way the record judges wrong. Yuanwu Keqin rejects specific reported explanations as misconstruals, including treating Mazu Daoyi's look as a symbolic pairing of sun and moon and taking Fayan Wenyi's fire-seeking exchange as a self-referential explanation. In the whisk case, Jinfeng raises the whisk and immediately tells the unnamed monk who assumes a listening posture that he has already misconstrued it. Wansong Xingxiu says that some readers reduce a recorded silence to a mere long pause; Dahui Zonggao warns against answering a question about one's birth-condition with only a home district. Shiyu Mingfang says that many people of his day misconstrue visible forms and identify gestures and shouts as the marvelous functioning of the six faculties; Fushi Tongxian retrospectively says that misconstruing one sentence from Master Zhan cost him several further years. The word is the sources' adverse verdict in interviews, commentary, warning, and self-report; this entry records what each named speaker rejects without inventing one universal correct interpretation.

Senses.Explanation: Zhong Kui is the legendary demon-queller, attested 70 times in 43 allowlisted texts. Chan records do not retell a complete outside biography; they put his name and familiar attributes to work in public answers, festival speech, verse, and appraisal. Asked for “the host within the guest,” Wuzu Fayan answers, “Zhong Kui's little sister” (鍾馗小妹). At the Double-Fifth festival, after a student says that a little ghost might display a trick, Wuzu Fayan replies, “Zhong Kui will frighten you” (鍾馗嚇你), then speaks of a protective talisman. Xiaoyin Xin makes the demon-queller dance eighteen beats (鍾馗解舞十八拍); Panshan Dabo Qian pictures him on a wall beside swords hanging in space (壁上畵鍾馗，空中懸劍戟); and Fushan Fayuan says at New Year that no strange thing is presently before them, so there is no need to paste up Zhong Kui (目前無異怪，不用貼鍾馗). His name can also be an unglossed answer: asked how to discuss words with no trace, Dongshan Shouchu says, “Zhong Kui does not read books” (鍾馗不讀書). The Zen-specific bend is this repeated deployment of the demon-catching figure, his household, dance, painted image, and protective posting as encounter answers and teaching-seat language; no further symbolic meaning is assigned.

Senses.Explanation: The Iron Ox of Shaanfu is a named object in a recurring case, while other iron-ox passages use the durable animal figure without naming that monument. The Shaanfu Iron Ox is the corpus's fixed place-named iron ox, distinct from an unplaced iron-ox figure. Chan masters make it an impossible moving stage-object and public answer. Fenyang Shanzhao answers a question about the student's turning place by saying to water the Shaanfu Iron Ox. Linxi Wenqing's hall address pairs it with the great image of Jiading and makes the two cross their named regions: the image comes through the pass while the Iron Ox enters western Shu. Baiyu Si says that a fire beneath Lake Tai frightens it into running to Silla. These place-name, pairing, watering, and travel predicates establish the recurring named object, but the stored witnesses do not establish what physical object it was or whether it was cast.

Senses.Note: The direct casting witness establishes a cast object locally but does not make every generic iron ox cast, nor does it retroactively identify the Shaanfu Iron Ox's material relation. Fixed longer forms such as the mechanism of an iron ox and the hornless iron ox are retained as family deployments; they do not independently define the bare headword. Mosquito, seal, barrier, and lineage uses are predicates and comparisons, not separate referents.

Senses.Explanation: This separate corpus sense names iron-ox figure, not the Shaanfu Iron Ox. The stored cases keep that referent explicit. An iron-ox figure is an unplaced ox image that Chan masters put into comparisons, mechanism language, and impossible actions. Yaoshan Weiyan compares his former position at Shitou Xiqian to a mosquito on an iron ox. Guishan Lingyou sharpens the physical scene: a mosquito on the iron ox has nowhere to put its mouth. Fengxue Yanzhao compares the patriarchal mind-seal to the mechanism of an iron ox and stages a public exchange over whether to apply the seal. Zhenjing Kewen has a hornless iron ox break an iron barrier, and Yandang Wenji places one in a lineage answer beside the barren woman who bears a child. Baichi Yuan's verse directly speaks of casting an iron ox, establishing a cast object in that occurrence without making casting part of every use. Hongzhi Zhengjue says one tug by the iron ox snaps a gold rope. These are deployments of the generic figure, not the specifically named Shaanfu Iron Ox.

Senses.Explanation: The mechanism of the iron ox is Fengxue Yanzhao's image for the ancestral seal as a working that cannot be handled by choosing motion or rest. His case says that when it goes the seal holds fast, when it stays the seal breaks, and then asks what happens when it neither goes nor stays. Yuanwu Keqin calls this mechanism impossible to cage; later masters quote the case in public interviews and demand an answer beyond merely repeating its terms. The iron ox supplies apparent immovability, while 機 makes that image an active test rather than a static object.

Senses.PreferredTarget: the public teaching front of a Chan house
Senses.Explanation: The outward teaching establishment through which a Chan house presents and conducts its public work. An unnamed questioner calls ordinary question and answer this public teaching front and asks whether there is anything beyond it. Panan Jicheng likewise calls even his capacious account of a shout a responsive public front and a temporary stopping place, not the treasure-place. Yongjue Yuanxian says his public front is uniformly straight, while Wuyi Yuanlai tells his assembly to know that there is a house-front before he speaks of branches sharing one source. Jinshan Tanying announces that his own front differs and has changed the tracks followed elsewhere. Li Pan warns that Juelang Daosheng's steep front is not merely the severity of rejecting people with sticks and shouts, while Zhean Fan says even outstanding visitors may receive word only through the attendant. Chan bends the household frontage image into the exposed working face of a named teaching house, but that institutional use is not the same referent as an actual entrance court.
Senses.Note: Frozen-corpus concordance: 1,569 exact hits in 313 files and 310 independent works. This sense names an institution's outward teaching arrangement, not masonry or spatial access. The lineage-style term names inherited style; the house-style term names a house's characteristic manner; this headword foregrounds the public-facing arrangement through which that manner is encountered.

Senses.Explanation: An actual gateway together with the entrance space it opens onto. On arriving at Sansheng Monastery, Konggu Daocheng reaches the hall gate, points with his staff, and calls that visible threshold 'this gate and court'; his next verbs are spatial—buddhas enter through it, patriarchs leave through it, and he comes there to reside. The setting, pointing gesture, and motion through the entrance make the architectural referent explicit. The same utterance recruits the structure for a Chan occasion, but its referent remains the physical threshold rather than the institution's public teaching arrangement.

Senses.Explanation: To open one’s mouth is the visible onset of speaking, repeatedly made the exact pressure point of a Chan exchange. In the Guizong case an unnamed monk is struck precisely when he is about to open his mouth; in Xuedou Chongxian’s meeting with Zhimen, the second blow falls at the same instant. Yuanwu stops Kaifu Daoning as soon as he begins, while Dahui threatens a hot iron wheel at the mere move. Other addresses demand that the assembly open its mouths or direct recognition to what precedes opening mouth and raising intention. Foyin’s portrait verse turns an open-mouthed smile into a public question. Zen bends an ordinary bodily transition into the timed boundary where an answer is demanded, interrupted, struck, or forestalled.

SearchAliases: open your mouth and be wrong
Senses.Explanation: “Open your mouth and you are already wrong” is spoken as both self-verdict and interview challenge, commonly paired with losing by silence or missing as soon as the mind frames an answer. Literally, open the mouth and immediately or already be wrong : "open your mouth and you are already wrong." The phrase occurs 43 times in 34 allowlisted texts; the variant "open your mouth and it is then wrong" occurs 13 times in 10. Its early defining exchange has an unnamed questioner ask Dabe to speak apart from removing the upper and taking away the lower. Dabe answers, "when I open my mouth I am already wrong" . The unnamed questioner calls Dabe his guide; Dabe replies, "today I died in the disciple's hands" , so the record shows the verdict catching Dabe’s own utterance. Later masters make it a portable paired formula: Po'an says, "open your mouth and you are already wrong; aim the mind and you immediately miss" . Other records pair it with "move a thought and immediately go against" . Wuzhun states the closed-mouth counterpart, "open your mouth and you are already wrong; close your mouth and you are already lost," then asks how communication is possible apart from opening and not opening . The phrase also becomes an encounter instruction: Baishan tells an unnamed questioner, "open your mouth and you are already wrong; move a thought and immediately go against; leave these two roads and speak quickly!" The unnamed questioner answers, "wrong," and Baishan answers with another stock retort. Chan thus bends an ordinary judgment of erroneous speech into a self-applying verdict, a fixed parallel line, and a demand used while requiring an answer; the records preserve the resulting replies rather than defining silence as the solution.

Senses.Explanation: Chan records use this verb for an awakening event that breaks open in a person and, in direct address, for bringing listeners to that event. Lamp compilers narrate Guling Shenzan, Angulimala, an unnamed monk, and Ashvaghosha as persons who open into awakening after an encounter, words, or a sound. The actors undergo the event; they do not utter its lexical label. Yongming Yanshou stresses that the event admits no intervening instant, Mazu Daoyi uses the verb causatively for opening his listeners into awakening, and Zhongfeng Mingben speaks of a time when it occurs naturally in sustained inquiry. Intransitive and causative syntax retain one core event while changing who undergoes or brings it about.

Senses.Explanation: To disclose or show something, including instruction shown in a public interview. An unnamed monk asks Baizhang Yuansu to disclose the intention of the patriarch’s coming from the west and receives “the mud ox swallows the huge wave”; the named layman He Changbai asks Juelang Daosheng for instruction for the Fushan assembly and receives a verse about clouds and snow. In the Longtan–Tianhuang case, Longtan Chongxin complains that he has long attended without being shown the essentials of mind. Tianhuang Daowu lists raising a hand when tea was brought and lowering his head when greeted, then asks, “Where was I not showing you the essentials of mind?” (那裏不是與你開示心要處). The Blue Cliff Record's compiler narrates that Jingqing Daofu used a responsive dynamic to “show later students” (開示後學); Jingqing is the person described, not the utterer of that clause. The monastery manager Chengyi tells Jifei Ruyi that he has received Jifei’s disclosure (承師開示), treating Jifei’s reply as instruction already given. Request, act, repeated conduct, and received instruction are stages of the same showing, not different lexical referents.

Senses.Explanation: The parent term's Chan use is verbal tangle; this orthographic form sharpens it to talk treated as idle or unnecessary. An early record warns people not to gather and talk idle vine-tangle, adding that the old man may catch and examine them. Two later verses call the whole great treasury of teachings 'idle vine-tangle': one immediately adds that the seventeen hundred cases trip people to death. A separate verse says that a massive volume already carries idle vine-tangle and puns that there is no need to send more 'idle furnishings.' The Zen deviation is the extension of the corpus's vine-language from individual words to gathered discussion, large books, the canon, and the case collection. The texts make those appraisals; this entry does not generalize them to every written record.

Senses.Explanation: The at-ease person of the Way appears chiefly in the compound “one at ease, with learning ended and nothing contrived,” which the records treat as a named condition rather than mere leisure. Literally, "an idle or at-ease person of the Way" . Chan usage bends ordinary idleness into a named epithet, most often in the full line "an at-ease person of the Way who has ended study and does nothing contrived" . Huangbo explains that people of old heard one statement and thereby "ended study" , and so received this name; he contrasts them with people seeking much knowledge and many explanations. Tianru explicitly lists "the great sea of extinction" , "the ground of actual principle" , and this full epithet as different names for "great rest" . The Mirror Record distinguishes accumulating study, ending study, and then passing beyond both, saying that only on reaching the end of study does one first draw near the Way. Other records deploy the shortened term in verse: the whole world is full of people seeking buddha, but an at-ease person of the Way is hard to find . The epithet therefore names a Chan roster type through explicit ending-study and great-rest definitions, not a generic loafer.

Senses.Explanation: An interrogative pronoun: 'who?' or, according to syntax, 'whom?' The records put it to several public uses. It asks the recorded questioner's identity inside the exchange 'what is buddha?' — 'who are you?' / 'so-and-so' / 'do you recognize so-and-so?' (汝是阿誰／某甲／汝識某甲否). It asks lineage in the stock interview formula 'whose song does the identified master sing; to whom does the house style succeed?' (師唱誰家曲，宗風嗣阿誰), agency in 'who can go?' (阿誰去得), authorship in 'who spoke this scripture?' (此經是阿誰說), and the beneficiary of activity in 'for whom are you busy every day?' (每日區區為阿誰). The Chan deviation lies in this concentration inside public identity, lineage, authorship, and accountability questions; the word itself remains the ordinary interrogative and does not name a special inward self.

Senses.Explanation: A monastery steward is the resident officer who handles a monastery’s practical affairs and answers for the institution in ordinary encounters. The role appears beside the named teaching figure and assembly rather than as another name for the abbot. Mazu’s steward asks after his illness; Yaoshan’s steward carries the assembly’s request for instruction. Linji questions a steward returning from selling the monastery’s yellow rice. At Wutai a steward asks whether Huihui bows to another or to himself; in the Pei Xiu case the steward answers for a temple’s wall image, and another temple steward answers an official about its protector image. The Danxia case makes the office’s custodial stake comic and sharp: Danxia burns a wooden buddha, and the steward who objects is said to lose his eyebrows. The Chan bend is the practical office entering famous public cases as the institution’s immediate custodian and interlocutor.

Senses.Explanation: Tao Yuanming is the poet whom these records recognize through wine, chrysanthemums, and his decision to return home. Masters make that literary figure work in public speech: 'if it were Tao Yuanming, he would frown and go home' dismisses a labored formulation, while other addresses pair his return with withdrawal from a crowded or defiled scene. He is therefore a pre-Chan figure as deployed by Chan speakers, not a lineage master and not merely a biographical name.

Senses.Explanation: The expression denotes go along with it in these Chan records. Its wording is "go along with it." In the named Dasui case, the recorded questioner asks whether "this" is destroyed when the world is destroyed by the kalpa fire. Dasui answers, "destroyed." the recorded questioner asks, "then it goes along with it?" and Dasui answers, "go along with it." Later collections repeatedly set this answer beside Longji's contrary "not destroyed" and preserve it as the case's answer-line. Elsewhere the same ordinary phrase can mean following a person or thing; the fixed Chan deployment is its repeated use for Dasui's answer.

Senses.Explanation: Records use this phrase for moving responsively with the occasion, but Feiyin Tongrong turns it into criticism when the historical monastic in Zhaozhou's cypress case drifts with discriminating thought. The image is “follow the waves and ride the swells,” one member of the Yunmen three-phrase frame. In the Blue Cliff Record, Yuanwu Keqin says a phrase can follow the waves when used on the road, meeting a knowing companion and distinguishing what the occasion calls for. His recorded sayings contrast going with the waves, where varied establishments are responsive at every point, with cutting off all streams and barring ordinary and sage. Hongzhi Zhengjue says Yunmen, steady in body and mind, knew how to follow the waves. Tianyin Yuanxiu's verse follows waves and wind in a small boat but turns back rather than remaining midstream. Ruibai Mingxue defines the phrase-function through a shout that answers an affair with the affair and principle with principle. Feiyin Tongrong, by contrast, criticizes a monastic whose discriminating mind follows the waves and misses what is directly present; Shiyu Mingfang similarly says Yunmen “only managed” to follow the waves in a disputed case.

Senses.Explanation: To follow conditions is to proceed in accordance with the circumstances that arise rather than insist on a fixed arrangement. Records apply it to eating, travelling, daily conduct, responding to people and things, and accepting ample or spare provisions. Some passages pair it with unconfined activity or say that responsive change does not lose the thing’s character. These are deployments of one manner of proceeding, not separate senses.
Senses.Note: The frozen corpus has 1,982 exact hits in 332 files representing 328 works. Seven anchors cover daily conduct, travel, provisions, responsive functioning, a biographical maxim, and a direct encounter question across independent works.

Senses.Explanation: “wherever” or “in every place.” Throughout the sampled corpus, its Chan value lies chiefly in the predicates whose scope it sets. Linji's record has the fixed line “act as host wherever you are; every place you stand is genuine” (隨處作主，立處皆真). Yuanwu preserves the paired formula “act as host wherever you are; on meeting conditions, they are the source” (隨處作主，遇緣即宗). A teaching-seat address defines the work of a lineage teacher with “wherever he is, he raises the guiding principle; he answers questions according to the occasion” (隨處提綱，應機問答). Other records use the same distributive word in “named wherever [it appears]” (隨處立名), “arise right here and perish wherever” (當處出生，隨處滅盡), and “clear wherever [you are]” (隨處明了). These predicates are distinct; the location word is not. No departure from its ordinary distributive meaning was found, and none is manufactured.

Senses.PreferredTarget: act as host wherever you are
AlternateTargets: make yourself host in every place
Senses.Explanation: Linji’s direct imperative ‘wherever you are, act as host’ is paired with ‘where you stand is genuine’ and with circumstances being unable to turn the person addressed. Literally, 'wherever the place, act as host.' The expression occurs 136 times in 85 allowed texts. Linji's record gives its best-known continuation twice: 'act as host wherever you are; every place you stand is genuine' (隨處作主，立處皆真). The first occurrence continues, 'circumstances come and cannot turn you around' (境來回換不得); the second says that whatever comes is not to be received. Later records most often pair the phrase with 'on meeting circumstances, it is immediately the source' (遇緣即宗). Yuanwu records variants including 'act as host wherever you are; on meeting circumstances, it is immediately the source' (隨處作主，遇緣即宗) and 'act as host wherever you are; on meeting circumstances, immediately act' (隨處作主，遇緣即行). A later collection reverses the order—'the teaching has no fixed form: on meeting circumstances, it is immediately the source; the Way does not travel in vain: act as host wherever you are' (法無定相，遇緣即宗；道不虗行，隨處作主)—and another places the phrase beside 'establish the source and set up the purport'. The records deploy it as a direct imperative, a quoted Linji saying, and a predicate within assembly addresses.
Senses.Note: The graph 'host/master' (主) is translated as 'host' in the preferred target because Linji's surrounding record repeatedly distinguishes guest and host; 'master' is retained as an alternate graph-literal rendering. The unpunctuated full Linji continuation 'act as host wherever you are; every place you stand is genuine' (隨處作主立處皆真) occurs twice in the Recorded Sayings of the Ancient Worthies. The phrase later circulates across houses with the circumstance/source pairing and is therefore corpus-wide rather than Linji-specific.

Senses.Explanation: Itinerant monks who travel between monasteries and are received, housed, counted, and fed by Chan communities. The compound occurs 789 times in 238 allowlisted texts. Hongzhi Zhengjue directly tells an addressee, 'Cloud-and-water is you; you are cloud-and-water,' immediately after describing a patch-robed monk taking a staff and circling the world. Sanshan Denglai counts cloud-and-water monks in the two halls; Wuzhun Shifan's biography records hundreds of rooms built to receive them; Fushi Tongxian directs visitors to the cloud-and-water hall; and Jie Weizhou recalls their doubled numbers during famine and the provisions used to sustain them. At the end of retreat, Tianyin Yuanxiu describes groups leaving the mountains in threes and twos as cloud-and-water roaming onward. The expanded noun 'cloud-and-water monk' occurs 17 times in 14 texts, while reception and hall constructions show that the shorter compound can name the same people without an explicit word for monk.
Senses.Note: The technical collective can stand without an explicit word for monk, as shown by reception and release-day contexts. No formula equates it with a prescribed activity. The sole exact question asks for the 'meaning of cloud-and-water' and receives a verse-like answer rather than a lexical definition.

Senses.Explanation: The white ox in the open ground. Changqing Da'an describes a water buffalo he tended during thirty years at Guishan, repeatedly pulling it back from crops until it changed into this white ox, plainly present and no longer needing to be driven. Other named speakers keep the animal imagery active: it grows horns, must not eat another's seedlings, bellows when Linji Yixuan asks about it, is cooked for a year-end communal meal, or has nowhere to be placed when snow makes everything one color. Chan thus uses the open-ground white ox as a publicly handled figure of an animal no longer straying or concealed, while interview answers and seasonal talks keep testing whether that description has become another object to possess.

Senses.Explanation: The exposed pillar is addressed, paired with the hearth, made to speak or bear offspring, and repeatedly inserted into public answers. Literally, an exposed or bare pillar : "the exposed pillar." It occurs 2,729 times in 325 allowlisted texts. In Chan halls it is not merely architecture: masters address it, strike it, point questioners to it, and pair it with the lantern. Danxia greets a pillar with joined palms as "World-Honored One"; when an unnamed questioner says, "Master, that is an exposed pillar," Danxia answers with a verse about crying blood to no use. Shitou answers "what is the meaning of coming from the west?" with "ask the exposed pillar" ; when the questioner cannot understand, Shitou says he understands even less. Asked to whom his teaching will be entrusted after his death, a later recorded answer is, "exposed pillar, fire stove" and reverses the pair after the follow-up. The pillar is also made an impossible animate figure: "like an exposed pillar bearing a child" , a phrase found 87 times in . Another verse says oxhide is stretched over the pillar, the pillar cries out, ordinary ears do not hear it, and the sages laugh. The Zen deviation is therefore concrete and institutional: a fixed hall support becomes a named interlocutor, recipient, speaker, and pregnant figure in encounters, commonly partnered with lantern or stove. These are the corpus's recorded actions; the entry adds no symbolic meaning.

Senses.Explanation: The numinous or divining tortoise appears with shell, omens, diagram, book, and a tail that leaves traces. The most frequent Chan family is “the numinous tortoise drags its tail” (靈龜曳尾). The corpus explains the material action: on the ground it wipes its track, but the track arises again (拂迹迹生, “it brushes away the trace and the trace appears”). The Blue Cliff Record says that even someone with flashing responsiveness cannot avoid the tortoise dragging its tail. A later comment applies the same action to the Buddha holding up the flower and says traces are hard to remove. Asked for the Five Ranks, Boshan Suru Han answers that the numinous tortoise has no omen-lines and its empty shell need not be drilled. Other addresses have the tortoise enter the sea and swallow the moon, or pair the river-horse carrying a diagram with the tortoise bearing a book. The Zen-specific bend is the repeated use of this divining animal's tail, track, shell, omen, diagram, and burden as public comment, answer, and teaching-seat image; the entry does not convert those actions into a single abstract lesson.

Senses.Explanation: Green bamboo is presented in the records as immediately displaying or being the body, and that claim is then publicly challenged; the phrase is therefore a tested claim rather than scenery. Literally “verdant green bamboo.” In the Chan corpus these four ordinary landscape words are overwhelmingly the first half of a disputed stock proposition: “verdant green bamboo is entirely the true-as-is” or “entirely the body of reality,” paired with “luxuriant yellow flowers are none other than complete discernment” (青青翠竹，盡是真如／法身；鬱鬱黃花，無非般若). The proposition is not a settled glossary equation. The Ancestral Hall Collection explicitly records that some call it a wrong saying while others accept it; elsewhere in the same text one named record subject answers “it does not pervade form”, and Dazhu Huihai rejects identifying the bamboo itself with the body of reality. Dahui preserves both sides and describes Nanyang Huizhong as maintaining “verdant green bamboo is entirely the body of reality” while Dazhu breaks it as “verdant green bamboo is not the body of reality” (國師主張青青翠竹盡是法身；大珠破青青翠竹不是法身). The phrase also enters interviews: asked “verdant green bamboo is entirely the true-as-is; what is the true-as-is?”, a named record subject answers, “a guest who turns tile into gold—one hears the name but does not see the form” (點瓦成金客，聞名不見形); asked for “the wish-granting pearl that follows color,” another answers “verdant green bamboo, luxuriant yellow flowers” (青青翠竹，鬱鬱黃花). Thus Zen bends a landscape phrase into a repeatedly quoted proposition, dispute, and question-answer case; the record itself refuses one uncontested equation.
Senses.Note: #0g deviation: this is not merely bamboo scenery. It functions as the fixed opening of a proposition repeatedly affirmed, denied, questioned, and commented on by Chan teachers. The paired phrase “luxuriant yellow flowers” (鬱鬱黃花) has 57 hits in 41 texts. Exact “verdant green bamboo is entirely the body of reality” (青青翠竹盡是法身) has 18 hits in 14 texts. Headword count: 116 hits in 68 texts. “True-as-is” and “body of reality” translate the two attested predicates without adding a definition beyond these recorded predicates.

SearchAliases: not the mind not the Buddha
Senses.Explanation: Not mind, not buddha: a recorded saying, answer, question, and the second member of the sequence beginning with 'this mind is this buddha' (即心即佛). The exact negative wording is (非心非佛). In the Mazu exchange, an unnamed monk asks why Mazu says 'this mind is this buddha'; Mazu Daoyi answers, 'to stop a small child crying' (為止小兒啼). Asked, 'What about when the crying stops?' (啼止時如何), he replies, 'not mind, not buddha' (非心非佛). Funiu Zizai explicitly classifies the pair: 'This mind is this buddha is a sentence seeking medicine where there is no illness; not mind, not buddha is a sentence countering medicine and illness' (即心即佛是無病求藥句，非心非佛是藥病對治句). Other records set it beside a longer 'not mind, not buddha, not a thing' expression, ask 'What is not mind, not buddha?' (如何是非心非佛), or treat it as a question answered with another recorded saying—Heshan Wuyin answers, 'Heshan knows how to beat the drum' (禾山解打鼓). Damei Fachang's case preserves an explicit contrast: told that Mazu now says 'not mind, not buddha,' Damei answers that he still keeps 'this mind is this buddha.' Zen bends a bare double negation into a mobile public-interview saying whose recorded force depends on its speaker, sequence, and answer rather than an imported abstract definition. Yuanwu Keqin tells the assembly to set ‘not mind, not buddha’ to one side; Songyuan Chongyue raises Mazu's paired sayings and asks whether they are false or real. These are stances toward the same quoted phrase, not new senses.
Senses.Note: The exact phrase occurs 837 times in 233 allowlisted storage files; the direct 'what is not mind, not buddha?' question occurs 55 times in 41. Two rare definition-form searches produced grammatical constructions but no fuller definition than Funiu Zizai's classification; exact search strings remain in WORK rather than appearing as unattested prose quotations. Paired and expanded forms remain related recorded expressions, not interchangeable formulas. The term is corpus-wide even though its best-known early occurrence belongs to Mazu's exchange.

Senses.Explanation: Facing the wall is recorded as a bodily action associated with Bodhidharma and Luzhu, and is repeatedly raised as an interview case rather than an imported exercise. Literally, to face a wall. The expression occurs 1,857 times in 308 allowlisted texts, and the Chan record makes it a named action rather than a general description of where someone sits. Bodhidharma's biography says that he sat facing the wall at Shaolin, remained silent throughout the day, and was called the wall-gazing brahman; the nine-year formula occurs 435 times in . The action is not confined to Bodhidharma: the records say that Luzu faced the wall whenever a visitor came, and later masters repeatedly ask why he did so. A verse on Luzu calls it the most effortless complete command, but immediately says that one who knows mind does not depend on a raised eyebrow to recognize another. Other masters criticize the inherited scenes: one calls Bodhidharma's nine years facing the wall a source of ghosts, while a verse collection preserves both praise and mockery around the same act. The corpus therefore records facing the wall as an action of masters, a recurring public-interview question, and an object of later criticism; it does not supply a single explanatory gloss for the act.

Senses.Explanation: The face or face-front: a bodily front imagined as a gate or opening. The graphs join 'face' (面) to 'gate or opening' (門), and the compound has 1,040 occurrences in 287 allowlisted texts. Its physical reference is explicit when Baozhi uses a finger to split open his face (以指𠢐面門) and when a fire-mass is said to scorch the face of anyone who comes near (近著即燎却面門). The record also uses verbs of impact with it: ‘press through the face’ (拶破面門) has 38 occurrences in 30 texts, while ‘scorch the face’ (燎却面門) has 53 in 34. In the repeatedly quoted Linji case, ‘the true person of no rank’ (無位真人) is said to be constantly entering and leaving through the faces of the people present (常在汝等諸人面門出入); ‘entering and leaving through the face’ (面門出入) occurs 223 times in 141 texts. Yuanwu also records ‘a dynamic at the face’ (面門一機) in a small address and tells his interlocutor that he remains unaware even when it has ‘pressed through his face’ (拶破面門). These are the attested bodily, spatial, and case-specific uses; the texts do not supply a separate abstract definition for the compound.
Senses.Note: The apparent definition-form hit for ‘face + one who’ (面門者) is not a definition: it occurs inside ‘how many people have split open the face?’ (󳮢破面門者幾人), where the final graph marks the person performing the verb. The inventory likewise found ‘the so-called face, nostrils, ears, eyes, heels, and brains’ (所謂面門、鼻孔、耳朵、眼睛、腳跟、頭腦), an enumeration rather than a gloss. The Linji occurrence is a raised case under Vinaya Master Bensong's section of the Five Lamps Compendium; Linji Yixuan remains the exact quoted utterer and Bensong the later raiser.

Senses.Explanation: The phrase pictures an extra eye at the crown of the head; speakers require, open, test, or attribute this eye in public encounters. The records use it with the verbs possess, open, look, illuminate, and strike blind, and with the adjective correct. Lushan Fazhen says that to understand the upward matter one must possess the crown-gate eye; possessing it accords with the heart of leaving home, and he then asks, “do you want to understand the crown-gate eye?” before saying that people in the four capitals put on clothes and eat while people in the two Zhejiang circuits are full and warm (欲明向上事，須具頂門眼；要會頂門眼麼？四京人著衣喫飯，兩浙人飽暖自如). Yuanwu invites “those who possess the crown-gate eye” to raise Xuansha's case (具頂門眼者，請試舉看), and says in verse that when the crown-gate eye is correct it has complete efficacy (頂門眼正有全功). Dahui says a flash of lightning opens the crown-gate eye (激電爍開頂門眼). In a direct exchange, the cited participant says the furnace has opened it; Chaozong Tongren asks what it is, the cited participant bows, and Chaozong Tongren strikes him and says, “it has been knocked blind” (擉瞎了也). A transmission record appraises Zhaozhou as possessing it while distinguishing black and white in a stone-struck spark (趙州具頂門眼，向擊石火裏分緇素). The term occurs 276 times in 123 allowlisted files. Jifei Ruyi directly turns the image back into a public question, asking, “What is the eye at the crown?” This questioning use concerns the same eye-image, not another object.

Senses.Explanation: Sumeru is the named cosmic mountain used as a vast landmark, comparison, carried burden, or direct answer. Chan records keep the mountain visible while making it stand in exchanges beside mustard seeds, oceans, nostrils, and the act of walking around it. The full "Mount Sumeru" (須彌山) occurs 1,052 times and the variant transliteration "Sumeru-lu" (須彌盧) 147. Chan records use the mountain's name in questions, comparisons, and statements of size or destruction. One Compendium saying places together "break Sumeru into fine dust" and "take the waters of the four great seas into one hair-pore" (破須彌為微塵，攝四大海水入一毛孔). A Continued Lamp address says, "if the lineage purport is raised, Sumeru must directly be shattered" (舉揚宗旨，須彌直須粉碎). A Dahui lamp witness says, "pick up Sumeru-lu in the palm and swing inside a needle's eye" (拈須彌盧於掌上，向針眼裡打鞦韆). Gulin Qingmao also supplies a local self-definition: "the so-called Mount Sumeru is precisely the move before living beings and buddhas were established" (所謂須彌山者，即是生佛未具已前一著子也). Public exchanges and addresses place a seamless stupa and an unstruck bell on Sumeru's summit, tie Sumeru with a lotus-root filament, and test the claim that a mustard seed contains it. These are the records' stated deployments; Gulin's equation does not replace the proper name throughout the corpus.

Senses.Explanation: The term names a verse composed on an old case, the genre formed by such verses, and the act of composing them. Guan Youwudang calls Xuedou Chongxian's hundred verses essential study material and names Yuanwu Keqin's appraisal of Xuedou's old-case verses. Puhui places verses on old cases beside picking up old cases as distinct literary activities. Lingshu Sengyuan says one hundred such verses formed a book. Dahui Zonggao describes participants presenting interpretations and composing old-case verses. Biographical narratives say Zhengdang Mingbian composed one hundred in retirement and Dahui composed one hundred and ten while living at Yunmen Hermitage. Count, title, compilation, and composition grammar all point to the same literary product and activity; noun and verb frames do not require separate senses.

Senses.Explanation: The records reject “stubborn emptiness” as an insensible blankness mistaken for oneself, and contrast it with concrete things and lively response. Literally “stubborn” or “insensible emptiness.” In Chan records the phrase is predominantly a rejected identification, not a praised condition. Caoshan's house verse commands, “students must first recognize their own house; do not mix the true boundary with stubborn emptiness” . Hongzhi likewise warns, “do not recognize stubborn emptiness as oneself” . A staff discourse makes the deployment concrete: the ordinary person calls the staff a staff, while the listener who “recognizes a stubborn emptiness” denies that there is a staff . A later address describes keeping stubborn emptiness at an idle corner, “entirely without openings,” and clinging to being a wooden puppet or a wall . A verse draws its own contrast: “do not dwell in stubborn emptiness; do not hide in dead water; directly you must be lively and splashing, like the sun shining at midday” . The recurring verbs are recognize, mix with, fall into, cling to, dwell in, and mistake for oneself; the recurrent contrasts are the true boundary, liveliness, things that appear, and the staff that is denied.

Senses.Explanation: The phrase denotes awakening characterized as sudden rather than staged gradually. Huineng says one's own nature awakens itself, with sudden awakening and sudden refinement and no gradual sequence. An unnamed monk contrasts sudden awakening of principle with gradual removal of affairs and asks Sanzu Chonghui for its principle. A case narrative describes Bao'en Xuance awakening suddenly at the fire-boy answer. Guxue Zhe likewise contrasts principle, which must be awakened to suddenly, with affairs removed gradually. Yongming Yanshou places sudden awakening in a fourfold matrix with gradual awakening and sudden or gradual refinement. Guifeng Zongmi defines turning from ordinary person to sage as sudden awakening. Yulin Tongxiu asks whether an addressee has the capacity for sudden awakening and sudden refinement. These uses distinguish sudden awakening from later refinement without forcing every record into one historical classification.
Senses.Note: Seven exact lexical witnesses across six distinct works cover self-awakening, encounter narration, sudden/gradual contrast, a fourfold matrix, direct definition, and capacity test. The longer Treatise on the Essential Gate of Entering the Way through Sudden Awakening title was excluded under the substring gate and buys no bare-headword depth.

Senses.Explanation: A paired contrast, literally 'sudden and gradual.' The term occurs 275 times in 104 allowed texts. The Platform Record reports that people spoke of Southern Huineng and Northern Shenxiu and therefore made a Southern/Northern division of sudden and gradual. Huineng's recorded correction is explicit: 'The teaching is originally one lineage; people are northern and southern. The teaching is one kind; seeing has slowness and speed. What is called sudden and gradual? The teaching has no sudden and gradual; people are sharp and dull, and therefore it is called sudden and gradual' (法本一宗，人有南北。法即一種，見有遲疾。何名頓漸？法無頓漸，人有利鈍，故名頓漸). Another recension puts it as 'seeing slowly is gradual, seeing quickly is sudden' (‘seeing slowly is gradual; seeing quickly is sudden’), again followed by 'the teaching has no gradual and sudden'. Later texts likewise say that sudden and gradual have no difference (頓漸無殊), or that whichever order is stated—'gradually refining, suddenly understanding' (漸修頓悟) or 'suddenly understanding, gradually refining' (頓悟漸修)—one must finally arrive personally once. The Record of the Source-Mirror enumerates four textual combinations: gradually refining and suddenly understanding, suddenly understanding and gradually refining, gradually refining and gradually understanding, and suddenly understanding and suddenly refining. That list records combinations of words; it does not override the Platform Record's direct correction or establish a hierarchy. The corpus contains five occurrences of 'the teaching has no sudden and gradual' (法無頓漸).
Senses.Note: The Platform Record locates slowness and speed in seeing and sharpness and dullness in people; later texts record the sudden/gradual combinations. In those cited combinations, 'refining' (修) translates the recorded graph literally.

Senses.PreferredTarget: put another head atop one's head
AlternateTargets: add a head on top of the head
set a head upon one's head
Senses.Explanation: Putting another head atop one's head is an image of needless addition to what is already complete. Chan records apply it when an interlocutor adds a name, assertion, attainment, or operation, and directly compare it with drawing feet on a snake, adding frost to snow, and fastening a shackle onto a cangue. Linji Yixuan follows it with the question, "what do you lack?" (是儞欠少甚麼). Baohua Xian pairs "you have finished eating gruel—putting another head atop your head" (喫粥了也，頭上安頭) with "go wash your bowl—drawing feet on a snake" (洗鉢盂去，為虵畫足). Yun'an Zhenjing separately calls his own added words "drawing feet on a snake". Other explicit parallels are Jingyin Facheng's "add frost atop snow" (霜加雪上) and Ruiyan Zihong's "put a shackle on a cangue" (枷上著杻). These corpus comparisons establish unnecessary addition without importing an external theory.
Senses.Note: The phrase is productive in binary naming tests: calling an object a staff may be "putting another head atop one's head," while denying it is a staff may be "cutting off the head to seek life" (斬頭覓活). Saying "mind itself is Buddha" (即心是佛) is likewise compared to putting another head atop one's head, while saying "neither mind nor Buddha" (非心非佛) is compared to losing the head and recognizing its shadow (迷頭認影). One community address explicitly lists "do not put another head atop your head" (不得頭上安頭) as the fourth of four ailments, after seeking another's spittle along the road, driving a stake while rocking an oar, and cutting off the head to seek life. The term names none of those other expressions; their value here is the corpus's own contrast set.

Senses.Explanation: To look around is to turn and look at a person, direction, or assembly. The verb retains that visual sense in Emperor Suzong's complaint that Nanyang Huizhong does not look at him and in an unnamed monk's looking east and west for the absent Changqing Da'an. Chan records also make it a recurrent teaching-seat stage direction. At an opening of the hall Xuedou Chongxian “looked around at the assembly” (顧視大眾) before speaking; Yungai Zhiyong follows the look with a shout and questions concerning host and guest. In one encounter Mazu Daoyi merely looks, Yangshan Huiji comments on the look, and the exchange ends. Ciji Cong compresses speech and action still further: “then he looked around at the assembly and said, ‘stop!’” (乃顧視大眾曰休). Yulin Tongxiu looks left and right, strikes the staff, and leaves the seat (顧視左右，卓拄杖，下座). Thus an ordinary look is bent into an observable public-address action of the teaching seat; the entry does not assign the look an unspoken symbolic message.

Senses.Explanation: The expression names Yunmen’s sequence: he looks toward the interlocutor, says “Look!”, and cuts off the attempted answer with “Hah!” Yunmen’s own record describes the interaction: he sometimes looked toward the recorded questioner and said “Look!”; when the questioner prepared to answer, Yunmen said “Hah!” The monasteries consequently named Yunmen by this look-and-two-utterance sequence. A collected transmission states the same sequence and adds that Deshan Yuanming later removed the initial look and called the shortened form “drawn look.” Later texts use the compact phrase as a named case, ask how it operates at face-to-face meeting, and place it alongside Yunmen’s other characteristic responses. The punctuation and speaker sequence matter: this is a recorded look and two utterances, not an abstract three-word maxim.
